=== p13 ===
Domain
Any dataset is said to come from a particular data domain, or a type of data.
Properties that deﬁne domains (How do these domains’ distributions diﬀer?):
● Language (English, Mandarin, Telugu, …)
● Genre (news articles, podcast transcripts, Reddit posts, novels, …)
● Dialect (British English, American English, Indian English, …)
● Register (formal writing, casual speech, text messages, …)
● Knowledge area (medicine, basketball, linguistics, DJing, …)
13
=== p14 ===
Discussion: Ground Truth
A data domain is deﬁned by a text distribution. This is the ground truth distribution.
Any corpus of text is a sample from its domain’s distribution (possibly a combination 
of easily nameable domains).
A language model PLM(W=w) is an approximation (or estimate) of the ground truth 
distribution.
How does the LM learn about the ground truth distribution?
What does the ground truth look like?
Can we ever access the ground truth?
14
=== p15 ===
Discussion
What does knowing the distribution of text in a language have to do with 
language understanding?
What advantages/disadvantages does the distributional view of 
language?
E.g., ﬂuency, hallucination, bias, etc.
Nice discussion: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.13638

Review: Autoregressive Language Model
A language model is a distribution over strings of a language.
An autoregressive factorization of a language model uses the chain rule to break up the 
joint probability PLM(w) into a product of conditional distributions PLM(wi|w<i), 
where each words probability is conditioned on its entire preﬁx (all the previous words).

Bigram language models instead give us conditional distributions where each word’s

The Markov Assumption
A Markov process is a stochastic process (a sequence sampled from a distribution) 
where the next event depends only on the current state.
The LM P(W) is a stochastic process. If we assume that it is a Markov process (i.e., 
we make the Markov assumption), then a bigram factorization is justiﬁed.

1. The keys to the cabinet are on the table.
2. The keys to the cabinet is on the table.
Which is greater, PLM(1) or PLM(2)?
Which PLM(are|The keys to the cabinet) or PLM(is|The keys to the cabinet)?

examples would pose a

call me IshmaelSOS EOS

=== p12 ===
We use a training corpus to estimate the conditional distributions for an n-gram model.
Count-based Estimating n-gram models
Bigram estimation:
 where #(w) is the number of times w 
occurs in the training corpus.
What is the general form of count-based estimation for an n-gram model?
Aside: Types vs. Tokens
A word type is a vocabulary entry. If a corpus has 10k types, it means you need 10k 
dictionary entries to deﬁne every word.
A word token is an instance of a word. When you are asked to write a 10k word essay, you 
count tokens. I.e., instances of the same word type are counted multiple times.
12
=== p13 ===
Exercise
Consider the following training corpus:
I am Sam EOS 
Sam I am EOS 
I do not like green eggs and ham EOS 
Estimate these bigram probabilities:
P(I | ε) P(Sam | ε) P(am | I)
P(EOS | Sam) P(Sam | am) P(do | I)
Estimate the unigram probabilities for I, Sam, EOS, eggs, like. 13
=== p14 ===
Why were n-gram models used?
Using count-based estimation for arbitrarily long contexts doesn’t work:
Making a simplifying assumption (the Markov assumption, or generalized Markov assumption) 
makes count-based estimation tractable in terms of memory.

=== p15 ===
On choosing n
The quality of text generation from an n-gram model generally improves for larger n.

=== p16 ===
Sparsity
…but the problem of data sparsity grows 
with the size of n. If the size of the 
vocabulary V is 10^4 (much smaller than 
the vocabulary of English), the number of 
possible 4-grams is 10^16!
The memory demands also grow roughly exponentially.
A partial solution is to choose a ﬁxed |V|, select the most 
frequent |V| words, and replace all other words with <UNK>.

=== p17 ===
Smoothing
Laplace smoothing (add-one smoothing) adds 1 to each count:
Intuition: we remove some 
probability mass from the 
observed n-grams, and 
distribute it evenly over 
unobserved n-grams.

=== p18 ===
Backoff
If we haven’t observed a particular n-gram, we can backoﬀ to the n-1 gram.
Note: This does not give a valid probability distribution.

The human “interrogator” has two 
conversations with “witnesses” – one human 
and one machine. Each witness tries to 
convince the interrogator that they are a real 
human. The interrogator (knowing that only 
one is human) must guess which is the real 
human. If they cannot do so reliably, the 
machine passes the Turing test: It is 
practically indistinguishable from a human.

Chinese Room Argument (Searle, 1980)
The subject, understanding no Chinese,

Chinese characters are delivered to the 
room, and the subject can follow the 
instructions, which tell them how to 
select new Chinese characters to send 
out of the room. By following the 
instructions, they can always produce 
appropriate responses to the input, 
convincing observers that the person in 
the room understands Chinese when 
they, in fact, do not.

=== p3 ===
Formal Languages, Definitions
● An alphabet Σ is a ﬁnite set of symbols, e.g., {a, b, c}
○ Capital Greek letters to denote alphabets
○ Lowercase Roman letters denote symbols
● Σ* is the set of strings over Σ, e.g., {ε, a, b, c, aa, ab, ac, ba, bb, bc, ca, cb, cc, aaa, …}
○ Σ* is called the Kleene closure of Σ.
○ Bold lowercase Roman letters denote strings in Σ*, e.g., y
● A language L is a subset of Σ*
● A subsequence of a string y is a sequence obtained by deleting symbols of y preserving the order.
○ A substring of y is a contiguous subsequence. 
■ yi:j denotes a substring of y ranging from ith symbol of y to the jth symbol, inclusive.
○ A preﬁx of y is a substring sharing the same ﬁrst symbol of y. 
■ y<i denotes the preﬁx of y ending before the ith symbol.
○ A suﬃx of y is a substring sharing the same last symbol of y. 
■ y>i denotes the suﬃx of y starting after ith symbol.

● An autoregressive LM factors this distribution using the chain rule:
PLM(W=w) = PLM(EOS | w) *          PLM(wi | w< i )

=== p8 ===
The EOS Symbol
The EOS symbol is necessary to ensure that PLM is a valid probability distribution. 
Why?
All probabilities of disjoint events must sum to 1. 
PLM(w) = PLM(EOS | w) *          PLM(wi | w< i )
In the previous example, a sequence and its preﬁxes are not disjoint events! Hence 
their probabilities don’t sum to 1. P(the | ε) = 0.2
P(cat | the) = 0.003
P(sat | the cat) = 0.01
P(on | the cat sat) = 0.4 
…
By stipulating that every string ends in EOS, 
and EOS occurs nowhere else, we create a set 
of disjoint events.

We often work with log probabilities when using LMs. Why?
P(the cat sat on the mat) = 0.00000000504
log(P(the cat sat on the mat)) = -19.1
An appealing alternative is surprisal:
SLM(w) = -log PLM(w)
Intuition: Low probability events are more surprising.
Surprisal is a measure of information (e.g., in bits).

Perplexity (PPL) measures how well a LM predicts the text of a corpus w:
PPLtotal(w) = PLM(w)-1

Intuition: PPL captures the expected number of times you would need to sample 
from PLM(W) in order to observe the test corpus w.
More typically, we measure PPL per word:
PPLword(w) = PLM(w)-1/|w|

## 1. Intro: what does it mean to "understand" language? (Session 1)

**Thought experiments:**
- **Turing Test (Turing):** an interrogator talks to a human and a machine and must guess which one is human. If they can't tell reliably, the machine passes. Jones & Bergen (2025) found that LMs pass.
- **Chinese Room (Searle, 1980):** a person follows rules to produce correct Chinese replies without understanding Chinese. The point is that manipulating symbols isn't understanding.
- **Octopus Test (Bender & Koller, 2020):** an octopus learns the statistics of English by listening in on telegraph messages. It fails when an islander asks for help fighting a bear. The point is that form alone gives you no grounding or reference.
- **Three parts of understanding:** form, reference, function.
- **Formal vs. functional competence (Mahowald et al., 2024):**
  - Formal competence is knowing that *"Colorless green ideas sleep furiously"* is grammatical.
  - Functional competence is knowing that it's nonsensical.

**History:**
- **Symbolic approach:** Chomsky's Generative Grammar. Chomsky (1957) argued that "grammatical" can't be the same as "high statistical approximation." His reason was that both (1) *Colorless green ideas…* and (2) *Furiously sleep ideas…* have probability around 0, yet only (1) is grammatical.
- **Rule-based NLU:** ELIZA (Weizenbaum, 1967) and grammar engineering such as HPSG (Pollard & Sag, 1994). These needed explicit, complete hand-written rules and huge manual effort.
- **Disillusionment:** Hutchins (1979) said machine translation was "led astray" by formal linguistics. Jelinek said, "Every time I fire a linguist, the performance of the speech recognizer goes up." Statistical, corpus-based methods took over in the 1980s–90s.
- **Connectionism:**
  - Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958).
  - Rumelhart, who was at UCSD and helped invent backpropagation.
  - The **past tense debate:** Rumelhart & McClelland (1986) against Pinker & Prince (1988). Berko's wug test (1958) is related.
- **Distributional Hypothesis:** "You shall know a word by the company it keeps" (Firth, 1957; also Harris, 1954). This led to LSA (Deerwester, 1990) and then word2vec (Mikolov, 2013).
- **Three eras of NLU:**
  1. Early 2010s: a separate network trained for each task.
  2. Late 2010s: **pretrain** on language modeling, then **fine-tune** a foundation model.
  3. 2020s: scale up and **prompt**. One set of weights handles nearly every task.
- **"Deep learning"** means neural networks with many layers trained on data.

---

## 2. Definition of a language model (Session 2)

**Formal language terms:**
- An **alphabet** Σ is a finite set of symbols.
- **Σ\*** (the **Kleene closure**) is the set of all *finite* strings over Σ, including the empty string ε. It is infinite.
- A **language** L ⊆ Σ\*.
- A **subsequence** comes from deleting symbols while keeping their order. A **substring** is a contiguous subsequence. y_{i:j} runs from position i to position j, inclusive.
- A **prefix** y_{<i} = y_{1:i−1}. A **suffix** y_{>i} = y_{i+1:|y|}.
- Mini-quiz answer: the Kleene closure of {0,…,9} is every finite string of digits, including ε and strings with leading zeros.

**LM definition:** a language model is a **probability distribution P_LM over Σ\***.

**Autoregressive factorization (chain rule):**

  P(w) = P(EOS | w) · ∏ᵢ P(wᵢ | w_{<i})

- Why factor it this way? The model's parameters give you **conditional next-word distributions**, not the joint probability directly. The chain rule is exact, so this loses nothing. You could also factor in another order, such as right-to-left.
- Why you need **EOS:** a string and its prefixes are not disjoint events, so without EOS the probabilities don't sum to 1. Every string must end in EOS, and EOS can appear nowhere else. That makes the strings disjoint and the distribution valid.

**Worked example:** P(the cat sat on the mat) = 0.2 × 0.003 × 0.01 × 0.4 × 0.5 × 0.06 × 0.07 = 5.04×10⁻⁹.

**Log probabilities:**
- They prevent numerical underflow and turn products into sums. log P = −19.1 in the example above.
- **Surprisal** S(w) = −log P(w). Low-probability events are more surprising. Surprisal measures information, in bits if you use log base 2.

**Perplexity:**
- PPL(w) = P(w)⁻¹ and PPL_word = P(w)^(−1/|w|). **Lower is better.**
- Intuition: roughly how many samples you'd need to draw from the model to see the test corpus. It also works as an effective "branching factor."
- Example: PPL_total = 1/5.04e-9 ≈ 198,412,698. PPL_word (with |w| = 7, counting EOS) ≈ **15.3**.

**What a string's probability reflects (GPT-2 surprisal examples):** typicality, semantic plausibility, grammaticality, word frequency, and **length** (longer strings get lower probability). So raw probability ≠ grammaticality. To isolate one property, compare minimal pairs that are matched on everything else.

**Domain and ground truth:**
- A domain is defined by its text distribution (language, genre, dialect, register, knowledge area). That distribution is the **ground truth**.
- A corpus is a *sample* from it. An LM is an *estimate* of the ground truth, which you can never observe directly.
- Discussion points on the distributional view: it explains fluency, but also hallucination and bias.

---

## 3. n-gram models (Session 3)

**Bigram model:** P(w) ≈ ∏ P(wᵢ | wᵢ₋₁), with SOS and EOS added.
- This equals the true joint probability **only under the Markov assumption**: the next event depends only on the current state. In general it's an *approximation*.

**n-gram model:** condition on the previous **n−1** words.
- Unigram: n = 1, no context.
- Bigram: n = 2. Trigram: n = 3.

**Long-distance agreement breaks bigrams:**
- Example: *"The keys to the cabinet **are/is**…"*. A real LM should prefer P(are | the keys to the cabinet). A bigram model only sees P(· | cabinet), so it prefers "is."
- Other failure cases: long-distance dependencies, filler–gap dependencies, coreference.

**Count-based (maximum likelihood) estimation:**

  P(wᵢ | w_{i−n+1:i−1}) = C(w_{i−n+1:i}) / C(w_{i−n+1:i−1})

**Types vs. tokens:** a **type** is a vocabulary entry. A **token** is one occurrence of a word.

**Exercise answers.** Corpus: *I am Sam EOS / Sam I am EOS / I do not like green eggs and ham EOS*

| Bigram | Answer | Unigram (17 tokens incl. EOS) | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| P(I \| ε) | 2/3 | P(I) | 3/17 |
| P(Sam \| ε) | 1/3 | P(Sam) | 2/17 |
| P(am \| I) | 2/3 | P(EOS) | 3/17 |
| P(EOS \| Sam) | 1/2 | P(eggs) | 1/17 |
| P(Sam \| am) | 1/2 | P(like) | 1/17 |
| P(do \| I) | 1/3 | | |

(If your professor leaves EOS out of the unigram denominator, use 14 instead of 17.)

**Why use n-grams at all?** Counting over arbitrarily long contexts is impossible, because almost every long prefix is unseen and memory explodes. The Markov assumption makes counting tractable.

**Choosing n:**
- A larger n generates better text, but **sparsity** gets much worse. With |V| = 10⁴, there are 10¹⁶ possible 4-grams, and memory grows roughly exponentially.
- A partial fix: keep the top-|V| words and map everything else to **`<UNK>`**.

**Laplace (add-one) smoothing:** P = (C(wᵢ₋₁wᵢ) + 1) / (C(wᵢ₋₁) + |V|). It takes probability mass from seen n-grams and spreads it evenly over unseen ones.

**Backoff:**
- If an n-gram was never seen, use the (n−1)-gram, multiplied by λ (stupid backoff).
- 0 < λ < 1 because the shorter context is less informative, so you discount it.
- **Backoff does not give a valid probability distribution.**

**Neural LMs** allow unlimited context. That's where the course goes next.

---

## 4. Linear and logistic regression, gradient descent (Session 4)

**Linear regression:**
- ŷ = b + Σ wⱼxⱼ = **w·x + b**. It predicts an unbounded continuous value.
- Objective: minimize the **squared error** Σ(ŷ − y)².
- House-price example: Model 2 gives 665k, 2.695M and 1.099M. Its squared error is about 1.0×10¹¹, against about 3.1×10¹¹ for Model 1, so **Model 2 is better.**

**Logistic regression (binary):**
- ŷ = **σ(w·x + b)**, where σ(z) = 1/(1 + e⁻ᶻ) maps (−∞, ∞) to (0, 1).
- z is the **logit**, because σ is the inverse of the log-odds function.

**Spam example:**
- Model 1 gives z = 11.8, 4.2, 3.5, so σ ≈ 1.0, 0.985, 0.97. That's wrong on x⁽³⁾, which is not spam.
- Model 2 gives z = 6.4, 3.9, 0.9, so σ ≈ 0.998, 0.98, 0.71. That's closer on x⁽³⁾.

**Multinomial logistic regression (k classes):**
- ŷ = **softmax(Wx + b)**, where softmax(z)ᵢ = e^{zᵢ} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ}.
- W is k × n, and **each row is one class's weight vector.**

**Loss:**
- Use the **negative log-likelihood** of the true class: L = −log ŷ_{true}.
- This equals the **cross-entropy** L = −Σₖ yₖ log ŷₖ when y is one-hot.

**Gradient descent:**
- Update rule: θ ← θ − η ∇_θ L, where η is the **learning rate**.
- Move *against* the slope. A positive slope means w goes down. Where the slope is 0, you're at a minimum.
- The **gradient** is the vector of partial derivatives and points in the direction of steepest ascent.
- For multinomial regression, the full gradient is a matrix with the same shape as [W | b].

**Logistic regression's gradient (memorize):**
- Binary: ∂L/∂wⱼ = **(σ(w·x + b) − y) · xⱼ**.
- Multinomial: ∂L/∂w_{k,j} = (ŷₖ − yₖ) xⱼ.
- Intuition: a bigger error, or a bigger feature value, means a bigger step.
- The logistic regression loss is **convex** (one minimum). Neural network losses are not.

**Batch types:**
- **Batch** gradient descent uses the whole dataset for each step, which is expensive.
- **SGD** uses one sample per step.
- **Minibatch** uses a small sample per step. It's more stable than SGD and cheaper than full batch.

---

## 5. MLPs and word embeddings (Session 5)

**Neural unit:** z = w·x + b, then the **activation** a = f(z). It works like logistic regression with any nonlinearity f.

**Activation functions:**

| | Sigmoid | tanh | ReLU |
|---|---|---|---|
| Range | (0, 1) | (−1, 1) | [0, ∞) |
| Zero-centered | No | Yes | No |
| Saturates | Both ends | Both ends | x ≤ 0 |
| Vanishing gradient | Severe | Moderate | Minimal |
| Sparse | No | No | Yes |
| Speed | Slow | Moderate | Fast |

**Fully connected layer:**
- **h = f(Wx + b)**. Output node i is f(wᵢᵀx), the i-th row of W times x.
- Worked example with a step function: W = [[.5, 1], [−1, −1], [1.5, 2]] and x = (2, −1) give ŷ = (0, 0, 1).

**Dimensions:**
- A layer that maps nᵢ inputs to nᵢ₊₁ outputs has a W of size **nᵢ₊₁ × nᵢ**.
- Its parameter count is nᵢ₊₁·nᵢ + nᵢ₊₁ (weights plus biases).

**Why use multiple layers?**
- A single perceptron can learn **AND** and **OR**, but **not XOR**, because XOR is not linearly separable.
- An MLP with one hidden layer can learn XOR.

**Why nonlinearity?**
- Without it, linear maps compose: U(Wx) = (UW)x = Vx. Any number of stacked linear layers collapses to one.
- U·f(Wx) does not collapse.

**Feedforward network:** at least one hidden layer. The output layer is just multinomial logistic regression (softmax).

**Backpropagation:**
- Draw the computation graph, then apply the **chain rule** backward from the loss.
- With softmax and cross-entropy, ∂L/∂z_out = **ŷ − y**. Then ∂L/∂W_out = (ŷ − y)hᵀ, and you multiply through Wᵀ and f′ for each earlier layer.

**Embeddings:**
- The output of every layer is an embedding. The set of embeddings a layer produces is an **embedding space**.
- Words can be vectors of features: noun, animate, "has a tail," co-occurs with "cat," and so on.
- **Feature engineering** (hand-crafted): interpretable and controllable, but labor-intensive and brittle.
- **Feature learning:** cheap and generalizable, but not interpretable.

**Distributional hypothesis:** a word's meaning comes from its contexts. Related issues: polysemy, morphology, word similarity.

**Count embeddings** (co-occurrence vectors) have two problems: they're as **long** as |V|, and they're **sparse**.

**GloVe:** learns dense vectors so that **wᵢ·wⱼ ≈ log P(co-occurrence)**.

**word2vec (skip-gram with negative sampling):**
- Train a **binary classifier**: do w and c co-occur within ±2 words?
- P(+ | w, c) = σ(c·w).
- L = −[log σ(c_pos·w) + Σ log σ(−c_neg·w)]. Minimize it over both W and C with SGD.

**Cosine similarity:** cos θ = a·b / (‖a‖‖b‖). The raw dot product is biased toward longer vectors, such as frequent words, and cosine normalizes for length.

**Analogies:**
- a : b :: c : d means a − b = c − d, so **c ≈ a − b + d**.
- Example: king − man + woman ≈ queen.

---

## 6. Attention and Transformers (Session 6)

**Why sentences are hard to embed:**
- There are infinitely many sentences, so you can't use a lookup table.
- Sentences vary in length.
- Sentences vary in how much information they carry.
- "You can't cram the meaning of a whole sentence into a single vector!" (Mooney)
- **Pooling** turns a variable-length sequence into a fixed-length one by summing, averaging or taking the max.

**Static vs. contextual embeddings:**
- **Static** (word2vec): one vector per word form.
- **Contextual:** the vector represents the word plus its (preceding) context.

**Elman RNN (1990):**
- hₜ = σ(Uxₜ + Vhₜ₋₁ + b).
- Output: softmax(σ(Whₜ + b₀)).
- It suffers from **vanishing gradients**: sensitivity to early inputs decays exponentially.

**LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber):** adds a **memory cell** and **3 gates** (forget, input, output).

**Why RNNs and LSTMs matter:**
- They were the first neural LMs.
- The first pretrained foundation models were LSTMs: **ULMFiT and ELMo (2018)**.
- They are more cognitively plausible.

**Why they were dropped:**
- They process tokens **sequentially**, which GPUs can't parallelize.
- Memory decay and vanishing gradients remain a problem.

**Attention:**
- A generalization of sum-pooling: a word's output is a **weighted sum** of value vectors.
- **Cross-attention** attends over *another* sequence, as in translation.
- **Self-attention** attends over the *same* sequence.

**Scaled dot-product attention (know cold):**
- qᵢ = W_Q xᵢ, kⱼ = W_K xⱼ, vⱼ = W_V xⱼ.
- s_{i,j} = kⱼᵀqᵢ / √d_k.
- aᵢ = softmax(sᵢ).
- x′ᵢ = Σⱼ a_{i,j} vⱼ.
- Matrix form: **softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k) V**.

**What Q, K, V mean:**
- Query: "whose output am I computing?"
- Key: "which token am I attending to?"
- Value: "what does that token contribute or mean?"

**Attention worked example:**
- Scores (0.2, 0.6, 2.0, 0.5) → weights (.10, .15, .61, .14).
- With the causal mask, s₂ = (1.1, 0.3, −∞, −∞) → (.69, .31, 0, 0).

**Causal masking:** set s_{i,j} = **−∞ for j > i** so tokens can't see the future. Softmax turns those scores into 0.

**Multi-head attention:**
- Each head h has its own W_Q⁽ʰ⁾, W_K⁽ʰ⁾, W_V⁽ʰ⁾ and output zᵢ⁽ʰ⁾.
- **Concatenate** the head outputs, then project: x′ = W_O[z⁽¹⁾; …; z⁽ᴴ⁾], with W_O ∈ ℝ^{d × H·d_v}.
- Usually d_head = d/H. For example, 768/12 = 64.

**Transformer:**
- Introduced in *"Attention Is All You Need"* (2017), which also introduced scaled dot-product attention.
- It replaced LSTMs because it is more efficient and solves memory decay and vanishing gradients.

**Transformer block:**
- Multi-head self-attention, then a feedforward network (FFN). Each sublayer has a **residual connection** and a **LayerNorm**.
- FFN = W₂ f(W₁x + b₁) + b₂, with d_ff ≈ 4d (for example, 3072 = 4 × 768).

**Deep Transformer LM:**
- Input embeddings + positional embeddings → N stacked blocks → **LM head**.
- The LM head is an unembedding (linear) layer followed by a softmax over the vocabulary.

**Positional embeddings:**
- Attention is **order-invariant**, so you add a position vector pₜ to each input embedding.
- They can be learned or fixed. The standard fixed choice is sinusoidal: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/10000^{2i/d}) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos/10000^{2i/d}).

**Why Transformers?**
- Training **parallelizes** across all time steps.
- They handle **long-range dependencies** well.
- The cost: runtime grows **quadratically** with sequence length (O(n²)), compared with **linearly** for RNNs.

**Hyperparameters to recognize:**

| Model | Params | Layers | d_model | Heads |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BERT-base | 110M | 12 | 768 | 12 |
| GPT-2 small | 124M | 12 | 768 | 12 |
| GPT-3 | 175B | 96 | 12,288 | 96 |

- **Grouped-query attention (GQA):** several query heads share one set of K/V heads. For example, Llama 3 uses 32 query heads with 8 KV heads.

---

## Likely exam question types
1. **Compute:**
   - A string's probability from conditionals, plus its surprisal and per-word perplexity.
   - Bigram or unigram MLE estimates from a toy corpus, with and without Laplace smoothing.
   - A logistic or softmax output from given weights; one gradient-descent step using (ŷ − y)x.
   - A layer's forward pass (Wx, then the activation); layer dimensions and parameter counts.
   - An attention step: scores → softmax → weighted sum, with a causal mask.
   - Cosine similarity, or an analogy using vector arithmetic.
2. **Explain why:**
   - EOS is needed.
   - We use log probabilities.
   - Bigrams fail on agreement.
   - Bigger n causes sparsity.
   - Backoff isn't a valid distribution.
   - Nonlinearity matters, and a single layer can't learn XOR.
   - Cosine beats the raw dot product.
   - We scale by √d_k (large dot products saturate the softmax).
   - We need positional embeddings.
   - Transformers replaced LSTMs.
3. **Concepts:**
   - The Turing test, Chinese Room and Octopus test.
   - Formal vs. functional competence.
   - Symbolic vs. statistical approaches and Chomsky's argument.
   - Static vs. contextual embeddings.
   - Cross- vs. self-attention.
   - The three eras of NLU.

**Reading:** Jurafsky & Martin ch. 3.1–3.6 (n-grams) was assigned. The later lectures follow J&M ch. 5–9 (logistic regression, embeddings, neural networks, RNNs, Transformers).

content.text:
The practice test already has its answer key, and I checked the math: it's correct. Below is what the test emphasizes, what each section needs, and some extra problems in the same style.

## Where the points are

| Section | Topic | Lecture | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | True/False (5) | Sessions 2, 4, 6 | Concepts |
| 2 | Short answer (5) | Sessions 3, 4, 6, plus 2 topics **not in your slides** | Concepts + 1 calculation |
| 3 | MLP forward pass + matrix form | Session 5 | **Hand calculation** |
| 4 | Bigram probabilities, Laplace smoothing, sparsity | Session 3 | **Hand calculation + explain** |
| 5 | Training loop arithmetic | **Not in your slides** | Calculation |
| 6 | Skip-gram LM: is the factorization valid? | Sessions 2–3 | **Proof-style reasoning** |

**Main takeaways:**
1. **n-grams are the biggest topic.** Section 4, Q2.5 and Section 6 are all count-based LMs or factorization. That's probably 35–40% of the exam.
2. **You need fast hand arithmetic.** Bigram tables, add-one smoothing, step-function MLPs, matrix dimensions and batch/token counts.
3. **Factorization validity gets a whole section.** Know exactly why chain rule + Markov makes a bigram valid, and why some other factorizations (like the skip-gram) are not.
4. **Logistic regression and word embeddings barely show up.** Only T/F #4 (bounded vs. unbounded output) and Q2.3 (batch size). Don't over-study word2vec or GloVe, but don't skip them either.
5. **Two topics aren't in Sessions 1–6:** seq2seq/encoder-decoder (Q2.2) and gradient accumulation/global batch/epochs (Section 5). Check whether a Session 7+ deck or the J&M reading covers them. They're on the practice test, so expect them.

---

## What each section needs

### 1. True/False
1. **T.** Ungrammatical sentences have higher surprisal than minimal grammatical pairs (the Session 2 GPT-2 table). The "minimal pair" part matters, because length and frequency also change surprisal.
2. **F.** Lower perplexity is better.
3. **F.** Layers *can* have different numbers of heads. The architecture doesn't force them to match. Watch for "must" and "always" in T/F questions.
4. **F.** It's backwards. Linear regression is unbounded; logistic regression is bounded to (0, 1) by the sigmoid.
5. **T.** Attention is order-invariant, so the model needs positional embeddings.

Other T/F statements you could see:
- "Backoff gives a valid distribution." **F**
- "Without nonlinearities, a deep network equals one layer." **T**
- "Logistic regression's loss is convex." **T**
- "Transformer runtime grows linearly with sequence length." **F** (quadratic)
- "word2vec embeddings are contextual." **F** (static)
- "EOS is needed for P_LM to sum to 1." **T**

### 2. Short answer: memorize one or two sentences each
- **Q, K, V:**
  - The query qᵢ is token i's "what am I looking for."
  - It is dot-producted with each key kⱼ (j ≤ i under the causal mask). Those scores are divided by √dₖ and softmaxed to get weights.
  - The output is the weighted sum of the value vectors vⱼ, which carry each token's content.
- **seq2seq examples:** translation, summarization. Others: question answering, speech recognition, grammar correction. An **encoder-decoder** model encodes the whole input, then decodes the output, usually using **cross-attention** to the encoder states.
- **Why bigger batches help:** the gradient estimate is closer to the full-dataset gradient, so training is lower-variance and more stable. The cost is more compute per step.
- **Dimensionality:** each head's value dimension is d_v = d / H. Here W_V⁽ⁱ⁾ is (d/H) × d, so 1024/8 = 128, giving **128 × 1024**. Write it as rows × columns: output dim × input dim.
- **Why count-based estimation of P(wᵢ | w₍<ᵢ₎) fails:** the context has unbounded length, so there are infinitely many possible contexts. Almost all are unseen in a finite corpus, so the counts are 0 (sparsity).

### 3. MLP by hand
- **Method:** each hidden unit is g(weighted sum of its inputs). Then the output is g(weighted sum of the hidden units).
- **Matrix form:** **y = g(W₂ g(W₁x))**.
  - Row i of W₁ is the set of weights going **into** hidden unit i.
  - W₁ is (#hidden × #inputs), here 3 × 2. W₂ is 1 × 3.
- **Easy mistake:** reading the diagram's edge labels into the wrong matrix cell. Label each edge xⱼ → Hᵢ as W₁[i, j].
- The real exam could add biases or use ReLU instead of a step function. Practice both.

### 4. Bigram tables
- **MLE:** divide each row by its **row sum**. Rows are wᵢ (the context); columns are wᵢ₊₁.
- **Sequence probability:** multiply P(first word | ε) through P(EOS | last word). **Always include the ε start and the EOS end.**
- **Any zero count makes the whole sequence 0.** That's why sequences 2 and 3 are 0, and it's the motivation for smoothing.
- **Laplace smoothing:** (count + 1) / (row sum + |V|).
  - Here |V| = 4 (a, b, c, EOS). **ε isn't a possible next word, so it isn't counted in |V|.**
  - Example: the b row is (0, 10, 10, 0) → (1, 11, 11, 1)/24.
- **Sparsity:** most n-grams are unseen, especially for large n. Their counts are 0, so any new sequence containing one gets P = 0. Add-one takes some probability mass from seen n-grams and gives every n-gram a nonzero share.
- **Limitations of add-one smoothing (know all three):**
  1. All unseen continuations of a context get the *same* probability, even though some are more plausible than others.
  2. A **rare** prefix hands relatively large probability to its unseen continuations, while a **frequent** prefix hands them very little.
  3. With a large vocabulary, too much probability mass moves to unseen n-grams.

### 5. Training loop arithmetic (not in your slides)
- **Global batch** = local batch × gradient-accumulation steps (× #GPUs if given). Here 10 × 100 = 1000 samples per update.
- **Total tokens seen** = updates × global batch × sequence length = 10³ × 10³ × 10³ = **10⁹**.
- **Epochs** = total tokens seen / dataset size = 10⁹ / 10⁷ = **100**.
- Know the vocabulary: an **update/step** is one optimizer step. **Gradient accumulation** sums gradients over several local batches before one update, which simulates a bigger batch on limited memory. An **epoch** is one full pass over the dataset.

### 6. Factorization validity (most important conceptual question)
- **Valid:** the chain rule P(w) = ∏ P(wᵢ | w₍<ᵢ₎) is exact. Replace each term using the Markov assumption, P(wᵢ | w₍<ᵢ₎) = P(wᵢ | wᵢ₋₁), and you get the bigram model, a valid distribution.
- **Invalid:** the skip-gram product ∏ P(wᵢ | wᵢ₋₁, wᵢ₊₁). Every chain-rule factorization, in any order, ends with one term conditioned on nothing (or only on BOS). In the skip-gram product every term is conditioned on two neighbors, so no chain-rule order can produce it. It isn't a valid joint distribution.
- **Variants to prepare** (these are my predictions):
  - "Is a right-to-left bigram, ∏ P(wᵢ | wᵢ₊₁), valid?" **Yes.** Apply the chain rule in reverse order, then the Markov assumption.
  - "Is a trigram valid?" **Yes**, under a second-order Markov assumption.
  - "Is backoff valid?" **No.** The probabilities don't sum to 1.
  - "Why is EOS needed?" Without it, a string and its prefixes overlap as events, so the probabilities don't sum to 1.

---

## Practice problems in the same style
1. **Heads:** H = 12, d = 768, with no W_O. What is W_V⁽ⁱ⁾? → **64 × 768**. Now add W_O: it's d × H·d_v = **768 × 768**.
2. **Training loop:** local batch 32, 8 accumulation steps, 4 GPUs, sequence length 2048, 500 updates, 1B-token dataset.
   - Global batch = 32 × 8 × 4 = **1024 samples**.
   - Tokens seen = 500 × 1024 × 2048 ≈ **1.05 × 10⁹**.
   - Epochs ≈ **1.05**.
3. **Smoothed sequence:** use the Laplace table from Section 4 to compute P(a b EOS).
   - P(a | ε) · P(b | a) · P(EOS | b) = 3/10 · 2/5 · 1/24 = **1/200 = 0.005**.
   - Compare: the unsmoothed answer is 0, because b → EOS was never observed.
4. **MLP with ReLU:** redo Section 3 with g = ReLU.
   - Hidden units: H = (6, 0, 0).
   - Output: y = ReLU(−3·6 + 0 + 0) = **0**.
   - With x = (−1, 1) instead: H₁ = ReLU(−2 − 2) = 0, H₂ = ReLU(1 + 1) = 2, H₃ = ReLU(−3 + 4) = 1. Then y = ReLU(0 + 4 + 1) = **5**.
5. **Perplexity:** a 4-token sequence (including EOS) has P = 1/16. What is its per-word perplexity? → 16^(1/4) = **2**.

## What to put on your notes sheet
- The chain rule, the Markov substitution, and the skip-gram argument.
- MLE and Laplace formulas, with the note that |V| includes EOS but not ε.
- The perplexity formula.
- The attention formula softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V, plus d_v = d/H and the matrix shapes.
- y = g(W₂ g(W₁x)), with the rule that W is (out × in).
- The batch, token and epoch formulas.
- σ and softmax, and the gradient (ŷ − y)x.
- The table of activation-function properties.

content.text:
# LIGN 167 Midterm Playbook

Each topic below follows the same pattern:
- **Spot it:** the cues that tell you which kind of question it is.
- **Concept:** what you need to understand.
- **How to do it:** step-by-step method.
- **Worked example:** a full solution.
- **Traps:** common mistakes that cost points.

---

## 0. Quick question-type finder

| If the question says… | It's this topic | Go to |
|---|---|---|
| "probability of the sequence", "co-occurrence matrix", "estimate" | n-gram counting | §3 |
| "add-one", "Laplace", "smoothing", "unobserved" | Smoothing | §4 |
| "valid factorization", "Markov assumption", "joint probability", a strange new model | Factorization validity | §2 |
| "surprisal", "perplexity", "log probability" | LM evaluation | §1 |
| A network diagram with weights, "compute the output", "step function" | MLP forward pass | §6 |
| "rewrite using matrices", "dimensionality of W" | Linear algebra / dimensions | §6, §9 |
| "sigmoid", "logit", "classifier", "bounded" | Logistic regression | §5 |
| "batch size", "gradient accumulation", "epochs", "tokens seen" | Training loop arithmetic | §7 |
| "query/key/value", "heads", "mask", "positional" | Attention / Transformer | §9 |
| "cosine", "analogy", "word2vec", "static vs contextual" | Embeddings | §8 |
| "vanishing gradient", "sequential", "why Transformers replaced" | RNN/LSTM vs Transformer | §9 |
| Turing, Chinese Room, Octopus, Chomsky | Concepts / history | §10 |

---

## 1. Language model basics: string probability, surprisal, perplexity

**Spot it:** you're given conditional probabilities and asked for P(sentence), surprisal, or perplexity.

**Concept:**
- An LM is a **probability distribution over all strings** (Σ\*).
- We compute it with the chain rule: multiply each word's probability given everything before it, then multiply by P(EOS | whole string).
- **Surprisal** = −log P. Rarer events are more surprising.
- **Perplexity** = P^(−1/N). Think of it as the "effective number of choices per word." **Lower is better.**

**How to do it:**
1. Write out every factor, **including the first word given ε/BOS and the final EOS**.
2. Multiply the factors.
3. Surprisal = −log₂(P) in bits, or use ln if the question says nats.
4. Per-word perplexity = P^(−1/N), where N = number of tokens **including EOS**. Check how your instructor counts N; the lecture counted EOS (7 tokens for "the cat sat on the mat").

**Worked example.** P(the | ε) = 0.5, P(dog | the) = 0.2, P(EOS | the dog) = 0.1.
- P = 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.1 = **0.01**
- Surprisal = −log₂(0.01) = **6.64 bits**
- Total perplexity = 1/0.01 = **100**
- Per-word perplexity = 100^(1/3) = **4.64**

**Why we use logs:** multiplying many small probabilities underflows to 0 on a computer. Logs turn products into sums.

**Why EOS is needed:** without EOS, "the" and "the dog" aren't disjoint events (one is a prefix of the other), so the probabilities wouldn't sum to 1. Ending every string with EOS makes them disjoint.

**Traps:**
- Forgetting EOS or the first P(w₁ | ε) term.
- Saying "higher perplexity = better." It's the opposite.
- **Probability reflects more than grammaticality:** it also depends on length, word frequency, plausibility and typicality. To test grammaticality, compare *minimal pairs* (sentences that differ in just one spot).

---

## 2. Is this factorization valid? (Markov assumption)

**Spot it:**
- "Can we apply the Markov assumption…"
- "Is this a valid distribution?"
- A new model that conditions on something unusual, such as the next word.

**Concept:**
- The **chain rule is always exact**, in any order:
  P(w₁w₂w₃) = P(w₁) · P(w₂ | w₁) · P(w₃ | w₁w₂) · P(EOS | w₁w₂w₃)
- The **Markov assumption** says only the last k words matter: P(wᵢ | w₍<ᵢ₎) = P(wᵢ | wᵢ₋ₖ…wᵢ₋₁).
- Substituting it into the chain rule gives you the n-gram model. Because it came from the chain rule, it's still a valid distribution.

**How to do it:**
1. Write the chain rule in some order: left-to-right, right-to-left, or any permutation.
2. Ask whether a Markov-style substitution turns each chain-rule term into the model's terms.
3. If yes for some order, it's **valid**. If no order works, it's **not valid**.
4. **Quick test:** every chain-rule expansion has **one term conditioned on nothing**: the first factor in whatever order you chose. If *every* term in the model is conditioned on something, the model can't come from the chain rule.

**Worked examples:**

| Model | Valid? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Bigram ∏P(wᵢ \| wᵢ₋₁) | ✅ | Left-to-right chain rule + first-order Markov |
| Trigram ∏P(wᵢ \| wᵢ₋₂wᵢ₋₁) | ✅ | Chain rule + second-order Markov |
| Right-to-left ∏P(wᵢ \| wᵢ₊₁) | ✅ | Chain rule in reverse order + Markov |
| Skip-gram ∏P(wᵢ \| wᵢ₋₁, wᵢ₊₁) | ❌ | Every term conditions on 2 neighbors. No chain-rule order gives that, and nothing is left unconditioned. |
| Backoff (×λ) | ❌ | The probabilities don't sum to 1 |

**Answer template:** "The chain rule gives P(w) = ∏P(wᵢ | w₍<ᵢ₎) exactly. Under the Markov assumption, each term becomes P(wᵢ | wᵢ₋₁), so the bigram product equals the joint distribution. For [model X], no ordering of the chain rule produces terms of the form [X's terms], because [reason], so it is not a valid factorization."

---

## 3. n-gram estimation from counts

**Spot it:** a training corpus or a count/co-occurrence matrix, followed by "estimate P(…)".

**Concept:** maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE).
P(next | context) = count(context, next) / count(context)
In a count matrix, that's **cell ÷ row sum**. Rows are the context; columns are the next word.

**How to do it (corpus):**
1. Add ε (or BOS) at the start and EOS at the end of each sentence.
2. Count every adjacent pair (bigram).
3. For each context word, divide each next-word count by the total number of times that word appeared *as a context*.
4. For a sequence: multiply P(w₁ | ε) × … × P(EOS | last word).

**Worked example.** Corpus: `a b EOS` / `a a b EOS` / `b a EOS`

Bigram counts:

| | a | b | EOS | row sum |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ε | 2 | 1 | 0 | 3 |
| a | 1 | 2 | 1 | 4 |
| b | 1 | 0 | 2 | 3 |

Probabilities (cell ÷ row sum):

| | a | b | EOS |
|---|---|---|---|
| ε | 2/3 | 1/3 | 0 |
| a | 1/4 | 1/2 | 1/4 |
| b | 1/3 | 0 | 2/3 |

- P(a b EOS) = 2/3 × 1/2 × 2/3 = **2/9**
- P(b b EOS) = 1/3 × **0** × … = **0**, because b→b was never seen.

**Unigram:** count(word) ÷ total tokens. Check whether EOS counts as a token.

**Traps:**
- Dividing by the column sum instead of the row sum.
- Forgetting the ε row or the EOS factor.
- Not noticing a 0 early. The moment one factor is 0, the whole product is 0, so say so and stop.
- Types vs. tokens: a **type** is a distinct word (a vocabulary entry); a **token** is one occurrence.

---

## 4. Laplace (add-one) smoothing, sparsity, backoff

**Spot it:** "add-one", "Laplace", "smoothing", "unobserved n-grams", "sparsity".

**Concept:**
- **Sparsity:** most possible n-grams never appear in training, so their MLE probability is 0. Any new sentence containing one gets P = 0.
- The number of possible n-grams is |V|ⁿ. With |V| = 10⁴, there are 10¹⁶ possible 4-grams, so sparsity gets much worse as n grows.
- **Laplace smoothing:** P = (count + 1) / (row sum + |V|).
- |V| = the number of *possible next tokens*. Include EOS. **Do not include ε/BOS**, because it can never be a next token.

**How to do it:**
1. Add 1 to every cell of the count table.
2. Add |V| to each row sum.
3. Divide.
4. Check that each row sums to 1.

**Worked example** (same counts as §3; |V| = 3 for {a, b, EOS}):

| | a | b | EOS |
|---|---|---|---|
| ε | 3/6 | 2/6 | 1/6 |
| a | 2/7 | 3/7 | 2/7 |
| b | 2/6 | 1/6 | 3/6 |

- P(b b EOS) = 2/6 × 1/6 × 3/6 = **1/36**. Unsmoothed, it was 0.

**Limitations (an essay answer):**
1. Every unseen continuation of a context gets the **same** probability, even when some are clearly more plausible than others.
2. A **rare context** (small row sum) gives a big share of probability to unseen words. A **frequent context** (large row sum) gives them very little.
3. With a large |V|, too much probability mass moves away from the observed n-grams.

**Backoff:** if the n-gram is unseen, use the (n−1)-gram probability multiplied by λ, where 0 < λ < 1. The shorter context is less specific, so you discount it. Backoff **does not** give a valid distribution.

**`<UNK>`:** keep the top-|V| words and map every other word to `<UNK>`. This handles unknown words.

**Why count-based estimation can't do P(wᵢ | all previous words):** the context has unbounded length, so there are infinitely many possible contexts. Almost all have count 0. That's why n-gram models cap the context at n−1 words.

---

## 5. Linear and logistic regression, softmax, loss, gradients

**Spot it:** "predict a value", "classifier", "sigmoid", "logit", "loss", "update the weights", "bounded".

**Concept:**

| | Linear regression | Logistic regression | Multinomial (softmax) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Output | w·x + b | σ(w·x + b) | softmax(Wx + b) |
| Range | (−∞, ∞), **unbounded** | (0, 1), **bounded** | Probability vector over k classes |
| Loss | Squared error | −log ŷ (negative log-likelihood, NLL) | Cross-entropy −log ŷ_true |

- σ(z) = 1/(1 + e⁻ᶻ).
- z is called the **logit** (σ is the inverse of the log-odds).
- softmax(z)ᵢ = e^{zᵢ} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ}.

**Sigmoid values to memorize:**
- σ(0) = 0.5
- σ(1) ≈ 0.73, σ(2) ≈ 0.88, σ(3) ≈ 0.95
- σ(−z) = 1 − σ(z)

**Gradient (logistic regression):**
- ∂L/∂wⱼ = **(ŷ − y)·xⱼ**
- ∂L/∂b = ŷ − y
- Update: w ← w − η·gradient, where η is the learning rate.

**Worked example.** w = (2, −1), b = 0.5, x = (1, 3), true label y = 1, η = 0.1.
1. z = 2·1 + (−1)·3 + 0.5 = **−0.5**
2. ŷ = σ(−0.5) ≈ **0.378**, which predicts class 0 (wrong)
3. Loss = −ln(0.378) ≈ **0.97**
4. Error = ŷ − y = −0.622
   - Gradient for w = −0.622 × (1, 3) = (−0.622, −1.866)
   - Gradient for b = −0.622
5. New w = (2, −1) − 0.1 × (−0.622, −1.866) = **(2.062, −0.813)**. New b = **0.562**.
   The weights move to push z up, toward the correct class.

**Softmax example:** z = (2, 1, 0).
- e^z = (7.39, 2.72, 1), which sums to 11.11.
- softmax = **(0.665, 0.245, 0.090)**.

**Gradient descent intuition:**
- If the slope is positive, decrease w. If it's negative, increase w. Where the slope is 0, you're at a minimum.
- The logistic regression loss is **convex**: it has one global minimum. Neural network losses are not convex.

---

## 6. MLP (feedforward network) by hand

**Spot it:** a diagram with input nodes, hidden nodes and weighted edges; "compute the output"; "rewrite with matrices".

**Concept:**
- Each unit computes h = g(Σ weight·input + bias).
- A whole layer is **h = g(Wx + b)**.
- **Row i of W holds the weights going *into* unit i.**
- Two layers: **y = g(W₂ g(W₁x + b₁) + b₂)**.

**How to do it:**
1. For each hidden unit, list its incoming edges, multiply each by its input, add them up (plus the bias), then apply g.
2. Use those hidden values as inputs to the output unit and repeat.
3. For the matrix form, build W₁ with one row per hidden unit and one column per input. Shape: **(#outputs × #inputs)**.

**Worked example** (ReLU with biases). x = (1, 2), W₁ = [[1, −1], [0, 2]], b₁ = (0, −1), W₂ = [1, 2], b₂ = −5.
- Hidden pre-activations: (1 − 2 + 0, 0 + 4 − 1) = (−1, 3)
- After ReLU: h = (0, 3)
- Output: y = 1·0 + 2·3 − 5 = **1**

**Activations:**
- **Step:** 1 if a > 0, else 0. Note that a = 0 gives 0.
- **ReLU:** max(0, a). Fast, sparse, minimal vanishing gradient.
- **Sigmoid:** range (0, 1). Saturates at both ends; severe vanishing gradient.
- **tanh:** range (−1, 1). Zero-centered; moderate vanishing gradient.

**Parameter count per layer** = (n_out × n_in) + n_out. In the example: (2×2 + 2) + (1×2 + 1) = **9**.

**Why nonlinearity:** U(Wx) = (UW)x, so stacked linear layers collapse into a single linear layer. Adding g between them prevents the collapse.

**XOR:** a single perceptron can't learn XOR, because no straight line separates {(0,1), (1,0)} from {(0,0), (1,1)}. One hidden layer fixes this:
- h₁ = step(x₁ + x₂ − 0.5), which acts as OR
- h₂ = step(x₁ + x₂ − 1.5), which acts as AND
- y = step(h₁ − h₂ − 0.5), which means "OR and not AND"

Check:
- (1, 0): h = (1, 0), y = step(0.5) = **1** ✓
- (1, 1): h = (1, 1), y = step(−0.5) = **0** ✓
- (0, 0): h = (0, 0), y = step(−0.5) = **0** ✓
- (0, 1): h = (1, 0), y = step(0.5) = **1** ✓

**Backpropagation:** use the chain rule from the loss backward through the network. At a softmax + cross-entropy output, ∂L/∂z = **ŷ − y**. The same "error × input" pattern as logistic regression repeats at every layer.

**Traps:**
- Mixing up rows and columns of W.
- Treating a = 0 as positive for the step function.
- Applying g to the final output when the question says the output layer is linear, or the reverse. Read the question carefully.

---

## 7. Training loop arithmetic

**Spot it:** "batch size", "gradient accumulation", "sequence length", "updates", "epochs", "tokens seen".

**Formulas:**
- **Global batch** (samples per update) = local batch × accumulation steps × #GPUs (if given)
- **Tokens per update** = global batch × sequence length
- **Total tokens seen** = updates × tokens per update
- **Epochs** = total tokens seen ÷ dataset size in tokens

**How to do it:** write each quantity with its units and cancel them, like a chemistry conversion. Use powers of 10 when you can.

**Worked example.** Local batch 32, 8 accumulation steps, 4 GPUs, sequence length 2048, 500 updates, 1B-token dataset.
- Global batch = 32 × 8 × 4 = **1024 samples**
- Tokens per update = 1024 × 2048 ≈ 2.1M
- Total = 500 × 2.1M ≈ **1.05 × 10⁹ tokens**
- Epochs ≈ **1.05**

**Concepts:**
- **Batch GD** uses the whole dataset per step. **SGD** uses one sample. **Minibatch** uses a few.
- **Bigger batches** give a better estimate of the full-dataset gradient, so training is more stable. The cost is more compute per step.
- **Gradient accumulation** sums gradients over several local batches before one update. It simulates a large batch when GPU memory is limited.

---

## 8. Word embeddings

**Spot it:** "cosine", "analogy", "similar words", "word2vec/GloVe", "feature engineering vs. learning".

**Concept:**
- **Distributional hypothesis:** words that appear in similar contexts have similar meanings ("know a word by the company it keeps").
- **Count vectors** are as long as |V| and sparse. **GloVe and word2vec** learn dense, short vectors.
  - **GloVe:** learns vectors so that w·c ≈ log of their co-occurrence probability.
  - **word2vec (skip-gram with negative sampling):** a binary classifier, P(co-occur) = σ(c·w). It pulls real context words closer and pushes random "negative" words away.
- **Static** embeddings (word2vec) give one vector per word form, so "bank" (river) = "bank" (money). **Contextual** embeddings (RNN or Transformer outputs) change with the surrounding words.
- **Feature engineering** (hand-made features): interpretable, but laborious and brittle. **Feature learning:** cheap and generalizes, but not interpretable.

**Cosine similarity** = a·b / (‖a‖‖b‖). The raw dot product favors longer vectors (often frequent words); cosine normalizes for length.

**Cosine example:** a = (1, 2), b = (2, 1).
- a·b = 4
- ‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = √5
- cos = 4/5 = **0.8**

**Analogy:** to complete a : b :: c : ?, compute **? ≈ b − a + c**, then find the nearest word by cosine. Example: man : king :: woman : ? gives king − man + woman ≈ **queen**.

---

## 9. RNNs, attention and Transformers

### RNN and LSTM
- **Elman RNN:** hₜ = σ(Uxₜ + Vhₜ₋₁ + b). It reads one token at a time and carries a fixed-size memory hₜ.
- **Problems:**
  1. **Vanishing gradients:** early tokens' influence shrinks exponentially.
  2. **Sequential processing:** it can't be parallelized on GPUs.
- **LSTM** adds a memory cell and 3 gates (forget, input, output) to reduce vanishing gradients.
- Historically, ELMo and ULMFiT (2018) were the first pretrained LSTM foundation models.

### Scaled dot-product attention (the main calculation)
**Spot it:** you're given q, k, v vectors or scores and asked for an attention output.

**How to do it, for token i:**
1. Scores: sᵢⱼ = (kⱼ · qᵢ) / √dₖ for each allowed j (j ≤ i under the causal mask).
2. Weights: aᵢ = softmax(sᵢ). Masked positions get a score of −∞, which becomes weight 0.
3. Output: x′ᵢ = Σⱼ aᵢⱼ vⱼ.

The matrix form is **softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V**.

**Worked example.** dₖ = 4 (so √dₖ = 2), token 2 attends to tokens 1 and 2.
- q₂ = (1, 0, 1, 0), k₁ = (1, 1, 0, 0), k₂ = (2, 0, 2, 0), v₁ = (1, 0), v₂ = (0, 1)
- Dot products: k₁·q₂ = 1, k₂·q₂ = 4. Scaled: (0.5, 2).
- Softmax: e^0.5 = 1.65, e^2 = 7.39, sum = 9.04, so the weights are **(0.18, 0.82)**.
- Output = 0.18·v₁ + 0.82·v₂ = **(0.18, 0.82)**.
- Token 1, under the mask, can only see itself, so its weight is 1 and its output is v₁.

**Intuitive Q/K/V answer:**
- The **query** is what the current token is looking for.
- Each **key** is what a token offers to be matched against. The query·key score says how relevant that token is.
- The **value** is the content that actually gets mixed into the output, weighted by relevance.

**Why divide by √dₖ:** dot products grow with dimension. Large scores make the softmax nearly one-hot, which saturates it and gives tiny gradients.

**Self- vs. cross-attention:**
- **Self-attention** attends within the same sequence.
- **Cross-attention** attends to another sequence: the decoder looks at the encoder's states.
- **Encoder-decoder (seq2seq)** tasks: translation, summarization, question answering, speech-to-text.

### Multi-head dimensions (a very likely question)
- Per-head size: dₖ = d_v = **d / H**.
- W_Q⁽ʰ⁾, W_K⁽ʰ⁾, W_V⁽ʰ⁾ are each **(d/H) × d**, written as (output dim × input dim).
- The head outputs are concatenated into a vector of size H·d_v = d. Then W_O is **d × H·d_v** (here d × d).
- Example: d = 1024, H = 8 gives W_V = **128 × 1024**. With d = 768, H = 12, it's **64 × 768**.
- Different layers *may* have different numbers of heads. They aren't required to match.

### Transformer block and LM
- **Block:** multi-head self-attention, then a feedforward network. Each sublayer has a **residual connection** (+x) and **LayerNorm**. The FFN hidden size is usually about 4d.
- **LM:** embeddings + positional embeddings → N blocks → LM head (linear layer + softmax over the vocabulary).
- **Positional embeddings are required** because attention ignores order: shuffling the tokens gives the same weights. They can be learned or sinusoidal.
- **Causal mask:** set scores to −∞ for future tokens, so each token predicts the next one without peeking.
- **Why Transformers replaced RNNs:**
  - Training parallelizes across all positions.
  - Every token can reach every other token directly, so there's no memory decay and fewer vanishing gradients.
  - The cost: attention takes **O(n²)** time in sequence length, compared with O(n) for an RNN.

---

## 10. Concepts and history (for T/F and short answers)
- **Turing Test:** if a judge can't tell the machine from a human, the machine passes. Jones & Bergen (2025) found that LMs pass.
- **Chinese Room (Searle):** following symbol rules ≠ understanding.
- **Octopus (Bender & Koller):** learning from form alone gives no grounding, so the octopus fails on a new real-world situation (the bear).
- **Formal vs. functional competence (Mahowald):**
  - Formal: knowing *"Colorless green ideas sleep furiously"* is grammatical.
  - Functional: knowing that it's nonsense.
- **Chomsky (1957):** "grammatical" ≠ "statistically likely." Both "colorless green ideas…" and its reversal have a corpus probability of about 0, yet only one is grammatical.
- **Jelinek:** "every time I fire a linguist, performance goes up." This marks the 1980s–90s shift to statistical methods.
- **Eras:** task-specific networks (early 2010s) → pretrain + fine-tune (late 2010s) → prompting a single scaled model (2020s).

---

## Study plan (in order of exam weight)
1. **n-grams:** MLE tables, Laplace smoothing, sparsity, and the limits of smoothing. Do two full corpus-to-probabilities problems.
2. **Factorization validity:** be able to write the chain-rule + Markov argument from memory, plus the skip-gram counterexample.
3. **MLP by hand:** one step-function problem and one ReLU-with-bias problem, each also in matrix form.
4. **Attention:** one full score → softmax → weighted-sum calculation, plus the multi-head dimension formula.
5. **Training loop arithmetic:** one problem.
6. **Short-answer phrases:** Q/K/V, seq2seq examples, batch size, why count-based estimation fails, why positional embeddings.
7. **T/F traps:** perplexity direction, which regression is bounded, "must" statements, backoff validity, O(n²) vs O(n).

To test yourself, cover the worked examples above and redo them. If you'd like, I can write a fresh practice exam with new numbers and grade your answers.

LIGN 167 Midterm Study Guide

Deep Learning & Natural Language Understanding · Sessions 1–6 + Practice Midterm
Exam format In class during normal meeting time · 40 points · 1 double-sided 8.5×11 page of handwritten notes allowed.
Where the points are (based on the practice midterm)
  1. n-gram models are the biggest topic (~35–40%): count tables, Laplace smoothing, sparsity, factorization validity.
  2. Hand calculations: bigram tables, add-one smoothing, MLP forward pass, matrix dimensions, training-loop arithmetic.
  3. Factorization validity gets a whole section: chain rule + Markov assumption, and why a skip-gram model is not valid.
  4. Attention: Q/K/V intuition and multi-head dimensions.
  5. Light coverage: logistic regression (bounded vs. unbounded), batch size, word embeddings.
  6. Not in the Session 1–6 slides but on the practice test: seq2seq / encoder-decoder, gradient accumulation / epochs. Covered in this guide.

Contents

0. Question-type finder
1. LM basics: probability, surprisal, perplexity
2. Factorization validity (Markov)
3. n-gram estimation from counts
4. Laplace smoothing, sparsity, backoff
5. Linear & logistic regression, gradients
6. MLP by hand
7. Training-loop arithmetic
8. Word embeddings
9. RNNs, attention, Transformers
10. Concepts & history
11. Practice midterm walkthrough
12. Extra practice problems
13. Notes-sheet checklist & study plan

Each topic follows the same pattern: Spot it How to do it Worked example Traps. Formulas follow the standard Jurafsky & Martin forms the course uses; check notation against your slides.

0. Question-Type Finder

Read the question, find the cue, jump to the section.

If the question says…It's this topicGo to
"probability of the sequence", "co-occurrence matrix", "estimate"n-gram counting§3
"add-one", "Laplace", "smoothing", "unobserved"Smoothing§4
"valid factorization", "Markov assumption", "joint probability", a strange new modelFactorization validity§2
"surprisal", "perplexity", "log probability"LM evaluation§1
Network diagram with weights, "compute the output", "step function"MLP forward pass§6
"rewrite using matrices", "dimensionality of W"Linear algebra / dimensions§6, §9
"sigmoid", "logit", "classifier", "bounded"Logistic regression§5
"batch size", "gradient accumulation", "epochs", "tokens seen"Training-loop arithmetic§7
"query/key/value", "heads", "mask", "positional"Attention / Transformer§9
"cosine", "analogy", "word2vec", "static vs. contextual"Embeddings§8
"vanishing gradient", "sequential", "why Transformers replaced…"RNN/LSTM vs. Transformer§9
"seq2seq", "encoder-decoder", "translation"Encoder-decoder / cross-attention§9
Turing, Chinese Room, Octopus, ChomskyConcepts / history§10

1. LM Basics: Probability, Surprisal, Perplexity

Spot itYou're given conditional probabilities and asked for P(sentence), surprisal, or perplexity.

Concept

  • A language model is a probability distribution over all strings Σ* (the Kleene closure: every finite string over the alphabet, including the empty string ε).
  • Autoregressive factorization (chain rule):
P(w) = P(EOS | w) · ∏i P(wi | w<i)
  • Surprisal S(w) = −log P(w). Rarer events are more surprising. In bits if log base 2.
  • Perplexity: PPLtotal = P(w)−1; PPLword = P(w)−1/N. Think "effective number of choices per word." Lower is better.
How to do it
  1. Write every factor, including P(w1 | ε) and the final P(EOS | …).
  2. Multiply.
  3. Surprisal = −log2(P) (or ln if asked for nats).
  4. Per-word PPL = P−1/N, N = number of tokens including EOS (the lecture counted EOS).
Worked example P(the | ε) = 0.5, P(dog | the) = 0.2, P(EOS | the dog) = 0.1
  • P = 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.01
  • Surprisal = −log2(0.01) = 6.64 bits
  • PPLtotal = 1/0.01 = 100; PPLword = 1001/3 = 4.64
Lecture example: P(the cat sat on the mat) = 5.04×10−9, log P = −19.1, PPLword (N=7) ≈ 15.3.
Why logs?Multiplying many small probabilities underflows to 0. Logs turn products into sums.
Why EOS?Without EOS, "the" and "the dog" aren't disjoint events (one is a prefix of the other), so probabilities wouldn't sum to 1. Ending every string in EOS makes them disjoint.
Traps
  • Forgetting EOS or the first P(w1 | ε) term.
  • "Higher perplexity = better" is false.
  • Probability reflects more than grammaticality: length, word frequency, plausibility, typicality. Compare minimal pairs to test grammaticality. (Under the ground-truth LM, ungrammatical sentences have higher surprisal than minimally different grammatical ones: True.)

Notation: substring yi:j (inclusive); prefix y<i = y1:i−1; suffix y>i = yi+1:|y|. A subsequence deletes symbols keeping order; a substring is a contiguous subsequence. A data domain (language, genre, dialect, register, topic) is defined by its ground-truth distribution; a corpus is a sample; an LM is an estimate.

2. Is This Factorization Valid? (Markov Assumption)

Spot it"Can we apply the Markov assumption…", "Is this a valid distribution?", or a new model that conditions on something unusual (e.g., the next word).

Concept

The chain rule is always exact, in any order:

P(w1w2w3) = P(w1) · P(w2 | w1) · P(w3 | w1w2) · P(EOS | w1w2w3)

The Markov assumption: the next event depends only on the current state (the last k words):

P(wi | w<i) = P(wi | wi−1)   (first order → bigram)

Substitute it into the chain rule and you get the n-gram model. Because it came from the chain rule, it is still a valid distribution.

How to do it
  1. Write the chain rule in some order (left-to-right, right-to-left, any permutation).
  2. Ask: does a Markov-style substitution turn each chain-rule term into the model's terms?
  3. Yes for some order → valid. No order works → not valid.
  4. Quick test: every chain-rule expansion has one term conditioned on nothing (the first factor). If every term in the model is conditioned on something, it can't come from the chain rule.
ModelValid?Why
Bigram ∏P(wi | wi−1)YesLeft-to-right chain rule + first-order Markov
Trigram ∏P(wi | wi−2wi−1)YesChain rule + second-order Markov
Right-to-left ∏P(wi | wi+1)YesChain rule in reverse order + Markov
Skip-gram ∏P(wi | wi−1, wi+1)NoEvery term conditions on 2 neighbors. No chain-rule order produces that, and nothing is left unconditioned.
Backoff (× λ)NoProbabilities don't sum to 1
Answer template "The chain rule gives P(w) = ∏P(wi | w<i) exactly. Under the Markov assumption each term becomes P(wi | wi−1), so the bigram product equals the joint distribution. For [model X], no ordering of the chain rule produces terms of the form [X's terms], because [e.g., every chain-rule expansion contains one term conditioned on nothing, but every X term is conditioned on two tokens], so it is not a valid factorization."
Why the autoregressive factorization? The model's parameters don't give P(w) directly; they give conditional next-word distributions. The chain rule turns those into a joint probability exactly. You could factorize in another order (e.g., right-to-left).

3. n-gram Estimation from Counts

Spot itA training corpus or a count / co-occurrence matrix, followed by "estimate P(…)".

Concept: maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE)

P(wi | wi−n+1:i−1) = C(wi−n+1:i) / C(wi−n+1:i−1)

In a count matrix: cell ÷ row sum. Rows = context wi; columns = next word wi+1.

An n-gram conditions on the previous n−1 words: unigram n=1 (no context), bigram n=2, trigram n=3.

How to do it (from a corpus)
  1. Add ε (BOS) at the start and EOS at the end of each sentence.
  2. Count every adjacent pair.
  3. For each context word, divide each next-word count by that word's total count as a context (the row sum).
  4. For a sequence: P(w1 | ε) × … × P(EOS | last word).
Worked example Corpus: a b EOS / a a b EOS / b a EOS
CountsabEOSrow sum
ε2103
a1214
b1023
MLEabEOS
ε2/31/30
a1/41/21/4
b1/302/3
  • P(a b EOS) = 2/3 × 1/2 × 2/3 = 2/9
  • P(b b EOS) = 1/3 × 0 × … = 0 (b→b never seen)
Lecture exercise (Sam I am) Corpus: I am Sam EOS / Sam I am EOS / I do not like green eggs and ham EOS
BigramAnswer
P(I | ε)2/3
P(Sam | ε)1/3
P(am | I)2/3
P(EOS | Sam)1/2
P(Sam | am)1/2
P(do | I)1/3
Unigram (17 tokens incl. EOS)Answer
P(I)3/17
P(Sam)2/17
P(EOS)3/17
P(eggs)1/17
P(like)1/17

If EOS is excluded from the unigram denominator, use 14 instead of 17.

Traps
  • Dividing by the column sum instead of the row sum.
  • Forgetting the ε row or the EOS factor.
  • Missing a 0: once any factor is 0, the product is 0. Say so and stop.
  • Types vs. tokens: a type is a vocabulary entry; a token is one occurrence.
Why bigrams fail "The keys to the cabinet are/is…": a real LM uses P(· | the keys to the cabinet) and prefers "are". A bigram only sees P(· | cabinet) and prefers "is". Long-distance agreement, filler-gap dependencies, and coreference all break short contexts.

4. Laplace Smoothing, Sparsity, Backoff

Spot it"add-one", "Laplace", "smoothing", "unobserved n-grams", "sparsity".

Concept

  • Sparsity: most possible n-grams never appear in training, so their MLE probability is 0, and any new sentence containing one gets P = 0. There are |V|n possible n-grams: with |V| = 104, there are 1016 possible 4-grams. Larger n = better text but worse sparsity and roughly exponential memory.
  • Laplace (add-one) smoothing:
PLaplace(wi | wi−1) = (C(wi−1wi) + 1) / (C(wi−1) + |V|)

|V| = number of possible next tokens. Include EOS. Do not include ε/BOS (it can never be a next token).

How to do it
  1. Add 1 to every cell of the count table.
  2. Add |V| to each row sum.
  3. Divide.
  4. Check each row sums to 1.
Worked example Same counts as §3; |V| = 3 ({a, b, EOS}).
LaplaceabEOS
ε3/62/61/6
a2/73/72/7
b2/61/63/6
P(b b EOS) = 2/6 × 1/6 × 3/6 = 1/36 (it was 0 before smoothing).
How smoothing addresses sparsity Adds a pseudo-count of 1 to every possible n-gram so every n-gram gets a small non-zero probability. It removes some probability mass from observed n-grams and distributes it evenly over all possible continuations.
Limitations of add-one (essay answer)
  1. All unseen continuations of a context get the same probability, even though some are more plausible.
  2. A rare context (small row sum) hands a big share of probability to unseen words; a frequent context hands them very little (arguably reasonable: more "missed chances" to observe them).
  3. With a large |V|, too much mass moves away from the observed n-grams.

Other fixes

  • Backoff: if the n-gram is unseen, use the (n−1)-gram probability × λ, with 0 < λ < 1 (the shorter context is less specific, so discount it). Not a valid distribution.
  • <UNK>: keep the top-|V| words; map all others to <UNK>.
Why count-based estimation can't do P(wi | w<i) The context w<i has arbitrary length, so there are infinitely many possible contexts. Almost all are unobserved in a finite corpus, so counts are 0 (very sparse). That's why n-gram models cap the context at n−1 words, and why neural LMs are needed for unlimited context.

5. Linear & Logistic Regression, Softmax, Loss, Gradients

Spot it"predict a value", "classifier", "sigmoid", "logit", "loss", "update the weights", "bounded".
Linear regressionLogistic regressionMultinomial (softmax)
Outputw·x + bσ(w·x + b)softmax(Wx + b)
Range(−∞, ∞) unbounded(0, 1) boundedProbability vector over k classes
LossSquared error Σ(ŷ − y)²NLL: −log ŷtrueCross-entropy: −Σ yk log ŷk
UseHouse price, sentence complexitySpam? Is it English?Part of speech, next word
σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e−z)      softmax(z)i = ezi / Σj ezj

z is the logit (σ is the inverse of the log-odds function). In softmax regression, W is k × n and each row is one class's weight vector.

Sigmoid values to memorize σ(0) = 0.5 · σ(1) ≈ 0.73 · σ(2) ≈ 0.88 · σ(3) ≈ 0.95 · σ(−z) = 1 − σ(z)

Gradient descent

θ ← θ − η ∇θL      ∂L/∂wj = (ŷ − y) · xj      ∂L/∂b = ŷ − y

Multinomial: ∂L/∂wk,j = (ŷk − yk) xj. Bigger error or bigger feature → bigger step. Positive slope → decrease w; negative → increase; slope 0 = minimum. The logistic regression loss is convex (one minimum); neural network losses are not.

Worked example: one logistic regression step w = (2, −1), b = 0.5, x = (1, 3), true y = 1, η = 0.1
  1. z = 2·1 + (−1)·3 + 0.5 = −0.5
  2. ŷ = σ(−0.5) ≈ 0.378 → predicts class 0 (wrong)
  3. Loss = −ln(0.378) ≈ 0.97
  4. Error ŷ − y = −0.622 → grad w = (−0.622, −1.866), grad b = −0.622
  5. New w = (2, −1) − 0.1·(−0.622, −1.866) = (2.062, −0.813); new b = 0.562. The weights move to push z up, toward the correct class.
Worked example: softmax z = (2, 1, 0) → ez = (7.39, 2.72, 1), sum = 11.11 → softmax = (0.665, 0.245, 0.090)
Lecture examples House price: Model 2 (β0=300k, 400/sq ft, −1000/yr, +20k pool) predicts 665k, 2.695M, 1.099M. Squared error ≈ 1.0×1011 vs. ≈ 3.1×1011 for Model 1 → Model 2 is better.
Spam filter: Model 1 gives z = 11.8, 4.2, 3.5 → σ ≈ 1.0, 0.985, 0.97 (wrong on x(3), not spam). Model 2 gives z = 6.4, 3.9, 0.9 → σ ≈ 0.998, 0.98, 0.71 (closer on x(3)).
Batch, SGD, minibatch Batch GD uses the whole dataset per step (expensive). SGD uses one sample. Minibatch uses a small set: more stable than SGD, cheaper than full batch. Larger batches give a better estimate of the full-dataset gradient → more stable training.

6. MLP (Feedforward Network) by Hand

Spot itA diagram with input nodes, hidden nodes and weighted edges; "compute the output"; "rewrite with matrices".

Concept

unit: h = g(w·x + b)     layer: h = g(Wx + b)     two layers: y = g(W2 g(W1x + b1) + b2)

Row i of W holds the weights going into unit i. Shape of W = (#outputs × #inputs) = ni+1 × ni. The output layer is just multinomial logistic regression.

How to do it
  1. For each hidden unit: list incoming edges, multiply each by its input, sum (+ bias), apply g.
  2. Use those hidden values as inputs to the output unit; repeat.
  3. Matrix form: build W1 with one row per hidden unit, one column per input. Label each edge xj → Hi as W1[i, j].
Worked example: practice midterm (step function) x = (1, −2), g(a) = 1 if a > 0 else 0
  • H1 = g(1·2 + (−2)(−2)) = g(6) = 1
  • H2 = g(1·(−1) + (−2)·1) = g(−3) = 0
  • H3 = g(1·3 + (−2)·4) = g(−5) = 0
  • y = g(1·(−3) + 0·2 + 0·1) = g(−3) = 0
Matrix form: y = g( [−3  2  1] · g( [[2, −2], [−1, 1], [3, 4]] · [1, −2]T ) ), i.e. y = g(W2 g(W1x)), with W1 3×2 and W2 1×3.
Worked example: ReLU with biases x = (1, 2), W1 = [[1, −1], [0, 2]], b1 = (0, −1), W2 = [1, 2], b2 = −5
  • Pre-activations: (1 − 2 + 0, 0 + 4 − 1) = (−1, 3) → ReLU → h = (0, 3)
  • y = 1·0 + 2·3 − 5 = 1
  • Parameters: (2×2 + 2) + (1×2 + 1) = 9
SigmoidtanhReLUStep
Formula1/(1+e−a)tanh(a)max(0, a)1 if a > 0 else 0
Range(0, 1)(−1, 1)[0, ∞){0, 1}
Zero-centeredNoYesNoNo
SaturatesBoth endsBoth endsa ≤ 0—
Vanishing gradientSevereModerateMinimal—
Sparse / speedNo / slowNo / moderateYes / fast—
Why nonlinearity?U(Wx) = (UW)x = Vx: stacked linear layers collapse into one. U·g(Wx) doesn't collapse.
BackpropChain rule backward through the computation graph. At softmax + cross-entropy output, ∂L/∂z = ŷ − y; ∂L/∂Wout = (ŷ − y)hT.
XOR needs a hidden layer A single perceptron can learn AND and OR but not XOR: no straight line separates {(0,1),(1,0)} from {(0,0),(1,1)}. h1 = step(x1 + x2 − 0.5) (OR), h2 = step(x1 + x2 − 1.5) (AND), y = step(h1 − h2 − 0.5) ("OR and not AND"). Check: (1,0)→1 ✓ · (0,1)→1 ✓ · (1,1)→0 ✓ · (0,0)→0 ✓
Traps
  • Mixing up rows and columns of W.
  • Treating a = 0 as positive for the step function (g(0) = 0).
  • Applying g to a linear output layer, or forgetting it on the output when the question applies it.

7. Training-Loop Arithmetic

Spot it"batch size", "gradient accumulation", "sequence length", "updates", "epochs", "tokens seen".
Global batch = local batch × accumulation steps (× #GPUs)
Tokens per update = global batch × sequence length
Total tokens seen = updates × tokens per update
Epochs = total tokens seen ÷ dataset size (tokens)
How to do itWrite each quantity with its units and cancel them like a unit conversion. Use powers of 10.
Practice midterm 1000 updates, 10M-token dataset, local batch 10, 100 accumulation steps, sequence length 1000.
  • Global batch = 10 × 100 = 1000 samples
  • Tokens = 103 updates × 101 × 102 × 103 tokens/sample = 109 tokens
  • Epochs = 109 / 107 = 100
Variant Local batch 32, 8 accumulation steps, 4 GPUs, sequence length 2048, 500 updates, 1B-token dataset. Global batch = 32 × 8 × 4 = 1024 · tokens ≈ 500 × 1024 × 2048 ≈ 1.05×109 · epochs ≈ 1.05
Vocabulary Update / step = one optimizer step. Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several local batches before one update, simulating a big batch on limited GPU memory. Epoch = one full pass over the dataset.

8. Word Embeddings

Spot it"cosine", "analogy", "similar words", "word2vec/GloVe", "feature engineering vs. learning".
  • Distributional hypothesis: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps" (Firth 1957; Harris 1954).
  • Feature engineering (hand-made): interpretable and controllable, but laborious and brittle. Feature learning: minimal labor and generalizes, but not interpretable.
  • Count vectors: problems are (1) length = |V| and (2) sparsity.
  • GloVe: dense vectors with wi·wj ≈ log P(co-occurrence).
  • word2vec (skip-gram w/ negative sampling): binary classifier "do w and c co-occur within ±2 words?" P(+ | w, c) = σ(c·w). L = −[log σ(cpos·w) + Σ log σ(−cneg·w)], minimized over W and C with SGD.
  • Static (word2vec): one vector per word form ("bank" = "bank"). Contextual (RNN/Transformer outputs): the vector depends on the surrounding words.
cos θ = (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖)      analogy a : b :: c : ?  →  ? ≈ b − a + c
Worked examples a = (1, 2), b = (2, 1): a·b = 4, ‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = √5 → cos = 0.8.
man : king :: woman : ? → king − man + woman ≈ queen (find the nearest word by cosine).
Raw dot product favors longer vectors (often frequent words); cosine normalizes for length.

9. RNNs, Attention & Transformers

From words to sentences

Networks take fixed-size vectors. Sentences are infinite in number (no lookup table), vary in length, and vary in information content. Pooling (sum / mean / max) gives a fixed-length vector. "You can't cram the meaning of a whole sentence into a single vector!" (Mooney).

RNN & LSTM

Elman RNN (1990): ht = σ(Uxt + Vht−1 + b)    P(wt+1 | w≤t) = softmax(Wht + bo)
  • Problems: vanishing gradients (early tokens' influence shrinks exponentially) and sequential processing (can't parallelize on GPUs).
  • LSTM adds a memory cell and 3 gates (forget, input, output).
  • First neural LMs were RNNs; first pretrained foundation models were LSTMs (ULMFiT, ELMo, 2018). RNNs are more cognitively plausible.

Scaled dot-product attention

Spot itYou're given q, k, v vectors or scores and asked for an attention output.
qi = WQxi,  kj = WKxj,  vj = WVxj     sij = kjTqi / √dk     ai = softmax(si)     x′i = Σj aij vj
Matrix form: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKT / √dk) V
How to do it (for token i)
  1. Scores: dot qi with each allowed key kj (j ≤ i with a causal mask), divide by √dk.
  2. Masked positions get −∞ → weight 0.
  3. Softmax the scores → weights.
  4. Output = weighted sum of value vectors.
Worked example dk = 4 (√dk = 2). q2 = (1,0,1,0), k1 = (1,1,0,0), k2 = (2,0,2,0), v1 = (1,0), v2 = (0,1)
  • Dots: k1·q2 = 1, k2·q2 = 4 → scaled (0.5, 2)
  • Softmax: e0.5 = 1.65, e2 = 7.39, sum 9.04 → weights (0.18, 0.82)
  • Output = 0.18·v1 + 0.82·v2 = (0.18, 0.82)
  • Token 1 under the mask sees only itself → weight 1, output = v1.
Lecture: scores (0.2, 0.6, 2.0, 0.5) → weights (.10, .15, .61, .14). Masked (1.1, 0.3, −∞, −∞) → (.69, .31, 0, 0).
Q / K / V intuition (short-answer) Query: what the current token (whose output we're computing) is looking for. Key: what each token offers to be matched against; query·key = how relevant that token is. Value: the content (syntactic/semantic) that actually gets mixed in. Output for token i = weighted sum of values vj for j ≤ i.
Why divide by √dk?Dot products grow with dimension; large scores make softmax nearly one-hot (saturated) → tiny gradients.
Self vs. cross-attentionSelf: attend within the same sequence. Cross: attend to another sequence (decoder → encoder states).
Encoder-decoder (seq2seq) Encode the whole input, then decode the output using cross-attention to the encoder. Examples: translation, summarization, question answering, speech-to-text, grammar correction.

Multi-head attention dimensions very likely

  • Per-head size: dk = dv = d / H.
  • WQ(h), WK(h), WV(h) are each (d/H) × d (output dim × input dim).
  • Concatenate head outputs → size H·dv = d. Then WO ∈ ℝd × H·dv (here d × d).
  • d = 1024, H = 8 → WV = 128 × 1024. d = 768, H = 12 → 64 × 768.
  • Different layers may have different numbers of heads; not required to match. GQA: several query heads share one set of K/V heads (Llama 3: 32 query, 8 KV).

Transformer

  • "Attention Is All You Need" (2017) introduced scaled dot-product attention and the Transformer.
  • Block: multi-head self-attention → feedforward network (FFN ≈ 4d hidden, e.g. 3072 = 4 × 768). Each sublayer has a residual connection and LayerNorm.
  • LM: static token embeddings + positional embeddings → N blocks → LM head (linear + softmax over vocab).
  • Positional embeddings are required: attention is order-invariant. Learned or sinusoidal: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/100002i/d), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(…).
  • Causal mask: scores = −∞ for future tokens.
  • Why Transformers: parallel training over all positions; direct long-range connections (no memory decay, fewer vanishing gradients). Cost: O(n²) in sequence length vs. O(n) for RNNs.

Chomsky (1957)"Grammatical" ≠ "statistically likely": both "Colorless green ideas…" and "Furiously sleep ideas…" have ~0 corpus probability, yet only one is grammatical. Symbolic approach = Generative Grammar.
Rule-based NLUELIZA (Weizenbaum, 1967); grammar engineering (HPSG). Explicit rules, huge manual effort.
DisillusionmentHutchins (1979): MT "led astray" by formal linguistics. Jelinek: "Every time I fire a linguist, performance goes up." Statistical methods took over in the '80s–'90s.
