1. LM Basics: Probability, Surprisal, Perplexity

Spot itYou're given conditional probabilities and asked for P(sentence), surprisal, or perplexity.

Concept

  • A language model is a probability distribution over all strings Σ* (the Kleene closure: every finite string over the alphabet, including the empty string ε).
  • Autoregressive factorization (chain rule):
P(w) = P(EOS | w) · ∏i P(wi | w<i)
  • Surprisal S(w) = −log P(w). Rarer events are more surprising. In bits if log base 2.
  • Perplexity: PPLtotal = P(w)−1; PPLword = P(w)−1/N. Think "effective number of choices per word." Lower is better.
How to do it
  1. Write every factor, including P(w1 | ε) and the final P(EOS | …).
  2. Multiply.
  3. Surprisal = −log2(P) (or ln if asked for nats).
  4. Per-word PPL = P−1/N, N = number of tokens including EOS (the lecture counted EOS).
Worked example P(the | ε) = 0.5, P(dog | the) = 0.2, P(EOS | the dog) = 0.1
  • P = 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.01
  • Surprisal = −log2(0.01) = 6.64 bits
  • PPLtotal = 1/0.01 = 100; PPLword = 1001/3 = 4.64
Lecture example: P(the cat sat on the mat) = 5.04×10−9, log P = −19.1, PPLword (N=7) ≈ 15.3.
Why logs?Multiplying many small probabilities underflows to 0. Logs turn products into sums.
Why EOS?Without EOS, "the" and "the dog" aren't disjoint events (one is a prefix of the other), so probabilities wouldn't sum to 1. Ending every string in EOS makes them disjoint.
Traps
  • Forgetting EOS or the first P(w1 | ε) term.
  • "Higher perplexity = better" is false.
  • Probability reflects more than grammaticality: length, word frequency, plausibility, typicality. Compare minimal pairs to test grammaticality. (Under the ground-truth LM, ungrammatical sentences have higher surprisal than minimally different grammatical ones: True.)

Notation: substring yi:j (inclusive); prefix y<i = y1:i−1; suffix y>i = yi+1:|y|. A subsequence deletes symbols keeping order; a substring is a contiguous subsequence. A data domain (language, genre, dialect, register, topic) is defined by its ground-truth distribution; a corpus is a sample; an LM is an estimate.

2. Is This Factorization Valid? (Markov Assumption)

Spot it"Can we apply the Markov assumption…", "Is this a valid distribution?", or a new model that conditions on something unusual (e.g., the next word).

Concept

The chain rule is always exact, in any order:

P(w1w2w3) = P(w1) · P(w2 | w1) · P(w3 | w1w2) · P(EOS | w1w2w3)

The Markov assumption: the next event depends only on the current state (the last k words):

P(wi | w<i) = P(wi | wi−1)   (first order → bigram)

Substitute it into the chain rule and you get the n-gram model. Because it came from the chain rule, it is still a valid distribution.

How to do it
  1. Write the chain rule in some order (left-to-right, right-to-left, any permutation).
  2. Ask: does a Markov-style substitution turn each chain-rule term into the model's terms?
  3. Yes for some order → valid. No order works → not valid.
  4. Quick test: every chain-rule expansion has one term conditioned on nothing (the first factor). If every term in the model is conditioned on something, it can't come from the chain rule.
ModelValid?Why
Bigram ∏P(wi | wi−1)YesLeft-to-right chain rule + first-order Markov
Trigram ∏P(wi | wi−2wi−1)YesChain rule + second-order Markov
Right-to-left ∏P(wi | wi+1)YesChain rule in reverse order + Markov
Skip-gram ∏P(wi | wi−1, wi+1)NoEvery term conditions on 2 neighbors. No chain-rule order produces that, and nothing is left unconditioned.
Backoff (× λ)NoProbabilities don't sum to 1
Answer template "The chain rule gives P(w) = ∏P(wi | w<i) exactly. Under the Markov assumption each term becomes P(wi | wi−1), so the bigram product equals the joint distribution. For [model X], no ordering of the chain rule produces terms of the form [X's terms], because [e.g., every chain-rule expansion contains one term conditioned on nothing, but every X term is conditioned on two tokens], so it is not a valid factorization."
Why the autoregressive factorization? The model's parameters don't give P(w) directly; they give conditional next-word distributions. The chain rule turns those into a joint probability exactly. You could factorize in another order (e.g., right-to-left).

3. n-gram Estimation from Counts

Spot itA training corpus or a count / co-occurrence matrix, followed by "estimate P(…)".

Concept: maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE)

P(wi | wi−n+1:i−1) = C(wi−n+1:i) / C(wi−n+1:i−1)

In a count matrix: cell ÷ row sum. Rows = context wi; columns = next word wi+1.

An n-gram conditions on the previous n−1 words: unigram n=1 (no context), bigram n=2, trigram n=3.

How to do it (from a corpus)
  1. Add ε (BOS) at the start and EOS at the end of each sentence.
  2. Count every adjacent pair.
  3. For each context word, divide each next-word count by that word's total count as a context (the row sum).
  4. For a sequence: P(w1 | ε) × … × P(EOS | last word).

Why bigrams fail "The keys to the cabinet are/is…": a real LM uses P(· | the keys to the cabinet) and prefers "are". A bigram only sees P(· | cabinet) and prefers "is". Long-distance agreement, filler-gap dependencies, and coreference all break short contexts.

4. Laplace Smoothing, Sparsity, Backoff

Spot it"add-one", "Laplace", "smoothing", "unobserved n-grams", "sparsity".

Concept

  • Sparsity: most possible n-grams never appear in training, so their MLE probability is 0, and any new sentence containing one gets P = 0. There are |V|n possible n-grams: with |V| = 104, there are 1016 possible 4-grams. Larger n = better text but worse sparsity and roughly exponential memory.
  • Laplace (add-one) smoothing:
PLaplace(wi | wi−1) = (C(wi−1wi) + 1) / (C(wi−1) + |V|)

|V| = number of possible next tokens. Include EOS. Do not include ε/BOS (it can never be a next token).

How to do it
  1. Add 1 to every cell of the count table.
  2. Add |V| to each row sum.
  3. Divide.
  4. Check each row sums to 1.
Worked example Same counts as §3; |V| = 3 ({a, b, EOS}).
LaplaceabEOS
ε3/62/61/6
a2/73/72/7
b2/61/63/6
P(b b EOS) = 2/6 × 1/6 × 3/6 = 1/36 (it was 0 before smoothing).
How smoothing addresses sparsity Adds a pseudo-count of 1 to every possible n-gram so every n-gram gets a small non-zero probability. It removes some probability mass from observed n-grams and distributes it evenly over all possible continuations.
Limitations of add-one (essay answer)
  1. All unseen continuations of a context get the same probability, even though some are more plausible.
  2. A rare context (small row sum) hands a big share of probability to unseen words; a frequent context hands them very little (arguably reasonable: more "missed chances" to observe them).
  3. With a large |V|, too much mass moves away from the observed n-grams.

Other fixes

  • Backoff: if the n-gram is unseen, use the (n−1)-gram probability × λ, with 0 < λ < 1 (the shorter context is less specific, so discount it). Not a valid distribution.
  • <UNK>: keep the top-|V| words; map all others to <UNK>.
Why count-based estimation can't do P(wi | w<i) The context w<i has arbitrary length, so there are infinitely many possible contexts. Almost all are unobserved in a finite corpus, so counts are 0 (very sparse). That's why n-gram models cap the context at n−1 words, and why neural LMs are needed for unlimited context.

z is the logit (σ is the inverse of the log-odds function). In softmax regression, W is k × n and each row is one class's weight vector.

Sigmoid values to memorize σ(0) = 0.5 · σ(1) ≈ 0.73 · σ(2) ≈ 0.88 · σ(3) ≈ 0.95 · σ(−z) = 1 − σ(z)

Gradient descent

θ ← θ − η ∇θL      ∂L/∂wj = (ŷ − y) · xj      ∂L/∂b = ŷ − y

Multinomial: ∂L/∂wk,j = (ŷk − yk) xj. Bigger error or bigger feature → bigger step. Positive slope → decrease w; negative → increase; slope 0 = minimum. The logistic regression loss is convex (one minimum); neural network losses are not.

Worked example: one logistic regression step w = (2, −1), b = 0.5, x = (1, 3), true y = 1, η = 0.1
  1. z = 2·1 + (−1)·3 + 0.5 = −0.5
  2. ŷ = σ(−0.5) ≈ 0.378 → predicts class 0 (wrong)
  3. Loss = −ln(0.378) ≈ 0.97
  4. Error ŷ − y = −0.622 → grad w = (−0.622, −1.866), grad b = −0.622
  5. New w = (2, −1) − 0.1·(−0.622, −1.866) = (2.062, −0.813); new b = 0.562. The weights move to push z up, toward the correct class.
Worked example: softmax z = (2, 1, 0) → ez = (7.39, 2.72, 1), sum = 11.11 → softmax = (0.665, 0.245, 0.090)
Lecture examples House price: Model 2 (β0=300k, 400/sq ft, −1000/yr, +20k pool) predicts 665k, 2.695M, 1.099M. Squared error ≈ 1.0×1011 vs. ≈ 3.1×1011 for Model 1 → Model 2 is better.
Spam filter: Model 1 gives z = 11.8, 4.2, 3.5 → σ ≈ 1.0, 0.985, 0.97 (wrong on x(3), not spam). Model 2 gives z = 6.4, 3.9, 0.9 → σ ≈ 0.998, 0.98, 0.71 (closer on x(3)).
Batch, SGD, minibatch Batch GD uses the whole dataset per step (expensive). SGD uses one sample. Minibatch uses a small set: more stable than SGD, cheaper than full batch. Larger batches give a better estimate of the full-dataset gradient → more stable training.

6. MLP (Feedforward Network) by Hand

Spot itA diagram with input nodes, hidden nodes and weighted edges; "compute the output"; "rewrite with matrices".

Concept

unit: h = g(w·x + b)     layer: h = g(Wx + b)     two layers: y = g(W2 g(W1x + b1) + b2)

Row i of W holds the weights going into unit i. Shape of W = (#outputs × #inputs) = ni+1 × ni. The output layer is just multinomial logistic regression.

How to do it
  1. For each hidden unit: list incoming edges, multiply each by its input, sum (+ bias), apply g.
  2. Use those hidden values as inputs to the output unit; repeat.
  3. Matrix form: build W1 with one row per hidden unit, one column per input. Label each edge xj → Hi as W1[i, j].
Worked example: practice midterm (step function) x = (1, −2), g(a) = 1 if a > 0 else 0
  • H1 = g(1·2 + (−2)(−2)) = g(6) = 1
  • H2 = g(1·(−1) + (−2)·1) = g(−3) = 0
  • H3 = g(1·3 + (−2)·4) = g(−5) = 0
  • y = g(1·(−3) + 0·2 + 0·1) = g(−3) = 0
Matrix form: y = g( [−3  2  1] · g( [[2, −2], [−1, 1], [3, 4]] · [1, −2]T ) ), i.e. y = g(W2 g(W1x)), with W1 3×2 and W2 1×3.
Worked example: ReLU with biases x = (1, 2), W1 = [[1, −1], [0, 2]], b1 = (0, −1), W2 = [1, 2], b2 = −5
  • Pre-activations: (1 − 2 + 0, 0 + 4 − 1) = (−1, 3) → ReLU → h = (0, 3)
  • y = 1·0 + 2·3 − 5 = 1
  • Parameters: (2×2 + 2) + (1×2 + 1) = 9
SigmoidtanhReLUStep
Formula1/(1+e−a)tanh(a)max(0, a)1 if a > 0 else 0
Range(0, 1)(−1, 1)[0, ∞){0, 1}
Zero-centeredNoYesNoNo

Sparse / speedNo / slowNo / moderateYes / fast—
Why nonlinearity?U(Wx) = (UW)x = Vx: stacked linear layers collapse into one. U·g(Wx) doesn't collapse.
BackpropChain rule backward through the computation graph. At softmax + cross-entropy output, ∂L/∂z = ŷ − y; ∂L/∂Wout = (ŷ − y)hT.
XOR needs a hidden layer A single perceptron can learn AND and OR but not XOR: no straight line separates {(0,1),(1,0)} from {(0,0),(1,1)}. h1 = step(x1 + x2 − 0.5) (OR), h2 = step(x1 + x2 − 1.5) (AND), y = step(h1 − h2 − 0.5) ("OR and not AND"). Check: (1,0)→1 ✓ · (0,1)→1 ✓ · (1,1)→0 ✓ · (0,0)→0 ✓
Traps
  • Mixing up rows and columns of W.
  • Treating a = 0 as positive for the step function (g(0) = 0).
  • Applying g to a linear output layer, or forgetting it on the output when the question applies it.

7. Training-Loop Arithmetic

Spot it"batch size", "gradient accumulation", "sequence length", "updates", "epochs", "tokens seen".
Global batch = local batch × accumulation steps (× #GPUs)
Tokens per update = global batch × sequence length
Total tokens seen = updates × tokens per update
Epochs = total tokens seen ÷ dataset size (tokens)
How to do itWrite each quantity with its units and cancel them like a unit conversion. Use powers of 10.
Practice midterm 1000 updates, 10M-token dataset, local batch 10, 100 accumulation steps, sequence length 1000.
  • Global batch = 10 × 100 = 1000 samples
  • Tokens = 103 updates × 101 × 102 × 103 tokens/sample = 109 tokens
  • Epochs = 109 / 107 = 100
Variant Local batch 32, 8 accumulation steps, 4 GPUs, sequence length 2048, 500 updates, 1B-token dataset. Global batch = 32 × 8 × 4 = 1024 · tokens ≈ 500 × 1024 × 2048 ≈ 1.05×109 · epochs ≈ 1.05
Vocabulary Update / step = one optimizer step. Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several local batches before one update, simulating a big batch on limited GPU memory. Epoch = one full pass over the dataset.

8. Word Embeddings

Spot it"cosine", "analogy", "similar words", "word2vec/GloVe", "feature engineering vs. learning".
  • Distributional hypothesis: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps" (Firth 1957; Harris 1954).
  • Feature engineering (hand-made): interpretable and controllable, but laborious and brittle. Feature learning: minimal labor and generalizes, but not interpretable.
  • Count vectors: problems are (1) length = |V| and (2) sparsity.
  • GloVe: dense vectors with wi·wj ≈ log P(co-occurrence).
  • word2vec (skip-gram w/ negative sampling): binary classifier "do w and c co-occur within ±2 words?" P(+ | w, c) = σ(c·w). L = −[log σ(cpos·w) + Σ log σ(−cneg·w)], minimized over W and C with SGD.
  • Static (word2vec): one vector per word form ("bank" = "bank"). Contextual (RNN/Transformer outputs): the vector depends on the surrounding words.
cos θ = (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖)      analogy a : b :: c : ?  →  ? ≈ b − a + c
Worked examples a = (1, 2), b = (2, 1): a·b = 4, ‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = √5 → cos = 0.8.
man : king :: woman : ? → king − man + woman ≈ queen (find the nearest word by cosine).
Raw dot product favors longer vectors (often frequent words); cosine normalizes for length.

9. RNNs, Attention & Transformers

From words to sentences

Networks take fixed-size vectors. Sentences are infinite in number (no lookup table), vary in length, and vary in information content. Pooling (sum / mean / max) gives a fixed-length vector. "You can't cram the meaning of a whole sentence into a single vector!" (Mooney).

RNN & LSTM

Elman RNN (1990): ht = σ(Uxt + Vht−1 + b)    P(wt+1 | w≤t) = softmax(Wht + bo)
  • Problems: vanishing gradients (early tokens' influence shrinks exponentially) and sequential processing (can't parallelize on GPUs).
  • LSTM adds a memory cell and 3 gates (forget, input, output).
  • First neural LMs were RNNs; first pretrained foundation models were LSTMs (ULMFiT, ELMo, 2018). RNNs are more cognitively plausible.

Scaled dot-product attention

Spot itYou're given q, k, v vectors or scores and asked for an attention output.
qi = WQxi,  kj = WKxj,  vj = WVxj     sij = kjTqi / √dk     ai = softmax(si)     x′i = Σj aij vj
Matrix form: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKT / √dk) V
How to do it (for token i)
  1. Scores: dot qi with each allowed key kj (j ≤ i with a causal mask), divide by √dk.
  2. Masked positions get −∞ → weight 0.
  3. Softmax the scores → weights.
  4. Output = weighted sum of value vectors.
Worked example dk = 4 (√dk = 2). q2 = (1,0,1,0), k1 = (1,1,0,0), k2 = (2,0,2,0), v1 = (1,0), v2 = (0,1)
  • Dots: k1·q2 = 1, k2·q2 = 4 → scaled (0.5, 2)
  • Softmax: e0.5 = 1.65, e2 = 7.39, sum 9.04 → weights (0.18, 0.82)
  • Output = 0.18·v1 + 0.82·v2 = (0.18, 0.82)
  • Token 1 under the mask sees only itself → weight 1, output = v1.
Lecture: scores (0.2, 0.6, 2.0, 0.5) → weights (.10, .15, .61, .14). Masked (1.1, 0.3, −∞, −∞) → (.69, .31, 0, 0).
Q / K / V intuition (short-answer) Query: what the current token (whose output we're computing) is looking for. Key: what each token offers to be matched against; query·key = how relevant that token is. Value: the content (syntactic/semantic) that actually gets mixed in. Output for token i = weighted sum of values vj for j ≤ i.
Why divide by √dk?Dot products grow with dimension; large scores make softmax nearly one-hot (saturated) → tiny gradients.
Self vs. cross-attentionSelf: attend within the same sequence. Cross: attend to another sequence (decoder → encoder states).
Encoder-decoder (seq2seq) Encode the whole input, then decode the output using cross-attention to the encoder. Examples: translation, summarization, question answering, speech-to-text, grammar correction.

Multi-head attention dimensions very likely

  • Per-head size: dk = dv = d / H.
  • WQ(h), WK(h), WV(h) are each (d/H) × d (output dim × input dim).
  • Concatenate head outputs → size H·dv = d. Then WO ∈ ℝd × H·dv (here d × d).
  • d = 1024, H = 8 → WV = 128 × 1024. d = 768, H = 12 → 64 × 768.
  • Different layers may have different numbers of heads; not required to match. GQA: several query heads share one set of K/V heads (Llama 3: 32 query, 8 KV).

Transformer

  • "Attention Is All You Need" (2017) introduced scaled dot-product attention and the Transformer.
  • Block: multi-head self-attention → feedforward network (FFN ≈ 4d hidden, e.g. 3072 = 4 × 768). Each sublayer has a residual connection and LayerNorm.
  • LM: static token embeddings + positional embeddings → N blocks → LM head (linear + softmax over vocab).
  • Positional embeddings are required: attention is order-invariant. Learned or sinusoidal: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/100002i/d), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(…).
  • Causal mask: scores = −∞ for future tokens.
  • Why Transformers: parallel training over all positions; direct long-range connections (no memory decay, fewer vanishing gradients). Cost: O(n²) in sequence length vs. O(n) for RNNs.

10. Concepts & History (T/F and short answer)

IdeaWhat to know
Turing TestIf a judge can't reliably tell machine from human, the machine passes. Jones & Bergen (2025): LMs pass.
Chinese Room (Searle, 1980)Following symbol rules ≠ understanding.
Octopus Test (Bender & Koller, 2020)Learning from form alone gives no grounding/reference; fails on the novel bear situation.
Form / Reference / FunctionThree aspects of language understanding.
Formal vs. functional competence (Mahowald et al., 2024)Formal: "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously" is grammatical. Functional: it's nonsense.
Chomsky (1957)"Grammatical" ≠ "statistically likely": both "Colorless green ideas…" and "Furiously sleep ideas…" have ~0 corpus probability, yet only one is grammatical. Symbolic approach = Generative Grammar.
Rule-based NLUELIZA (Weizenbaum, 1967); grammar engineering (HPSG). Explicit rules, huge manual effort.
DisillusionmentHutchins (1979): MT "led astray" by formal linguistics. Jelinek: "Every time I fire a linguist, performance goes up." Statistical methods took over in the '80s–'90s.
ConnectionismPerceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958); Rumelhart (UCSD, backprop); past tense debate: Rumelhart & McClelland (1986) vs. Pinker & Prince (1988); Berko wug test (1958).
Distributional statisticsFirth (1957) / Harris (1954) → LSA (Deerwester, 1990) → word2vec (Mikolov, 2013).
Three eras of NLUTask-specific networks (early 2010s) → pretrain + fine-tune a foundation model (late 2010s) → prompting a single scaled model (2020s).
"Deep learning"Neural networks with many layers trained on data.

StatementAnswer

Without nonlinearities, a deep network equals one linear layer.T
Logistic regression's loss is convex.T
Transformer runtime grows linearly with sequence length.F (quadratic)
word2vec embeddings are contextual.F (static)
EOS is needed for PLM to sum to 1.T
A single perceptron can learn XOR.F

Watch for absolute words like "must", "always", "all" in T/F.

In the skip-gram formula every wi is conditioned on exactly two tokens, so the product can never be derived from the chain rule.

1. LM Basics: Probability, Surprisal, Perplexity

Spot itYou're given conditional probabilities and asked for P(sentence), surprisal, or perplexity.

Concept

  • A language model is a probability distribution over all strings Σ* (the Kleene closure: every finite string over the alphabet, including the empty string ε).
  • Autoregressive factorization (chain rule):
P(w) = P(EOS | w) · ∏i P(wi | w<i)
  • Surprisal S(w) = −log P(w). Rarer events are more surprising. In bits if log base 2.
  • Perplexity: PPLtotal = P(w)−1; PPLword = P(w)−1/N. Think "effective number of choices per word." Lower is better.
How to do it
  1. Write every factor, including P(w1 | ε) and the final P(EOS | …).
  2. Multiply.
  3. Surprisal = −log2(P) (or ln if asked for nats).
  4. Per-word PPL = P−1/N, N = number of tokens including EOS (the lecture counted EOS).
Worked example P(the | ε) = 0.5, P(dog | the) = 0.2, P(EOS | the dog) = 0.1
  • P = 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.01
  • Surprisal = −log2(0.01) = 6.64 bits
  • PPLtotal = 1/0.01 = 100; PPLword = 1001/3 = 4.64
Lecture example: P(the cat sat on the mat) = 5.04×10−9, log P = −19.1, PPLword (N=7) ≈ 15.3.
Why logs?Multiplying many small probabilities underflows to 0. Logs turn products into sums.
Why EOS?Without EOS, "the" and "the dog" aren't disjoint events (one is a prefix of the other), so probabilities wouldn't sum to 1. Ending every string in EOS makes them disjoint.
Traps
  • Forgetting EOS or the first P(w1 | ε) term.
  • "Higher perplexity = better" is false.
  • Probability reflects more than grammaticality: length, word frequency, plausibility, typicality. Compare minimal pairs to test grammaticality. (Under the ground-truth LM, ungrammatical sentences have higher surprisal than minimally different grammatical ones: True.)

Notation: substring yi:j (inclusive); prefix y<i = y1:i−1; suffix y>i = yi+1:|y|. A subsequence deletes symbols keeping order; a substring is a contiguous subsequence. A data domain (language, genre, dialect, register, topic) is defined by its ground-truth distribution; a corpus is a sample; an LM is an estimate.

2. Is This Factorization Valid? (Markov Assumption)

Spot it"Can we apply the Markov assumption…", "Is this a valid distribution?", or a new model that conditions on something unusual (e.g., the next word).

Concept

The chain rule is always exact, in any order:

P(w1w2w3) = P(w1) · P(w2 | w1) · P(w3 | w1w2) · P(EOS | w1w2w3)

The Markov assumption: the next event depends only on the current state (the last k words):

P(wi | w<i) = P(wi | wi−1)   (first order → bigram)

Substitute it into the chain rule and you get the n-gram model. Because it came from the chain rule, it is still a valid distribution.

How to do it
  1. Write the chain rule in some order (left-to-right, right-to-left, any permutation).
  2. Ask: does a Markov-style substitution turn each chain-rule term into the model's terms?
  3. Yes for some order → valid. No order works → not valid.
  4. Quick test: every chain-rule expansion has one term conditioned on nothing (the first factor). If every term in the model is conditioned on something, it can't come from the chain rule.
ModelValid?Why
Bigram ∏P(wi | wi−1)YesLeft-to-right chain rule + first-order Markov
Trigram ∏P(wi | wi−2wi−1)YesChain rule + second-order Markov
Right-to-left ∏P(wi | wi+1)YesChain rule in reverse order + Markov
Skip-gram ∏P(wi | wi−1, wi+1)NoEvery term conditions on 2 neighbors. No chain-rule order produces that, and nothing is left unconditioned.
Backoff (× λ)NoProbabilities don't sum to 1
Answer template "The chain rule gives P(w) = ∏P(wi | w<i) exactly. Under the Markov assumption each term becomes P(wi | wi−1), so the bigram product equals the joint distribution. For [model X], no ordering of the chain rule produces terms of the form [X's terms], because [e.g., every chain-rule expansion contains one term conditioned on nothing, but every X term is conditioned on two tokens], so it is not a valid factorization."
Why the autoregressive factorization? The model's parameters don't give P(w) directly; they give conditional next-word distributions. The chain rule turns those into a joint probability exactly. You could factorize in another order (e.g., right-to-left).

3. n-gram Estimation from Counts

Spot itA training corpus or a count / co-occurrence matrix, followed by "estimate P(…)".

Concept: maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE)

P(wi | wi−n+1:i−1) = C(wi−n+1:i) / C(wi−n+1:i−1)

In a count matrix: cell ÷ row sum. Rows = context wi; columns = next word wi+1.

An n-gram conditions on the previous n−1 words: unigram n=1 (no context), bigram n=2, trigram n=3.

How to do it (from a corpus)
  1. Add ε (BOS) at the start and EOS at the end of each sentence.
  2. Count every adjacent pair.
  3. For each context word, divide each next-word count by that word's total count as a context (the row sum).
  4. For a sequence: P(w1 | ε) × … × P(EOS | last word).

  • Missing a 0: once any factor is 0, the product is 0. Say so and stop.
  • Types vs. tokens: a type is a vocabulary entry; a token is one occurrence.
Why bigrams fail "The keys to the cabinet are/is…": a real LM uses P(· | the keys to the cabinet) and prefers "are". A bigram only sees P(· | cabinet) and prefers "is". Long-distance agreement, filler-gap dependencies, and coreference all break short contexts.

4. Laplace Smoothing, Sparsity, Backoff

Spot it"add-one", "Laplace", "smoothing", "unobserved n-grams", "sparsity".

Concept

  • Sparsity: most possible n-grams never appear in training, so their MLE probability is 0, and any new sentence containing one gets P = 0. There are |V|n possible n-grams: with |V| = 104, there are 1016 possible 4-grams. Larger n = better text but worse sparsity and roughly exponential memory.
  • Laplace (add-one) smoothing:
PLaplace(wi | wi−1) = (C(wi−1wi) + 1) / (C(wi−1) + |V|)

|V| = number of possible next tokens. Include EOS. Do not include ε/BOS (it can never be a next token).

How to do it
  1. Add 1 to every cell of the count table.
  2. Add |V| to each row sum.
  3. Divide.
  4. Check each row sums to 1.
Worked example Same counts as §3; |V| = 3 ({a, b, EOS}).
LaplaceabEOS
ε3/62/61/6
a2/73/72/7
b2/61/63/6
P(b b EOS) = 2/6 × 1/6 × 3/6 = 1/36 (it was 0 before smoothing).
How smoothing addresses sparsity Adds a pseudo-count of 1 to every possible n-gram so every n-gram gets a small non-zero probability. It removes some probability mass from observed n-grams and distributes it evenly over all possible continuations.
Limitations of add-one (essay answer)
  1. All unseen continuations of a context get the same probability, even though some are more plausible.
  2. A rare context (small row sum) hands a big share of probability to unseen words; a frequent context hands them very little (arguably reasonable: more "missed chances" to observe them).
  3. With a large |V|, too much mass moves away from the observed n-grams.

Other fixes

  • Backoff: if the n-gram is unseen, use the (n−1)-gram probability × λ, with 0 < λ < 1 (the shorter context is less specific, so discount it). Not a valid distribution.
  • <UNK>: keep the top-|V| words; map all others to <UNK>.
Why count-based estimation can't do P(wi | w<i) The context w<i has arbitrary length, so there are infinitely many possible contexts. Almost all are unobserved in a finite corpus, so counts are 0 (very sparse). That's why n-gram models cap the context at n−1 words, and why neural LMs are needed for unlimited context.

5. Linear & Logistic Regression, Softmax, Loss, Gradients

Spot it"predict a value", "classifier", "sigmoid", "logit", "loss", "update the weights", "bounded".
Linear regressionLogistic regressionMultinomial (softmax)
Outputw·x + bσ(w·x + b)softmax(Wx + b)
Range(−∞, ∞) unbounded(0, 1) boundedProbability vector over k classes
LossSquared error Σ(ŷ − y)²NLL: −log ŷtrueCross-entropy: −Σ yk log ŷk
UseHouse price, sentence complexitySpam? Is it English?Part of speech, next word
σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e−z)      softmax(z)i = ezi / Σj ezj

z is the logit (σ is the inverse of the log-odds function). In softmax regression, W is k × n and each row is one class's weight vector.

Sigmoid values to memorize σ(0) = 0.5 · σ(1) ≈ 0.73 · σ(2) ≈ 0.88 · σ(3) ≈ 0.95 · σ(−z) = 1 − σ(z)

Gradient descent

θ ← θ − η ∇θL      ∂L/∂wj = (ŷ − y) · xj      ∂L/∂b = ŷ − y

Multinomial: ∂L/∂wk,j = (ŷk − yk) xj. Bigger error or bigger feature → bigger step. Positive slope → decrease w; negative → increase; slope 0 = minimum. The logistic regression loss is convex (one minimum); neural network losses are not.

Worked example: one logistic regression step w = (2, −1), b = 0.5, x = (1, 3), true y = 1, η = 0.1
  1. z = 2·1 + (−1)·3 + 0.5 = −0.5
  2. ŷ = σ(−0.5) ≈ 0.378 → predicts class 0 (wrong)
  3. Loss = −ln(0.378) ≈ 0.97
  4. Error ŷ − y = −0.622 → grad w = (−0.622, −1.866), grad b = −0.622
  5. New w = (2, −1) − 0.1·(−0.622, −1.866) = (2.062, −0.813); new b = 0.562. The weights move to push z up, toward the correct class.
Worked example: softmax z = (2, 1, 0) → ez = (7.39, 2.72, 1), sum = 11.11 → softmax = (0.665, 0.245, 0.090)
Lecture examples House price: Model 2 (β0=300k, 400/sq ft, −1000/yr, +20k pool) predicts 665k, 2.695M, 1.099M. Squared error ≈ 1.0×1011 vs. ≈ 3.1×1011 for Model 1 → Model 2 is better.
Spam filter: Model 1 gives z = 11.8, 4.2, 3.5 → σ ≈ 1.0, 0.985, 0.97 (wrong on x(3), not spam). Model 2 gives z = 6.4, 3.9, 0.9 → σ ≈ 0.998, 0.98, 0.71 (closer on x(3)).
Batch, SGD, minibatch Batch GD uses the whole dataset per step (expensive). SGD uses one sample. Minibatch uses a small set: more stable than SGD, cheaper than full batch. Larger batches give a better estimate of the full-dataset gradient → more stable training.

6. MLP (Feedforward Network) by Hand

Spot itA diagram with input nodes, hidden nodes and weighted edges; "compute the output"; "rewrite with matrices".

Concept

unit: h = g(w·x + b)     layer: h = g(Wx + b)     two layers: y = g(W2 g(W1x + b1) + b2)

Row i of W holds the weights going into unit i. Shape of W = (#outputs × #inputs) = ni+1 × ni. The output layer is just multinomial logistic regression.

How to do it
  1. For each hidden unit: list incoming edges, multiply each by its input, sum (+ bias), apply g.
  2. Use those hidden values as inputs to the output unit; repeat.
  3. Matrix form: build W1 with one row per hidden unit, one column per input. Label each edge xj → Hi as W1[i, j].
Worked example: practice midterm (step function) x = (1, −2), g(a) = 1 if a > 0 else 0
  • H1 = g(1·2 + (−2)(−2)) = g(6) = 1
  • H2 = g(1·(−1) + (−2)·1) = g(−3) = 0
  • H3 = g(1·3 + (−2)·4) = g(−5) = 0
  • y = g(1·(−3) + 0·2 + 0·1) = g(−3) = 0
Matrix form: y = g( [−3  2  1] · g( [[2, −2], [−1, 1], [3, 4]] · [1, −2]T ) ), i.e. y = g(W2 g(W1x)), with W1 3×2 and W2 1×3.
Worked example: ReLU with biases x = (1, 2), W1 = [[1, −1], [0, 2]], b1 = (0, −1), W2 = [1, 2], b2 = −5
  • Pre-activations: (1 − 2 + 0, 0 + 4 − 1) = (−1, 3) → ReLU → h = (0, 3)
  • y = 1·0 + 2·3 − 5 = 1
  • Parameters: (2×2 + 2) + (1×2 + 1) = 9
SigmoidtanhReLUStep
Formula1/(1+e−a)tanh(a)max(0, a)1 if a > 0 else 0
Range(0, 1)(−1, 1)[0, ∞){0, 1}
Zero-centeredNoYesNoNo
SaturatesBoth endsBoth endsa ≤ 0—
Vanishing gradientSevereModerateMinimal—
Sparse / speedNo / slowNo / moderateYes / fast—
Why nonlinearity?U(Wx) = (UW)x = Vx: stacked linear layers collapse into one. U·g(Wx) doesn't collapse.
BackpropChain rule backward through the computation graph. At softmax + cross-entropy output, ∂L/∂z = ŷ − y; ∂L/∂Wout = (ŷ − y)hT.
XOR needs a hidden layer A single perceptron can learn AND and OR but not XOR: no straight line separates {(0,1),(1,0)} from {(0,0),(1,1)}. h1 = step(x1 + x2 − 0.5) (OR), h2 = step(x1 + x2 − 1.5) (AND), y = step(h1 − h2 − 0.5) ("OR and not AND"). Check: (1,0)→1 ✓ · (0,1)→1 ✓ · (1,1)→0 ✓ · (0,0)→0 ✓
Traps
  • Mixing up rows and columns of W.
  • Treating a = 0 as positive for the step function (g(0) = 0).
  • Applying g to a linear output layer, or forgetting it on the output when the question applies it.

7. Training-Loop Arithmetic

Spot it"batch size", "gradient accumulation", "sequence length", "updates", "epochs", "tokens seen".
Global batch = local batch × accumulation steps (× #GPUs)
Tokens per update = global batch × sequence length
Total tokens seen = updates × tokens per update
Epochs = total tokens seen ÷ dataset size (tokens)
How to do itWrite each quantity with its units and cancel them like a unit conversion. Use powers of 10.
Practice midterm 1000 updates, 10M-token dataset, local batch 10, 100 accumulation steps, sequence length 1000.
  • Global batch = 10 × 100 = 1000 samples
  • Tokens = 103 updates × 101 × 102 × 103 tokens/sample = 109 tokens
  • Epochs = 109 / 107 = 100
Variant Local batch 32, 8 accumulation steps, 4 GPUs, sequence length 2048, 500 updates, 1B-token dataset. Global batch = 32 × 8 × 4 = 1024 · tokens ≈ 500 × 1024 × 2048 ≈ 1.05×109 · epochs ≈ 1.05
Vocabulary Update / step = one optimizer step. Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several local batches before one update, simulating a big batch on limited GPU memory. Epoch = one full pass over the dataset.

8. Word Embeddings

Spot it"cosine", "analogy", "similar words", "word2vec/GloVe", "feature engineering vs. learning".
  • Distributional hypothesis: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps" (Firth 1957; Harris 1954).
  • Feature engineering (hand-made): interpretable and controllable, but laborious and brittle. Feature learning: minimal labor and generalizes, but not interpretable.
  • Count vectors: problems are (1) length = |V| and (2) sparsity.
  • GloVe: dense vectors with wi·wj ≈ log P(co-occurrence).
  • word2vec (skip-gram w/ negative sampling): binary classifier "do w and c co-occur within ±2 words?" P(+ | w, c) = σ(c·w). L = −[log σ(cpos·w) + Σ log σ(−cneg·w)], minimized over W and C with SGD.
  • Static (word2vec): one vector per word form ("bank" = "bank"). Contextual (RNN/Transformer outputs): the vector depends on the surrounding words.
cos θ = (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖)      analogy a : b :: c : ?  →  ? ≈ b − a + c
Worked examples a = (1, 2), b = (2, 1): a·b = 4, ‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = √5 → cos = 0.8.
man : king :: woman : ? → king − man + woman ≈ queen (find the nearest word by cosine).
Raw dot product favors longer vectors (often frequent words); cosine normalizes for length.

9. RNNs, Attention & Transformers

From words to sentences

Networks take fixed-size vectors. Sentences are infinite in number (no lookup table), vary in length, and vary in information content. Pooling (sum / mean / max) gives a fixed-length vector. "You can't cram the meaning of a whole sentence into a single vector!" (Mooney).

RNN & LSTM

Elman RNN (1990): ht = σ(Uxt + Vht−1 + b)    P(wt+1 | w≤t) = softmax(Wht + bo)
  • Problems: vanishing gradients (early tokens' influence shrinks exponentially) and sequential processing (can't parallelize on GPUs).
  • LSTM adds a memory cell and 3 gates (forget, input, output).
  • First neural LMs were RNNs; first pretrained foundation models were LSTMs (ULMFiT, ELMo, 2018). RNNs are more cognitively plausible.

Scaled dot-product attention

Spot itYou're given q, k, v vectors or scores and asked for an attention output.
qi = WQxi,  kj = WKxj,  vj = WVxj     sij = kjTqi / √dk     ai = softmax(si)     x′i = Σj aij vj
Matrix form: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKT / √dk) V
How to do it (for token i)
  1. Scores: dot qi with each allowed key kj (j ≤ i with a causal mask), divide by √dk.
  2. Masked positions get −∞ → weight 0.
  3. Softmax the scores → weights.
  4. Output = weighted sum of value vectors.
Worked example dk = 4 (√dk = 2). q2 = (1,0,1,0), k1 = (1,1,0,0), k2 = (2,0,2,0), v1 = (1,0), v2 = (0,1)
  • Dots: k1·q2 = 1, k2·q2 = 4 → scaled (0.5, 2)
  • Softmax: e0.5 = 1.65, e2 = 7.39, sum 9.04 → weights (0.18, 0.82)
  • Output = 0.18·v1 + 0.82·v2 = (0.18, 0.82)
  • Token 1 under the mask sees only itself → weight 1, output = v1.
Lecture: scores (0.2, 0.6, 2.0, 0.5) → weights (.10, .15, .61, .14). Masked (1.1, 0.3, −∞, −∞) → (.69, .31, 0, 0).
Q / K / V intuition (short-answer) Query: what the current token (whose output we're computing) is looking for. Key: what each token offers to be matched against; query·key = how relevant that token is. Value: the content (syntactic/semantic) that actually gets mixed in. Output for token i = weighted sum of values vj for j ≤ i.
Why divide by √dk?Dot products grow with dimension; large scores make softmax nearly one-hot (saturated) → tiny gradients.
Self vs. cross-attentionSelf: attend within the same sequence. Cross: attend to another sequence (decoder → encoder states).
Encoder-decoder (seq2seq) Encode the whole input, then decode the output using cross-attention to the encoder. Examples: translation, summarization, question answering, speech-to-text, grammar correction.

Multi-head attention dimensions very likely

  • Per-head size: dk = dv = d / H.
  • WQ(h), WK(h), WV(h) are each (d/H) × d (output dim × input dim).
  • Concatenate head outputs → size H·dv = d. Then WO ∈ ℝd × H·dv (here d × d).
  • d = 1024, H = 8 → WV = 128 × 1024. d = 768, H = 12 → 64 × 768.
  • Different layers may have different numbers of heads; not required to match. GQA: several query heads share one set of K/V heads (Llama 3: 32 query, 8 KV).

Transformer

  • "Attention Is All You Need" (2017) introduced scaled dot-product attention and the Transformer.
  • Block: multi-head self-attention → feedforward network (FFN ≈ 4d hidden, e.g. 3072 = 4 × 768). Each sublayer has a residual connection and LayerNorm.
  • LM: static token embeddings + positional embeddings → N blocks → LM head (linear + softmax over vocab).
  • Positional embeddings are required: attention is order-invariant. Learned or sinusoidal: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/100002i/d), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(…).
  • Causal mask: scores = −∞ for future tokens.
  • Why Transformers: parallel training over all positions; direct long-range connections (no memory decay, fewer vanishing gradients). Cost: O(n²) in sequence length vs. O(n) for RNNs.

10. Concepts & History (T/F and short answer)

IdeaWhat to know
Turing TestIf a judge can't reliably tell machine from human, the machine passes. Jones & Bergen (2025): LMs pass.
Chinese Room (Searle, 1980)Following symbol rules ≠ understanding.
Octopus Test (Bender & Koller, 2020)Learning from form alone gives no grounding/reference; fails on the novel bear situation.
Form / Reference / FunctionThree aspects of language understanding.
Formal vs. functional competence (Mahowald et al., 2024)Formal: "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously" is grammatical. Functional: it's nonsense.
Chomsky (1957)"Grammatical" ≠ "statistically likely": both "Colorless green ideas…" and "Furiously sleep ideas…" have ~0 corpus probability, yet only one is grammatical. Symbolic approach = Generative Grammar.
Rule-based NLUELIZA (Weizenbaum, 1967); grammar engineering (HPSG). Explicit rules, huge manual effort.
DisillusionmentHutchins (1979): MT "led astray" by formal linguistics. Jelinek: "Every time I fire a linguist, performance goes up." Statistical methods took over in the '80s–'90s.
ConnectionismPerceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958); Rumelhart (UCSD, backprop); past tense debate: Rumelhart & McClelland (1986) vs. Pinker & Prince (1988); Berko wug test (1958).
Distributional statisticsFirth (1957) / Harris (1954) → LSA (Deerwester, 1990) → word2vec (Mikolov, 2013).
Three eras of NLUTask-specific networks (early 2010s) → pretrain + fine-tune a foundation model (late 2010s) → prompting a single scaled model (2020s).
"Deep learning"Neural networks with many layers trained on data.

True/False traps

StatementAnswer

All Transformer layers must have the same number of heads.F
Transformers need positional encodings to know token order.T
Ungrammatical sentences have higher surprisal than minimal grammatical pairs (ground-truth LM).T
Backoff gives a valid probability distribution.F
Without nonlinearities, a deep network equals one linear layer.T
Logistic regression's loss is convex.T
Transformer runtime grows linearly with sequence length.F (quadratic)
word2vec embeddings are contextual.F (static)
EOS is needed for PLM to sum to 1.T
A single perceptron can learn XOR.F

Watch for absolute words like "must", "always", "all" in T/F.

Section 6: skip-gram LM

Pskipgram(w) = ∏i=1|w| P(wi | wi−1, wi+1),   w0 = BOS, w|w|+1 = EOS

Can the Markov assumption make this valid? No. The Markov assumption substitutes P(wi | w<i) = P(wi | wi−1) into chain-rule terms. Every chain-rule factorization, in any order, ends up with a "singleton" term conditioned on nothing (for bigrams, P(w1 | BOS)). In the skip-gram formula every wi is conditioned on exactly two tokens, so the product can never be derived from the chain rule.

1. LM Basics: Probability, Surprisal, Perplexity

Spot itYou're given conditional probabilities and asked for P(sentence), surprisal, or perplexity.

Concept

  • A language model is a probability distribution over all strings Σ* (the Kleene closure: every finite string over the alphabet, including the empty string ε).
  • Autoregressive factorization (chain rule):
P(w) = P(EOS | w) · ∏i P(wi | w<i)
  • Surprisal S(w) = −log P(w). Rarer events are more surprising. In bits if log base 2.
  • Perplexity: PPLtotal = P(w)−1; PPLword = P(w)−1/N. Think "effective number of choices per word." Lower is better.
How to do it
  1. Write every factor, including P(w1 | ε) and the final P(EOS | …).
  2. Multiply.
  3. Surprisal = −log2(P) (or ln if asked for nats).
  4. Per-word PPL = P−1/N, N = number of tokens including EOS (the lecture counted EOS).
Worked example P(the | ε) = 0.5, P(dog | the) = 0.2, P(EOS | the dog) = 0.1
  • P = 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.01
  • Surprisal = −log2(0.01) = 6.64 bits
  • PPLtotal = 1/0.01 = 100; PPLword = 1001/3 = 4.64
Lecture example: P(the cat sat on the mat) = 5.04×10−9, log P = −19.1, PPLword (N=7) ≈ 15.3.
Why logs?Multiplying many small probabilities underflows to 0. Logs turn products into sums.
Why EOS?Without EOS, "the" and "the dog" aren't disjoint events (one is a prefix of the other), so probabilities wouldn't sum to 1. Ending every string in EOS makes them disjoint.
Traps
  • Forgetting EOS or the first P(w1 | ε) term.
  • "Higher perplexity = better" is false.
  • Probability reflects more than grammaticality: length, word frequency, plausibility, typicality. Compare minimal pairs to test grammaticality. (Under the ground-truth LM, ungrammatical sentences have higher surprisal than minimally different grammatical ones: True.)

Notation: substring yi:j (inclusive); prefix y<i = y1:i−1; suffix y>i = yi+1:|y|. A subsequence deletes symbols keeping order; a substring is a contiguous subsequence. A data domain (language, genre, dialect, register, topic) is defined by its ground-truth distribution; a corpus is a sample; an LM is an estimate.

2. Is This Factorization Valid? (Markov Assumption)

Spot it"Can we apply the Markov assumption…", "Is this a valid distribution?", or a new model that conditions on something unusual (e.g., the next word).

Concept

The chain rule is always exact, in any order:

P(w1w2w3) = P(w1) · P(w2 | w1) · P(w3 | w1w2) · P(EOS | w1w2w3)

The Markov assumption: the next event depends only on the current state (the last k words):

P(wi | w<i) = P(wi | wi−1)   (first order → bigram)

Substitute it into the chain rule and you get the n-gram model. Because it came from the chain rule, it is still a valid distribution.

How to do it
  1. Write the chain rule in some order (left-to-right, right-to-left, any permutation).
  2. Ask: does a Markov-style substitution turn each chain-rule term into the model's terms?
  3. Yes for some order → valid. No order works → not valid.
  4. Quick test: every chain-rule expansion has one term conditioned on nothing (the first factor). If every term in the model is conditioned on something, it can't come from the chain rule.
ModelValid?Why
Bigram ∏P(wi | wi−1)YesLeft-to-right chain rule + first-order Markov
Trigram ∏P(wi | wi−2wi−1)YesChain rule + second-order Markov
Right-to-left ∏P(wi | wi+1)YesChain rule in reverse order + Markov
Skip-gram ∏P(wi | wi−1, wi+1)NoEvery term conditions on 2 neighbors. No chain-rule order produces that, and nothing is left unconditioned.
Backoff (× λ)NoProbabilities don't sum to 1
Answer template "The chain rule gives P(w) = ∏P(wi | w<i) exactly. Under the Markov assumption each term becomes P(wi | wi−1), so the bigram product equals the joint distribution. For [model X], no ordering of the chain rule produces terms of the form [X's terms], because [e.g., every chain-rule expansion contains one term conditioned on nothing, but every X term is conditioned on two tokens], so it is not a valid factorization."
Why the autoregressive factorization? The model's parameters don't give P(w) directly; they give conditional next-word distributions. The chain rule turns those into a joint probability exactly. You could factorize in another order (e.g., right-to-left).

3. n-gram Estimation from Counts

Spot itA training corpus or a count / co-occurrence matrix, followed by "estimate P(…)".

Concept: maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE)

P(wi | wi−n+1:i−1) = C(wi−n+1:i) / C(wi−n+1:i−1)

In a count matrix: cell ÷ row sum. Rows = context wi; columns = next word wi+1.

An n-gram conditions on the previous n−1 words: unigram n=1 (no context), bigram n=2, trigram n=3.

How to do it (from a corpus)
  1. Add ε (BOS) at the start and EOS at the end of each sentence.
  2. Count every adjacent pair.
  3. For each context word, divide each next-word count by that word's total count as a context (the row sum).
  4. For a sequence: P(w1 | ε) × … × P(EOS | last word).

Why bigrams fail "The keys to the cabinet are/is…": a real LM uses P(· | the keys to the cabinet) and prefers "are". A bigram only sees P(· | cabinet) and prefers "is". Long-distance agreement, filler-gap dependencies, and coreference all break short contexts.

4. Laplace Smoothing, Sparsity, Backoff

Spot it"add-one", "Laplace", "smoothing", "unobserved n-grams", "sparsity".

Concept

  • Sparsity: most possible n-grams never appear in training, so their MLE probability is 0, and any new sentence containing one gets P = 0. There are |V|n possible n-grams: with |V| = 104, there are 1016 possible 4-grams. Larger n = better text but worse sparsity and roughly exponential memory.
  • Laplace (add-one) smoothing:
PLaplace(wi | wi−1) = (C(wi−1wi) + 1) / (C(wi−1) + |V|)

|V| = number of possible next tokens. Include EOS. Do not include ε/BOS (it can never be a next token).

How to do it
  1. Add 1 to every cell of the count table.
  2. Add |V| to each row sum.
  3. Divide.
  4. Check each row sums to 1.
Worked example Same counts as §3; |V| = 3 ({a, b, EOS}).
LaplaceabEOS
ε3/62/61/6
a2/73/72/7

P(b b EOS) = 2/6 × 1/6 × 3/6 = 1/36 (it was 0 before smoothing).
How smoothing addresses sparsity Adds a pseudo-count of 1 to every possible n-gram so every n-gram gets a small non-zero probability. It removes some probability mass from observed n-grams and distributes it evenly over all possible continuations.
Limitations of add-one (essay answer)
  1. All unseen continuations of a context get the same probability, even though some are more plausible.
  2. A rare context (small row sum) hands a big share of probability to unseen words; a frequent context hands them very little (arguably reasonable: more "missed chances" to observe them).
  3. With a large |V|, too much mass moves away from the observed n-grams.

Other fixes

  • Backoff: if the n-gram is unseen, use the (n−1)-gram probability × λ, with 0 < λ < 1 (the shorter context is less specific, so discount it). Not a valid distribution.
  • <UNK>: keep the top-|V| words; map all others to <UNK>.
Why count-based estimation can't do P(wi | w<i) The context w<i has arbitrary length, so there are infinitely many possible contexts. Almost all are unobserved in a finite corpus, so counts are 0 (very sparse). That's why n-gram models cap the context at n−1 words, and why neural LMs are needed for unlimited context.

Batch, SGD, minibatch Batch GD uses the whole dataset per step (expensive). SGD uses one sample. Minibatch uses a small set: more stable than SGD, cheaper than full batch. Larger batches give a better estimate of the full-dataset gradient → more stable training.

6. MLP (Feedforward Network) by Hand

Spot itA diagram with input nodes, hidden nodes and weighted edges; "compute the output"; "rewrite with matrices".

Concept

unit: h = g(w·x + b)     layer: h = g(Wx + b)     two layers: y = g(W2 g(W1x + b1) + b2)

Row i of W holds the weights going into unit i. Shape of W = (#outputs × #inputs) = ni+1 × ni. The output layer is just multinomial logistic regression.

How to do it
  1. For each hidden unit: list incoming edges, multiply each by its input, sum (+ bias), apply g.
  2. Use those hidden values as inputs to the output unit; repeat.
  3. Matrix form: build W1 with one row per hidden unit, one column per input. Label each edge xj → Hi as W1[i, j].
Worked example: practice midterm (step function) x = (1, −2), g(a) = 1 if a > 0 else 0

  • y = g(1·(−3) + 0·2 + 0·1) = g(−3) = 0

Practice midterm 1000 updates, 10M-token dataset, local batch 10, 100 accumulation steps, sequence length 1000.

8. Word Embeddings

Spot it"cosine", "analogy", "similar words", "word2vec/GloVe", "feature engineering vs. learning".
  • Distributional hypothesis: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps" (Firth 1957; Harris 1954).
  • Feature engineering (hand-made): interpretable and controllable, but laborious and brittle. Feature learning: minimal labor and generalizes, but not interpretable.
  • Count vectors: problems are (1) length = |V| and (2) sparsity.
  • GloVe: dense vectors with wi·wj ≈ log P(co-occurrence).
  • word2vec (skip-gram w/ negative sampling): binary classifier "do w and c co-occur within ±2 words?" P(+ | w, c) = σ(c·w). L = −[log σ(cpos·w) + Σ log σ(−cneg·w)], minimized over W and C with SGD.
  • Static (word2vec): one vector per word form ("bank" = "bank"). Contextual (RNN/Transformer outputs): the vector depends on the surrounding words.
cos θ = (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖)      analogy a : b :: c : ?  →  ? ≈ b − a + c
Worked examples a = (1, 2), b = (2, 1): a·b = 4, ‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = √5 → cos = 0.8.
man : king :: woman : ? → king − man + woman ≈ queen (find the nearest word by cosine).
Raw dot product favors longer vectors (often frequent words); cosine normalizes for length.

9. RNNs, Attention & Transformers

From words to sentences

Networks take fixed-size vectors. Sentences are infinite in number (no lookup table), vary in length, and vary in information content. Pooling (sum / mean / max) gives a fixed-length vector. "You can't cram the meaning of a whole sentence into a single vector!" (Mooney).

RNN & LSTM

Elman RNN (1990): ht = σ(Uxt + Vht−1 + b)    P(wt+1 | w≤t) = softmax(Wht + bo)
  • Problems: vanishing gradients (early tokens' influence shrinks exponentially) and sequential processing (can't parallelize on GPUs).
  • LSTM adds a memory cell and 3 gates (forget, input, output).
  • First neural LMs were RNNs; first pretrained foundation models were LSTMs (ULMFiT, ELMo, 2018). RNNs are more cognitively plausible.

Scaled dot-product attention

Spot itYou're given q, k, v vectors or scores and asked for an attention output.
qi = WQxi,  kj = WKxj,  vj = WVxj     sij = kjTqi / √dk     ai = softmax(si)     x′i = Σj aij vj
Matrix form: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKT / √dk) V
How to do it (for token i)
  1. Scores: dot qi with each allowed key kj (j ≤ i with a causal mask), divide by √dk.
  2. Masked positions get −∞ → weight 0.
  3. Softmax the scores → weights.
  4. Output = weighted sum of value vectors.
Worked example dk = 4 (√dk = 2). q2 = (1,0,1,0), k1 = (1,1,0,0), k2 = (2,0,2,0), v1 = (1,0), v2 = (0,1)
  • Dots: k1·q2 = 1, k2·q2 = 4 → scaled (0.5, 2)
  • Softmax: e0.5 = 1.65, e2 = 7.39, sum 9.04 → weights (0.18, 0.82)
  • Output = 0.18·v1 + 0.82·v2 = (0.18, 0.82)
  • Token 1 under the mask sees only itself → weight 1, output = v1.
Lecture: scores (0.2, 0.6, 2.0, 0.5) → weights (.10, .15, .61, .14). Masked (1.1, 0.3, −∞, −∞) → (.69, .31, 0, 0).
Q / K / V intuition (short-answer) Query: what the current token (whose output we're computing) is looking for. Key: what each token offers to be matched against; query·key = how relevant that token is. Value: the content (syntactic/semantic) that actually gets mixed in. Output for token i = weighted sum of values vj for j ≤ i.
Why divide by √dk?Dot products grow with dimension; large scores make softmax nearly one-hot (saturated) → tiny gradients.
Self vs. cross-attentionSelf: attend within the same sequence. Cross: attend to another sequence (decoder → encoder states).
Encoder-decoder (seq2seq) Encode the whole input, then decode the output using cross-attention to the encoder. Examples: translation, summarization, question answering, speech-to-text, grammar correction.

Multi-head attention dimensions very likely

  • Per-head size: dk = dv = d / H.
  • WQ(h), WK(h), WV(h) are each (d/H) × d (output dim × input dim).
  • Concatenate head outputs → size H·dv = d. Then WO ∈ ℝd × H·dv (here d × d).
  • d = 1024, H = 8 → WV = 128 × 1024. d = 768, H = 12 → 64 × 768.
  • Different layers may have different numbers of heads; not required to match. GQA: several query heads share one set of K/V heads (Llama 3: 32 query, 8 KV).

Transformer

  • "Attention Is All You Need" (2017) introduced scaled dot-product attention and the Transformer.
  • Block: multi-head self-attention → feedforward network (FFN ≈ 4d hidden, e.g. 3072 = 4 × 768). Each sublayer has a residual connection and LayerNorm.
  • LM: static token embeddings + positional embeddings → N blocks → LM head (linear + softmax over vocab).
  • Positional embeddings are required: attention is order-invariant. Learned or sinusoidal: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/100002i/d), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(…).
  • Causal mask: scores = −∞ for future tokens.
  • Why Transformers: parallel training over all positions; direct long-range connections (no memory decay, fewer vanishing gradients). Cost: O(n²) in sequence length vs. O(n) for RNNs.

Section 6: skip-gram LM

Pskipgram(w) = ∏i=1|w| P(wi | wi−1, wi+1),   w0 = BOS, w|w|+1 = EOS

Can the Markov assumption make this valid? No. The Markov assumption substitutes P(wi | w<i) = P(wi | wi−1) into chain-rule terms. Every chain-rule factorization, in any order, ends up with a "singleton" term conditioned on nothing (for bigrams, P(w1 | BOS)). In the skip-gram formula every wi is conditioned on exactly two tokens, so the product can never be derived from the chain rule.

content.text:
# Smoothing

## The problem it solves
An n-gram model learns probabilities by counting:

  P(next | context) = count(context, next) / count(context)

Most word pairs never appear in a finite training corpus. Their count is 0, so their probability is 0.

A single zero makes the whole sentence's probability zero, because the sentence probability is a product:

  P(sentence) = P(w₁|ε) × P(w₂|w₁) × … × **0** × … = **0**

So a perfectly reasonable new sentence can be marked as impossible just because one word pair never showed up in training. That's the **sparsity problem**. It gets worse as n grows, because there are |V|ⁿ possible n-grams and most of them are never seen.

**Smoothing** fixes this by giving every unseen n-gram a small non-zero probability.

## Laplace (add-one) smoothing
Pretend you saw every possible next word **one extra time**:

  P_Laplace(next | context) = (count(context, next) **+ 1**) / (count(context) **+ |V|**)

- The **+1 on top** is a fake count for every possible next word, including the ones never seen.
- The **+|V| on the bottom** keeps each row summing to 1. You added 1 to each of the |V| cells, so the row total grows by |V|.
- **|V| = the number of possible next tokens.** Include EOS. Don't include ε/BOS, because nothing can ever be followed *by* the start symbol.

## Worked example
After the word "b", the training counts are:

| next → | a | b | EOS | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| count | 1 | 0 | 2 | 3 |
| **MLE** | 1/3 | **0** | 2/3 | |
| **+1** | 2 | 1 | 3 | 3 + 3 = 6 |
| **Laplace** | 2/6 | **1/6** | 3/6 | |

- "b b" went from **0 → 1/6**, so it's no longer impossible.
- The seen continuations went **down**: a dropped from 1/3 to 2/6 (no change here), and EOS dropped from 2/3 to 1/2.

**Intuition:** smoothing takes some probability mass from the n-grams you've seen and spreads it evenly over the ones you haven't. The total stays 1; it just gets redistributed.

## How much it changes things depends on the row size
| Context | Row count | Unseen word gets | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rare word (seen 3 times) | 3 | 1/(3 + \|V\|) | **Big** share for unseen words. The real data is mostly drowned out. |
| Frequent word (seen 10,000 times) | 10,000 | 1/(10,000 + \|V\|) | Tiny share. The real counts dominate. |

This is reasonable in one sense: for a frequent context, you had many chances to see a continuation and didn't, so it really is probably unlikely.

## Limitations (a likely exam question)
1. **Every unseen continuation gets the same probability.** "the cat **purred**" and "the cat **photosynthesized**" both get 1/(count + |V|), even though one is clearly more plausible.
2. **Rare contexts get over-smoothed.** Their few real observations are swamped by the fake counts.
3. **A big vocabulary moves too much mass.** With |V| = 50,000, the row total grows by 50,000 for *every* context, so the observed n-grams lose a large share of their probability.

## Related fixes from lecture
- **Backoff:** if the trigram is unseen, use the bigram probability (× λ, where 0 < λ < 1). This is smarter than giving equal shares, because it uses the shorter context's information. But it's **not a valid probability distribution**: the probabilities don't sum to 1.
- **`<UNK>`:** handles *unknown words* rather than unseen *combinations*. Keep the top |V| words and map every other word to `<UNK>`.

## How to answer smoothing questions
- **"Compute the smoothed table":** add 1 to every cell, add |V| to every row total, divide, and check each row sums to 1.
- **"What is sparsity and how does smoothing help?":** unseen n-grams → zero counts → zero probability for whole sentences. Add-one gives every n-gram a pseudo-count, so nothing is zero. It takes mass from observed n-grams and spreads it over unobserved ones.
- **"Limitations?":** give the three points above: equal shares for all unseen words, rare contexts over-smoothed, too much mass moved when |V| is large.

# MLP forward pass (Section 6)

## The big picture
An MLP (multilayer perceptron) is layers of simple units. Each unit does the same two steps:

1. **Weighted sum:** multiply each input by a weight, add them up, and add a bias.
2. **Activation:** pass that number through a function g, such as a step function, ReLU or sigmoid.

That's it. A whole network is this repeated, with each layer's outputs becoming the next layer's inputs.

---

## The formulas, building up

### 1. One unit
  **h = g(w · x + b)**

- **x** = the inputs, e.g. (x₁, x₂)
- **w** = the weights on the edges coming into this unit, e.g. (w₁, w₂)
- **w · x** = the dot product: w₁x₁ + w₂x₂
- **b** = the bias (a constant added on)
- **g** = the activation function
- **h** = the unit's output (its "activation")

**Example:** inputs x = (1, −2), weights w = (2, −2), bias 0, step function.
- w · x = 2·1 + (−2)·(−2) = 2 + 4 = 6
- g(6) = 1, because 6 > 0

Without g, this is just linear regression. With g = sigmoid, it's exactly logistic regression.

### 2. A whole layer (several units at once)
  **h = g(Wx + b)**

When you have several units, you stack each unit's weight vector as **one row** of a matrix W. The matrix-vector product Wx then computes every unit's weighted sum at once:

```
        W            x          Wx
  ┌ 2   −2 ┐               ┌ 2·1 + (−2)(−2) ┐   ┌  6 ┐  ← H1
  │−1    1 │  ×  ┌ 1 ┐  =  │ −1·1 + 1·(−2)  │ = │ −3 │  ← H2
  └ 3    4 ┘     └−2 ┘     └ 3·1 + 4·(−2)   ┘   └ −5 ┘  ← H3
```

Then apply g to each entry: g(6, −3, −5) = **(1, 0, 0)**.

**Key rule: row i of W = the weights going *into* unit i.**
- Each **row** belongs to one output unit, so there are 3 rows for H1, H2, H3.
- Each **column** belongs to one input, so there are 2 columns for x₁, x₂.
- **Shape = (#outputs × #inputs)**. Here W₁ is **3 × 2**.

### 3. Two layers stacked
  **y = g(W₂ · g(W₁x + b₁) + b₂)**

Read it from the inside out:
1. **W₁x + b₁**: the hidden layer's weighted sums
2. **g(…)**: the hidden activations h = (H1, H2, H3)
3. **W₂h + b₂**: the output unit's weighted sum over the hidden units
4. **g(…)**: the final output y

The practice-exam diagram has no biases, so it's just **y = g(W₂ g(W₁x))**.

---

## Walking through the practice problem
From the diagram, the edge weights are:

| Edge | x₁ → | x₂ → |
|---|---|---|
| into H1 | 2 | −2 |
| into H2 | −1 | 1 |
| into H3 | 3 | 4 |

and the weights from H1, H2, H3 into y are −3, 2, 1.

**Step 1: hidden layer.** With x = (1, −2):
- H1 = g(1·2 + (−2)·(−2)) = g(6) = **1**
- H2 = g(1·(−1) + (−2)·1) = g(−3) = **0**
- H3 = g(1·3 + (−2)·4) = g(−5) = **0**

**Step 2: output layer.** It takes h = (1, 0, 0):
- y = g(1·(−3) + 0·2 + 0·1) = g(−3) = **0**

**Step 3: matrix form.**
```
W₁ = ┌ 2  −2 ┐      W₂ = [ −3  2  1 ]      x = ┌  1 ┐
     │−1   1 │           (1 × 3)                └ −2 ┘
     └ 3   4 ┘
     (3 × 2)

y = g( W₂ · g( W₁ · x ) )
```

**Dimension check:** W₁ (3×2) times x (2×1) gives a 3×1 vector. Then W₂ (1×3) times that 3×1 vector gives 1×1, a single number. ✓

---

## How to set up W from a diagram (where people lose points)
1. List the **destination** units of the layer (H1, H2, H3). Each one becomes a **row**.
2. List the **source** units (x₁, x₂). Each one becomes a **column**.
3. The weight on the edge x_j → H_i goes in **row i, column j**.

**Check:** the number of columns in W must equal the length of the vector you're multiplying.

## Why "the output layer is just multinomial logistic regression"
If the last layer uses softmax instead of a step function, the last layer is softmax(W₂h + b₂). That's exactly multinomial logistic regression, except its input is the learned hidden features h instead of the raw x. The hidden layers learn useful features; the last layer classifies them.

## Why g matters
Without g, two layers collapse into one: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x, which is just a single matrix. The nonlinearity is what lets an MLP learn things a single layer can't, like XOR.

## Common mistakes
- **Putting a unit's weights in a column instead of a row.** Rows are destinations, columns are sources.
- **The step function at exactly 0:** g(0) = 0, because the rule is a > 0.
- **Forgetting g on the output layer** when the question applies it there, or applying it when the output is meant to be linear.
- **Forgetting the bias** when the diagram includes one.

# The "Sam I am" exercise, step by step

## Step 0: The corpus
```
Sentence 1:  ε  I   am  Sam  EOS
Sentence 2:  ε  Sam I   am   EOS
Sentence 3:  ε  I   do  not  like  green  eggs  and  ham  EOS
```
- **ε** (empty string, also written BOS or SOS) marks the start of each sentence. It's what the first word is conditioned on.
- **EOS** marks the end.

---

## Part 1: Bigram probabilities

### The formula
  **P(next | prev) = count(prev followed by next) / count(prev)**

In words: out of all the times you saw the previous word, what fraction of the time came the next word?

**How to do it:**
1. Find every place the **conditioning word** (the one after the bar "|") appears.
2. Look at the word right after each one.
3. The fraction where it's the target word is the answer.

### P(I | ε): how often does a sentence start with "I"?
| Sentence | First word |
|---|---|
| 1 | **I** ✓ |
| 2 | Sam |
| 3 | **I** ✓ |

There are 3 sentence starts, and 2 of them are "I", so **2/3**.

### P(Sam | ε): how often does a sentence start with "Sam"?
Of the same 3 starts, only sentence 2 begins with "Sam", so **1/3**.

Check: 2/3 + 1/3 = 1. Every possible first word is accounted for. ✓

### P(am | I): after "I", how often comes "am"?
Find every "I" and look at the next word:

| Where | Next word |
|---|---|
| Sentence 1: **I** am | **am** ✓ |
| Sentence 2: Sam **I** am | **am** ✓ |
| Sentence 3: **I** do | do |

"I" appears 3 times and is followed by "am" twice, so **2/3**.

### P(do | I): after "I", how often comes "do"?
Same 3 occurrences of "I"; only one is followed by "do", so **1/3**.

Check: P(am | I) + P(do | I) = 2/3 + 1/3 = 1. ✓

### P(EOS | Sam): after "Sam", how often does the sentence end?
| Where | Next word |
|---|---|
| Sentence 1: am **Sam** EOS | **EOS** ✓ |
| Sentence 2: **Sam** I | I |

"Sam" appears 2 times and is followed by EOS once, so **1/2**.

### P(Sam | am): after "am", how often comes "Sam"?
| Where | Next word |
|---|---|
| Sentence 1: I **am** Sam | **Sam** ✓ |
| Sentence 2: I **am** EOS | EOS |

"am" appears 2 times and is followed by "Sam" once, so **1/2**.

---

## Part 2: Unigram probabilities

### The formula
  **P(word) = count(word) / total number of tokens**

A unigram ignores context entirely. It just asks how common the word is overall.

### Count the tokens
| Sentence | Tokens | Count |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | I, am, Sam, EOS | 4 |
| 2 | Sam, I, am, EOS | 4 |
| 3 | I, do, not, like, green, eggs, and, ham, EOS | 9 |
| **Total** | | **17** |

ε is **not** a token. It's only a start marker and is never predicted.

### Count each word
| Word | Where it appears | Count | P |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | s1, s2, s3 | 3 | **3/17** |
| Sam | s1, s2 | 2 | **2/17** |
| EOS | end of s1, s2, s3 | 3 | **3/17** |
| eggs | s3 | 1 | **1/17** |
| like | s3 | 1 | **1/17** |

### About "use 14 instead of 17"
Some instructors don't count EOS as a word. Then the total is 17 − 3 = 14 tokens, so P(I) = 3/14, and so on. Follow whatever convention your lecture used. The lecture slides counted EOS in sentence lengths, so 17 is the safer choice.

---

## The key difference
| | Bigram | Unigram |
|---|---|---|
| Question | "Given the previous word, how likely is this word?" | "How common is this word overall?" |
| Denominator | Count of the **previous** word | **Total** tokens |
| Example | P(am \| I) = 2/3 | P(am) = 2/17 |

## Common mistakes
1. **Using the wrong denominator for a bigram.** For P(am | I), divide by how many times "**I**" appears (3), not how many times "am" appears or the total token count.
2. **Forgetting ε.** P(I | ε) counts sentence *starts*: the denominator is the number of sentences (3).
3. **Forgetting EOS as a "next word."** "Sam" at the end of sentence 1 is followed by EOS, and that counts.
4. **Sanity check:** for any fixed conditioning word, the probabilities of all possible next words must sum to 1. After "I": am (2/3) + do (1/3) = 1 ✓.

# Softmax, explained

## What it does
Softmax turns any list of numbers (called **logits** or **scores**) into a **probability distribution**: every value lands between 0 and 1, and they all sum to 1.

  **softmax(z)ᵢ = e^(zᵢ) / Σⱼ e^(zⱼ)**

In words: exponentiate each number, then divide each one by the total.

## The example, step by step
Start with z = (2, 1, 0). These could be scores for three classes, such as noun, verb and adjective.

**Step 1: exponentiate each score.**
- e² = 7.39
- e¹ = 2.72
- e⁰ = 1

**Step 2: add them up.**
- 7.39 + 2.72 + 1 = 11.11

**Step 3: divide each by the sum.**
- 7.39 / 11.11 = **0.665**
- 2.72 / 11.11 = **0.245**
- 1 / 11.11 = **0.090**

**Check:** 0.665 + 0.245 + 0.090 = 1.00 ✓

So the model gives class 1 a 66.5% probability, class 2 24.5%, and class 3 9%.

## Why exponentiate?
1. **It makes everything positive.** Probabilities can't be negative, but logits can be. For example, e^(−3) = 0.05, which is still positive.
2. **It keeps the order.** A bigger score always gets a bigger probability.
3. **It exaggerates gaps.** A score difference of 1 becomes a probability ratio of e ≈ 2.7×. Here, 0.665 / 0.245 ≈ 2.7.

## Useful properties for the exam
- **Adding the same number to every score changes nothing.** (2, 1, 0) and (102, 101, 100) give the same softmax. Only the *differences* between scores matter, so subtract the largest score first to keep the numbers small.
- **Equal scores give a uniform distribution.** (5, 5, 5) → (1/3, 1/3, 1/3).
- **A score of −∞ gives probability 0.** This is how the **causal attention mask** works: future positions get score −∞, so their weight is 0.
- **Large score differences make it nearly one-hot.** (10, 0, 0) → about (0.9999, 0.00005, 0.00005). This is why attention divides by √dₖ: it keeps scores from getting so large that softmax saturates.
- **With 2 classes, softmax is the sigmoid.** softmax(z, 0)₁ = e^z/(e^z + 1) = σ(z).

## Where softmax appears in this course
| Place | What gets softmaxed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Multinomial logistic regression | Wx + b (one score per class) | Class probabilities |
| MLP output layer | W₂h + b₂ | Class probabilities |
| LM head | One score per vocabulary word | P(next word) |
| Attention | Scaled scores q·k/√dₖ | Attention weights |

## Exponentials worth memorizing, in case there's no calculator
| e⁰ | e^0.5 | e¹ | e² | e³ | e^(−1) | e^(ln 2) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.65 | 2.72 | 7.39 | 20.1 | 0.37 | 2 |

**Quick practice.** z = (1, 1, 0):
- e^z = (2.72, 2.72, 1), which sums to 6.44.
- softmax = **(0.42, 0.42, 0.16)**

Mostly no. Two short lines are enough, and you can work out the rest if you understand the terms.

**Why it's low priority:**
- The practice exam never asked about activation properties directly.
- The MLP question **gave you** the step-function definition. Expect the same on the real exam: if they want ReLU or sigmoid, they'll probably define it.
- The table was on a lecture slide (Session 5), so a T/F question is possible. For example: "ReLU suffers from severe vanishing gradients" (false), or "tanh is zero-centered" (true). Two lines on your sheet cover that.

**Compact version for your sheet:**
```
σ: (0,1), saturates both ends, severe vanishing grad | tanh: (−1,1), zero-centered, moderate
ReLU = max(0,a): [0,∞), fast, sparse, minimal vanishing (dead for a≤0) | step: 1 if a>0 else 0 (g(0)=0!)
```

**Understand the terms instead of memorizing the table:**
- **Range:** the possible outputs. Sigmoid squashes to (0, 1); tanh to (−1, 1); ReLU cuts off negatives.
- **Zero-centered:** outputs are balanced around 0. Only tanh is; the other three never go negative.
- **Saturates:** the curve goes flat, so its slope is about 0. Sigmoid and tanh flatten at both ends. ReLU is flat (slope 0) for every negative input.
- **Vanishing gradient:** backpropagation multiplies the slopes layer by layer. Sigmoid's largest slope is only 0.25, so the product shrinks quickly through many layers (severe). tanh's largest slope is 1 (moderate). ReLU's slope is exactly 1 for positive inputs, so the gradient doesn't shrink (minimal).
- **Sparse:** many outputs are exactly 0. ReLU outputs 0 for every negative input, so lots of units are "off."
- **Speed:** ReLU is just a comparison with 0, which is cheap. Sigmoid and tanh need exponentials.

If you understand saturation and vanishing gradients, you can rebuild every row of the table yourself. Use your cheat-sheet space for the n-gram, factorization and attention material instead.

**Yes for the multi-head dimensions. No for most of the rest.**

## Definitely include: multi-head dimensions
The practice exam tested exactly this (Q2.4: 8 heads, d = 1024 → W_V is 128 × 1024). A similar question with different numbers is very likely.

```
d_head = d/H     W_Q,W_K,W_V per head: (d/H) × d   [out × in]
concat heads → H·(d/H) = d     W_O: d × (H·d_v)  = d × d
ex: d=1024,H=8 → 128×1024    d=768,H=12 → 64×768
```

**Why the dimensions work out,** so you can rebuild it if you blank:
1. Each token's embedding x has size **d**. That's the **input** dimension, so it's the number of **columns**.
2. Each head makes its own smaller q, k, v vectors of size **d/H**. That's the **output** dimension, so it's the number of **rows**. This gives **(d/H) × d**.
3. Concatenating all H head outputs gives H × (d/H) = **d**, back to the original size.
4. W_O maps that size-d concatenation back to size d, so it's **d × d**.

**Trap:** if a question says there's "no W_O," the concatenation itself must equal d. That forces d_head = d/H.

## Include in a short form: the Transformer facts (one line each)
These are likely T/F or short-answer material. Write keywords, not sentences:
```
Block: MHSA → FFN (≈4d), each + residual + LayerNorm
Pos. embeddings REQUIRED (attention is order-invariant); learned or sinusoidal
Causal mask: future scores = −∞ → weight 0
Why Transformer > RNN: parallel training, long-range, no memory decay | cost O(n²) vs O(n)
Heads per layer NOT required to match
```

## Leave off
- **The sinusoidal formula.** You only need to know that fixed sinusoidal encodings exist; you won't be asked to compute one.
- **The model table.** You won't be asked GPT-3's layer count. At most, BERT-base/GPT-2 (768 = 12 × 64) is a handy check on d/H, and the formula above already covers it.
- **GQA and "Attention Is All You Need" (2017).** These are trivia, unlikely to be worth points.

**Yes. This is one of the most important blocks**, but write it compressed. Practice Q2.1 asked for exactly the Q/K/V intuition, and a hand calculation of attention is a natural exam question.

## Compact version (about 6 lines)
```
q=W_Q x, k=W_K x, v=W_V x     s_ij = k_j·q_i / √d_k     a_i = softmax(s_i)     out_i = Σ a_ij v_j
Matrix: softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k) V
Steps: dot q with each key (j≤i) → ÷√d_k → mask future = −∞ → softmax → weighted sum of v's
Q = what I'm looking for | K = what each token offers to match | V = content that gets mixed in
√d_k: big dims → big dots → softmax saturates (one-hot) → tiny gradients
Self = same sequence | Cross = other sequence (decoder→encoder; seq2seq: translation, summarization)
Ex: scores (0.5, 2) → e: 1.65, 7.39 → (.18, .82)
```

## What to drop
- **The full worked example.** The one-line version above is enough to remind you of the process.
- **The lecture's 4-score example.** It's redundant.

## Make sure you can do it without the sheet
The sheet gives you the formula, but you have to be fast at the steps:
1. **Dot product:** multiply matching entries and add. (1,0,1,0)·(2,0,2,0) = 2 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 4.
2. **Divide by √dₖ.** dₖ is the length of the q/k vectors, so for length 4, divide by 2.
3. **Softmax:** exponentiate, sum, divide. Use the e-values on your sheet: e^0.5 = 1.65, e¹ = 2.72, e² = 7.39.
4. **Weighted sum:** multiply each v by its weight and add the vectors entry by entry.

**Common mistakes:**
- Forgetting the √dₖ.
- Including future tokens when the question says "causal" or "masked."
- Mixing up the roles: the scores come from **q and k**; the output is built from **v**.

# The practice question with a unigram model instead

## What changes
A **unigram** model ignores context completely. Each word's probability is just how common it is overall:

  **P(w) = count(w) / total tokens**

and a sequence's probability is

  **P(w₁…wₙ) = P(w₁) · P(w₂) · … · P(wₙ) · P(EOS)**

Still multiply by P(EOS) at the end, so the probabilities over all strings sum to 1. **ε is not a token**; it's only a start marker and is never predicted.

---

## Step 1: Get each token's count from the matrix
Go back to the original **count** matrix from the practice exam, not the probability table:

| | a | b | c | EOS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ε | 2 | 0 | 3 | 1 |
| a | 1 | 3 | 0 | 2 |
| b | 0 | 10 | 10 | 0 |
| c | 3 | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| **column sum** | **6** | **14** | **15** | **4** |

**Use the column sums.** Every time a token appears, it's the "next word" after something, so the column total counts every occurrence of that token. Total tokens = 6 + 14 + 15 + 4 = **39**.

(Side note: this toy matrix isn't from a real corpus, so its row sums don't match its column sums. For example, b is a context 20 times but appears only 14 times. Don't let that confuse you; the columns are the right thing to count.)

## Step 2: Unigram probabilities
| Token | P |
|---|---|
| a | 6/39 ≈ 0.154 |
| b | 14/39 ≈ 0.359 |
| c | 15/39 ≈ 0.385 |
| EOS | 4/39 ≈ 0.103 |

## Step 3: The three sequences
**1. abccbc**

P = P(a) · P(b) · P(c) · P(c) · P(b) · P(c) · P(EOS)
  = (6 · 14 · 15 · 15 · 14 · 15 · 4) / 39⁷
  = 15,876,000 / 137,231,006,679 ≈ **1.16 × 10⁻⁴**

**2. ccbbaa**

P = P(c)² · P(b)² · P(a)² · P(EOS)
  = (15² · 14² · 6² · 4) / 39⁷
  = 6,350,400 / 39⁷ ≈ **4.63 × 10⁻⁵**

**3. bbccaa**

It's the same set of tokens as #2 (two each of a, b, c, plus EOS), just in a different order:
  = **4.63 × 10⁻⁵**, identical to #2.

---

## Comparison: bigram vs. unigram
| Sequence | Bigram | Unigram |
|---|---|---|
| abccbc | 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ | 1.16 × 10⁻⁴ |
| ccbbaa | **0** (b→a never seen) | 4.63 × 10⁻⁵ |
| bbccaa | **0** (never starts with b) | 4.63 × 10⁻⁵ |

**Takeaways:**
1. **Unigrams ignore order.** Any rearrangement of the same tokens gets the same probability, so #2 = #3. That's why unigrams are bad language models: "dog bites man" = "man bites dog" = "bites man dog."
2. **Unigrams rarely produce zeros.** A sequence gets probability 0 only if a word *never appears at all*. Bigrams get zeros whenever a *pair* was never seen, which happens far more often. That's the sparsity problem, and it gets worse as n grows.
3. **The trade-off:** larger n captures more context but has more sparsity. Smaller n has less sparsity but ignores context.

## Quick recipe
| Model | Probability of each word | Denominator |
|---|---|---|
| Unigram | count(w) / N | **Total tokens** (EOS included, ε not) |
| Bigram | count(prev, w) / count(prev) | **How often the previous word appears as a context** (its row sum) |
