content.text:
A filter card on a dashboard doesn't pop up by itself. You have to turn it on from one of the charts. Your **TR TransDate** filter is already on P16b's Filters shelf (the green pill), so you just need to show it.

**1. Show the filter card**
- On the **P16a dashboard**, click the top chart (P16b) so it gets the gray border.
- Click the small **▼ arrow** on that border → **Filters** → **TR TransDate**.

You can also do it on the P16b sheet: right-click the **TR TransDate** pill on Filters → **Show Filter**.

**2. Make it a range slider**
- Click the **▼** on the filter card → choose **Range of Dates**.
- If you don't see that option, the pill is set to discrete. Right-click **TR TransDate** on the Filters shelf → **Continuous**, then edit the filter and pick **Range of Dates**.

**3. Make it filter both charts**
- Click **▼** on the filter card → **Apply to Worksheets** → **Selected Worksheets…** → check **P16b** and **P16c** → OK.

**4. Place it and remove the title**
- Drag the card **across the bottom of the whole dashboard**. Drop it when the gray shaded area spans the full width under both charts.
- Click **▼** on the card → uncheck **Show Title**.

**Heads-up:** P16b still has a **YEAR(TR TransDate)** filter set to 2015. With it on, the slider will only cover 2015, not 1/1/2012–12/31/2015 like the video. If your slider looks stuck on 2015, remove that YEAR filter from P16b, and from P16c if it has one too.

39	1 Introduction
40	Tableau is a data visualization tool. You connect it to data, drag fields onto a canvas, and it draws
41	charts, maps, and dashboards without you writing formulas or code for the drawing itself. What
42	you do write, when the built in options run out, is a small amount of formula style logic that looks
43	a lot like an Excel IF statement.
44	You already have the two skills this module builds on. In Module 1 you used PivotTables to
45	summarize Excel data by dragging fields into rows, columns, and values, and Tableau’s canvas
46	works the same way, drag a field, watch the chart update. In Module 2 you used JOIN to combine
47	tables that share a key, and this module’s data connection does that same combining before you
48	ever open a worksheet, using the same inner and left join logic.
49	Business angle
50	Business intelligence tools like Tableau (Power BI is the other major one) exist because a
51	spreadsheet or a raw query result is not something you hand to a vice president. A VP wants
52	a chart of sales by region that updates itself every morning, or a dashboard she can click
53	through without asking you for a new report every time a filter changes. Tableau, Power BI,
54	and similar tools are what analysts use to turn a query result into something a non technical

210	5 Joining the tables
211	Transactions is the center of a star, every other table exists to describe one column of Transactions
212	in more detail. This is the exact same shape as the Northwind database in Module 2, one busy
213	transactional table (there, OrderDetails, here, Transactions) surrounded by smaller lookup tables
214	that each describe one dimension of it.
215	How the tables relate.Each transaction is either a sale, a purchase, or a return. Every transac-
216	tion hasexactly onesite, one employee (the manager), and one entity (the customer or supplier).
217	Going the other way, a site, an employee, or an entity can have zero or many transactions.
218	Materials and products work differently. A transaction haszero or onematerial andzero or one
219	product. A sale is linked to a product but not to a material. A purchase is linked to a material but
220	not to a product. So every row matches one of the two tables, never both, and the joins must allow
221	for that.
222	Join to Type Matching columns
223	Sites inner Transactions.TR SiteCode = Sites.Site SiteCode
224	Employee Master inner Transactions.TR Manager = Employee Master.Emp EmployeeID
225	Entity Master inner Transactions.TR EntityID = Entity Master.Ent EntityID
226	Material Master left outer Transactions.TR Item = Material Master.Mat Material
227	Product Master left outer Transactions.TR Item = Product Master.Prod Product

229	innerjoins because every transaction genuinely has a site, a manager, and a customer or supplier,
230	an inner join loses no rows here. Material Master and Product Master useleft outerjoins for the
231	opposite reason,TR Itemis a material code on a purchase row and a product code on a sales row,
232	never both, so an inner join to either table alone would silently drop half your data. A left join
233	keeps every transaction and simply leaves the non matching lookup columns blank.
234	The Data Source page is Module 2’sJOIN ... ONwith a mouse instead of a keyboard. It is the
235	same operation, not a similar one. When you drag a table on and pick the two matching columns,
236	Tableau writesJOIN Sites ON Transactions.TR SiteCode = Sites.Site SiteCodefor you and

238	same two you saw there.

389	7 Dimensions and measures
390	Tableau splits every field into one of two roles, shown as two groups in the Data pane.Dimensions
391	are fields that describe or categorize a row, a name, a code, a date, a category, things you group by.
392	Measuresare fields that hold a number you aggregate, sum, average, count, things you calculate
393	with. Older versions of Tableau print the words Dimensions and Measures as headers over the two
394	groups. Newer versions print nothing at all, just a light gray line, dimensions above it and measures
395	below.
396	Vocabulary
397	Dimension.Discrete data that either cannot be aggregated (summing every customer name
398	is meaningless) or has no practical meaning when aggregated (summing every zip code is
399	meaningless).
400	Measure.Numerical data that is meaningful when aggregated, for example the sum of
401	TR Quantityacross sales rows tells you total units sold.
402	The picture below shows why the role matters. It is the same field both times, and the two roles
403	produce two completely different charts.
404	TR Quantity
405	1
406	2
407	3
408	4
409	four rows of data
410	Used as a dimension
411	1 2 3 4
412	it slices,
413	four marks, one per value
414	Used as a measure
415	10
416	SUM
417	it aggregates,
418	one mark, one number
419	Tableau guesses a field’s role from its data type when you connect, and it guesses wrong more often
420	than you would expect. Any column of numbers, even an ID number likeTR EntityIDor a zip
421	code, is imported as a measure by default, because it is numeric, even though summing a customer
422	ID number is meaningless. You have to fix these by hand.
423	What the role changes.You can use a field either way, but the role sets Tableau’s default
424	behavior. DragTR Itemonto Rows while it is a measure and Tableau showsSUM(TR Item), which
425	adds up item codes. Convert it to a dimension, drag it onto Rows again, and Tableau now groups
426	by item and aggregates your other measures within each group. You can still override this for one
427	chart. Right click a dimension pill and choose Continuous or a function like Sum. It is simply easier
428	when every field starts in the right role.

718	EXCLUDEremoves a field from the view’s grouping.

1 Introduction
Tableau is a data visualization tool. You connect it to data, drag fields onto a canvas, and it draws
charts, maps, and dashboards without you writing formulas or code for the drawing itself. What
you do write, when the built in options run out, is a small amount of formula style logic that looks
a lot like an Excel IF statement.
You already have the two skills this module builds on. In Module 1 you used PivotTables to
summarize Excel data by dragging fields into rows, columns, and values, and Tableau’s canvas
works the same way, drag a field, watch the chart update. In Module 2 you used JOIN to combine
tables that share a key, and this module’s data connection does that same combining before you
ever open a worksheet, using the same inner and left join logic.
Business angle
Business intelligence tools like Tableau (Power BI is the other major one) exist because a
spreadsheet or a raw query result is not something you hand to a vice president. A VP wants
a chart of sales by region that updates itself every morning, or a dashboard she can click
through without asking you for a new report every time a filter changes. Tableau, Power BI,
and similar tools are what analysts use to turn a query result into something a non technical
audience can actually use, and fluency with one of them is a near universal requirement in
analyst job postings.
This module uses a different dataset than Modules 1 and 2. You will work with four years of
transactions, 2012 through 2015, from a hip implant manufacturer with five manufacturing and
distribution sites across the country. Every site buys raw materials from suppliers and sells finished
implants to hospitals and distributors, so the data supports two very different business questions,
procurement (what are we buying, from whom, and at what cost) and sales (what are we selling,
to whom, and how well).
2

=====PAGE=====
MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
2 Getting Tableau installed
Tableau Desktop is commercial software, normally licensed per user per year. UCSD has an aca-
demic partnership that gives you a free one year license for as long as you are a student, so set this
up once and it will be ready for every remaining class session.
T ry it now, installing T ableau
1. Create a new Tableau account with your school issued email. If you already have an
account under your UCSD email, sign into that account instead.
2. Once signed in, go to the Academic Quick Start page and clickDownload Tableau
Desktop. On the release page, sign in if asked, then pick the download for your computer
(Windows or Mac). Do not download Tableau Public or Tableau Prep. Those are different,
more limited products.
3. Install and open Tableau Desktop. When it asks you to register, enter your UCSD email,
UC San Diego as the organization, and Student as your job title.
4. To activate, go toHelp,Manage Product Keys, clickActivate, then chooseActivate
with a product keyand paste the product key.
Business angle
A perpetual Tableau Creator license runs a company on the order of a thousand dollars per
user per year at list price. That cost is one reason many companies standardize on a single
BI tool company wide rather than letting every team pick its own, and it is also why analysts
who arrive already fluent in whichever tool a company has standardized on have a real hiring
advantage.
3

=====PAGE=====
MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
3 The business scenario and the data
The data in this module comes from a fictional hip implant manufacturer with five sites, one each
in California, Florida, Illinois, New York, and Texas. Each site runs two sides of the business. On
the purchasing side, aProduction Managerbuys raw materials, titanium, stainless steel, cobalt
chrome, ceramic, two grades of polyethylene, silicone, and plaster, from outside suppliers. On the
sales side, aSales Managersells finished hip implants, built from those raw materials, to hospitals
and distributors. Every row in the transaction data is either a purchase or a sale, never both, which
is exactly the kind of detail a calculated field later in this module has to account for.
File Rows What it holds
Transactions.txt 258,602 One row per purchase or sale, site, manager, customer or sup-
plier, item, quantity, price, dates, dollar subtotal
Sites.txt 5 One row per site, a two letter code and the state name
Employee Master.txt 57 One row per manager, name, site, position (Sales Manager or
Production Manager), and order approval authority
Entity Master.txt 1,072 One row per customer or supplier, contact information, address,
and type (S for customer, O for supplier)
Material Master.txt 8 One row per raw material, category and description
Product Master.txt 6 One row per finished implant, category and description
This should feel familiar. Module 2 spent real time on the idea that a relational database keeps one
fact in one place rather than duplicating it, and this data is designed the same way.TR Subtotal
holds a dollar amount regardless of whether the row is a sale or a purchase, andTR TransType
(Sfor sale,Ofor purchase order) is what tells you which one you are looking at. You will build a
calculated field in Section 6 that readsTR TransTypeand routesTR Subtotalinto the right bucket.
T urn and talk
Materials and Products are two separate tables even though every product is built from
materials. Why not just add a MaterialUsed column directly onto the Product Master table?
What would go wrong if a hip implant used more than one raw material?
4

5 Joining the tables
Transactions is the center of a star, every other table exists to describe one column of Transactions
in more detail. This is the exact same shape as the Northwind database in Module 2, one busy
transactional table (there, OrderDetails, here, Transactions) surrounded by smaller lookup tables
that each describe one dimension of it.
How the tables relate.Each transaction is either a sale, a purchase, or a return. Every transac-
tion hasexactly onesite, one employee (the manager), and one entity (the customer or supplier).
Going the other way, a site, an employee, or an entity can have zero or many transactions.
Materials and products work differently. A transaction haszero or onematerial andzero or one
product. A sale is linked to a product but not to a material. A purchase is linked to a material but
not to a product. So every row matches one of the two tables, never both, and the joins must allow
for that.
Join to Type Matching columns
Sites inner Transactions.TR SiteCode = Sites.Site SiteCode
Employee Master inner Transactions.TR Manager = Employee Master.Emp EmployeeID
Entity Master inner Transactions.TR EntityID = Entity Master.Ent EntityID
Material Master left outer Transactions.TR Item = Material Master.Mat Material
Product Master left outer Transactions.TR Item = Product Master.Prod Product
Notice the pattern from Module 2 repeating itself. Sites, Employee Master, and Entity Master use
innerjoins because every transaction genuinely has a site, a manager, and a customer or supplier,
an inner join loses no rows here. Material Master and Product Master useleft outerjoins for the
opposite reason,TR Itemis a material code on a purchase row and a product code on a sales row,
never both, so an inner join to either table alone would silently drop half your data. A left join
keeps every transaction and simply leaves the non matching lookup columns blank.
The Data Source page is Module 2’sJOIN ... ONwith a mouse instead of a keyboard. It is the
same operation, not a similar one. When you drag a table on and pick the two matching columns,
Tableau writesJOIN Sites ON Transactions.TR SiteCode = Sites.Site SiteCodefor you and
runs it. Inner and left mean exactly what they meant in SQL, and the two pictures below are the
same two you saw there.

Why the product join must be Left
Two sale rows, both returns dated 10/19/2015, haveTR Item7053. That code is not in
Product Master, so their product columns stay null. An inner join to Product Master would
silently drop them. With every join set correctly, the result has11,268 purchase rowsand
247,334 sale rows, 258,602 in total.
T ry it now, see what goes wrong with an inner join
Change the Material Master join toInnerfor a moment and sort the preview by
TR TransType. Every row is now an O, and the record count on Sheet 1 drops from 258,602 to
11,268. All 247,334 sales are gone, because only purchases have a matching material. Change
it back toLeftbefore you continue.
Common mistake
The single most common mistake with this data is leaving Material Master and Product
Master as inner joins. Because a purchase’sTR Itemnever matches Product Master and a
sale’sTR Itemnever matches Material Master, two inner joins here do not just lose a few
rows, they can wipe out an entire transaction type if you are not careful about how Tableau
chains the joins together. If your record count drops by roughly the number of purchase or
sale rows, this is the first thing to check.
Business angle
This is what a supply chain analyst means by a single source of truth. Before this join exists,
procurement has one spreadsheet of purchases and sales has another, and the two never quite
agree on which supplier codes map to which raw materials. After the join, everyone in the
company who opens this workbook is working from the same five joined tables, which is most
of what a well built data warehouse is actually for.

6 Calculated fields
A calculated field is a new column you define with a formula, built from columns that already exist.
This is the helper column from Module 1, the one where you typed=IF(...)in the first cell of an
empty column and filled it down the sheet. Same idea, one difference. In Excel the formula lived
in every cell, so the column was as tall as the data. In Tableau you write it once and it applies
to all 258,602 rows, and it applies again on its own if the data grows. Once created, a calculated
field behaves exactly like any other field. You can drag it onto Rows, Columns, or Color, same as
TR Subtotalitself. The syntax is close to an Excel IF formula, written a little differently.
IF syntax
IF condition THEN result END
IF condition1 THEN result1 ELSEIF condition2 THEN result2 ELSE result3 END
Recall from Section 3 thatTR Subtotalholds a dollar amount for every transaction, and
TR TransTypetells you whether that row is a sale (S) or a purchase order (O). We need four
calculated fields that each isolate one slice of that single column.
Why bother?DragTR Subtotalonto Rows andTR SiteCodeonto Columns. California shows
a little over one billion dollars. That number is meaningless, because it adds sales, returns, and
purchases together. Now dragTR TransTypeinto the view as well. California splits into roughly
323 million in purchases and$688M in sales over the four years. You could add a filter every time
to keep only sales or only purchases, but that is easy to forget. Calculated fields solve this once.
The four fields and what they mean
Sales.Gross sales, before returns.
Returns.Negative sales, shown as a positive number.
Net sales.Sales after returns are taken out.
Purchases.The total of all purchase orders.
You could create similar fields for quantity, tax, or unit price too.

7 Dimensions and measures
Tableau splits every field into one of two roles, shown as two groups in the Data pane.Dimensions
are fields that describe or categorize a row, a name, a code, a date, a category, things you group by.
Measuresare fields that hold a number you aggregate, sum, average, count, things you calculate
with. Older versions of Tableau print the words Dimensions and Measures as headers over the two
groups. Newer versions print nothing at all, just a light gray line, dimensions above it and measures
below.
Vocabulary
Dimension.Discrete data that either cannot be aggregated (summing every customer name
is meaningless) or has no practical meaning when aggregated (summing every zip code is
meaningless).
Measure.Numerical data that is meaningful when aggregated, for example the sum of
TR Quantityacross sales rows tells you total units sold.
The picture below shows why the role matters. It is the same field both times, and the two roles
produce two completely different charts.

Tableau guesses a field’s role from its data type when you connect, and it guesses wrong more often
than you would expect. Any column of numbers, even an ID number likeTR EntityIDor a zip
code, is imported as a measure by default, because it is numeric, even though summing a customer
ID number is meaningless. You have to fix these by hand.
What the role changes.You can use a field either way, but the role sets Tableau’s default
behavior. DragTR Itemonto Rows while it is a measure and Tableau showsSUM(TR Item), which
adds up item codes. Convert it to a dimension, drag it onto Rows again, and Tableau now groups
by item and aggregates your other measures within each group. You can still override this for one
chart. Right click a dimension pill and choose Continuous or a function like Sum. It is simply easier
when every field starts in the right role.

Line, or drag one from theAnalyticspane. The dialog has four types at the top,Line,
Band,Distribution, andBox Plot.
Line
1. ChooseLineand set the value toAverage. An average line appears. You can also choose
Total, Sum, Minimum, Maximum, Median, or a constant.
2.Scope.Entire Table draws one line across all the data. Per Pane draws a separate line in
each pane. Per Cell draws one in each cell. This matters once you add another dimension
to Rows, such asTR SiteCode. Entire Table gives one average for all sites, while Per Pane
gives each site its own average.
3.Label.Choose None, Computation, Value (for example the actual average of Purchases),
or Custom, where you type your own text. You can also format the line and fill the area
above or below it.
Band
1. ChooseBand. Set a lower and an upper value, for example Minimum to Maximum, or
Average to Maximum, or constants.
2. Change the formatting to add lines at the edges of the band. If you checkShow recal-
culated band for highlighted or selected data points, the band changes when you
select points.
Distribution
1. ChooseDistribution. Instead of fixed values, the band comes from a calculation, such as
percentages, percentiles, quantiles, or standard deviation.
2. For example, set percentiles to 5 and 95 to shade the middle 90 percent of the data.
Quantiles splits the data into equal groups.
3. ChooseStandard Deviationand set the factor to 2. The band now runs from two
standard deviations below the average to two above. As before, choose Entire Table or
Per Pane.
23

=====PAGE=====
MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
Business angle, control charts
A two standard deviation band turns your chart into acontrol chart. If a business process,
such as generating sales, normally varies around an average, points outside the band may
signal something abnormal. One catch, data with an upward trend will naturally drift above
the band later on, without anything being wrong. Two fixes help. Use a Percent Difference
quick table calculation to remove the slope, or addTR TransDateby year to Rows so each
year gets its own average and band, Per Pane.
T utorial 10, level of detail expressions (LOD)
Build the chart first.
1. Open a new sheet. DragTR SiteCode,Emp LastName, andTR UnitPriceonto Rows. Set
the unit price toAverage.
2. DragTR TransDateonto Columns and choose the lowerMonthoption (month with year).
3. DragTR TransTypeonto Filters and keep onlyO. You now see each employee’s average
monthly unit price paid for purchases, grouped by site.
Where reference lines stop.Add a reference line, Average, Per Pane. Each employee gets
their own average, for example 4.225 for one and 4.724 for another. Switch it to Entire Table
and every employee shows the same company average, about 3.347. But what if you want
each employee compared with theirsite’saverage? A reference line cannot do that. You need
an LOD expression.
What an LOD expression does.It aggregates the data by fields you choose, even fields
that are not in the view. You create one as a calculated field, written inside curly brackets.
There are three types.
24

=====PAGE=====
MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
The three LOD types
EXCLUDEremoves a field from the view’s grouping.
{EXCLUDE [Emp LastName] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])}
The view groups by site, employee, and month. This keeps site and month but drops employee,
so it gives thesiteaverage for each month.
INCLUDEadds a field to the view’s grouping.
{INCLUDE [TR Item] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])}
This averages each employee’s unit price for each item, and the view then averages those
averages.
FIXEDsets its own grouping, independent of the view.
{FIXED [TR SiteCode], [TR TransType] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])}
This gives one average per site and transaction type, no matter what else is in the view.
Separate the grouping from the aggregate with acolon, not a semicolon.
T ry it now, add each LOD to the chart
1.EXCLUDE.Right click in the Data pane, choose Create Calculated Field, and enter the
EXCLUDE expression above. Drag it onto Rows. If Tableau shows it as an attribute
(ATTR), right click it, chooseMeasure, thenAverage. Right click its axis, chooseDual
Axis, set it to Line,Synchronize Axis, and hide the right header. Within each site,
every employee now shows the same line, the site’s average for each month. In California
it moves between about 3.22 and 3.78. Florida has its own line, between 3.16 and 3.89.
2.INCLUDE.Duplicate the sheet. Replace the EXCLUDE field with the INCLUDE ex-
pression above and repeat the dual axis steps. For example, in June 2014 Baro (CA)
bought three items, with average unit prices of 2.40, 6.08, and 1.77. The INCLUDE line
shows 3.42, the average of those three. His actual average unit price that month is 3.57,
because it averages every transaction. The two would only match if he bought each item
the same number of times.
3.FIXED.Duplicate the sheet again and use the FIXED expression above. The lines are
now flat over time, and differ slightly by site, for example 3.518 for California and 3.500
for Illinois.
4.Why include TR TransType in FIXED?FIXED ignores what is in the view. Without
TR TransType, it would average sales and purchases together. Including it keeps them
separate, and the filter then keeps only the purchase groups.
5.Make FIXED vary by month.Create a calculated field namedTransaction Date
MonthwithMONTH([TR TransDate]), and add it to the FIXED grouping. The site
averages now change from month to month.
25

=====PAGE=====
MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
Common mistake, averages of averages
An LOD returns its results first, and the view may then aggregate them further. If the LOD
groups at a finer level than the view, as with INCLUDE or a FIXED that names more fields
than the view, the view takes an average of averages. That is usually not the same as the
plain average of all transactions.
T utorial 11, ranking and filtering T op N within categories
Goal, show the top two employees by purchases within each site.
1. Open a new sheet. DragTR SiteCodeandEmp LastNameonto Rows andPurchasesonto
Columns. Filter out null purchases.
2. Sort the employees by purchases, largest first, so the top employees in each site are easy
to see.
3. DragPurchasesonto Columns asecondtime, so you keep the original bars. Right click
the second pill, chooseQuick Table Calculation, thenRank.
4. Check the ranks. By default Tableau ranks across the entire table, so only one employee
in the whole company is number 1. That is not what you want.
5. Right click the rank pill, chooseEdit Table Calculation, and set Compute Using to
Pane (down), so the ranking restarts within each site. Now each site reads 1, 2, 3, 4,
and so on.
6. Drag the rank pill ontoFilters(hold Ctrl, or Option on a Mac, to copy it instead of
moving it) and keep only ranks 1 to 2. Click Apply. You now see the top two employees
in each site.
Tableau’s own guides show another way to do this, using the INDEX() function. It works well
but is less intuitive.
26

=====PAGE=====
MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
9 Building your first chart
Every Tableau worksheet has the same handful of parts, and once you can name them the rest
of this module is just combinations of them. Dragging a field onto any shelf changes the chart
immediately, there is no separate step to run or refresh. Here is the whole window.
Dimensions
fields you group by
(names, codes, dates)
Measures
numbers you aggregate
(sum, average, count)
Data pane
a thin gray line is
all that separates
the two groups
Columns shelfwhat goes across, the x axis
Rows shelfwhat goes up and down, the y axis
Marks card
chart type
Color, Size, Label,
Detail, Tooltip
how each
mark is drawn
Canvas
the chart itself, redrawn on every drag
TheData paneon the left lists every field, dimensions above the line and measures below it. The
ColumnsandRowsshelves decide what sits on each axis. TheMarks cardcontrols how each
data point is drawn, and its five buttons matter later in this module, Color and Size encode a
measure visually, Label prints the value on the mark, Detail splits the marks finer without adding
a row or column, and Tooltip is what appears on hover.
T ry it now, your first bar chart
1. Open a new worksheet.
2. DragMat MaterialDescriptiononto Columns.
3. DragPurchasesonto Rows.
Check your result, a bar chart, one bar per raw material, height equal to total purchases of
that material across all four years. Tableau automatically aggregates a measure with SUM
when you drop it onto a shelf, this is the same automatic aggregation you saw with GROUP
BY in Module 2, except here it happens the instant you drag the field, with no GROUP BY
clause to write.
A few formatting moves come up in nearly every problem in this module. Right click an axis and
choose Format to control decimals, currency symbols, or a fixed start and end point for the scale.
Right click a field on a shelf and choose Rotate Label to change its orientation. The Marks card’s
Label button turns on or off the little text values drawn directly on each bar or point.
27

=====PAGE=====
MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
Quick table calculations
Right click a measure already on a shelf, choose Quick Table Calculation, and pick from
options including Percent of Total, Running Total, Difference, and Rank. A quick table
calculation does not change the underlying data, it recomputes the value already on the shelf
relative to the other values in the view, for example turning a dollar amount into that value’s
share of the total across everything currently shown.
Common mistake
A Percent of Total quick table calculation defaults to computing across the entire table, which
is not always what you want. Right click the pill again, go to Compute Using, and choose
which dimension the percentages should add up to 100 percent within, for example Table
(across everything) versus a specific field (within each group separately). Getting this setting
wrong is the most common reason a percentage chart’s bars do not add up the way you expect.
28

=====PAGE=====
MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
10 Dates and axes
Dates get special treatment in Tableau, and half the confusion in Problems 6 through 10 comes
from not knowing which of two things a date pill is doing. DragTR TransDateonto Columns and
Tableau gives youYEAR(TR TransDate)with a little plus sign on it. Click the plus and it drills
down, year to quarter to month to day.
Two ways to put a date on a shelf
Date part.Quarter on its own, so every Q1 from every year piles into one position. Four
positions total across four years of data. Tableau writes this asQUARTER([TR TransDate]).
Truncated date.Quarter and year together, so 2012 Q1 and 2015 Q1 stay separate. Sixteen
positions across four years. Tableau writes this asDATETRUNC(’quarter’, [TR TransDate]),
and the right click menu on a date pill lists both options, the truncated versions grouped lower
down and showing a full date like May 2012.
Adiscrete(blue) date pill makes headers and separate panes. Acontinuous(green) date
pill makes a real axis you can add a trend line to.
Common mistake
Problems 6 through 10 all want quarter and year together, sixteen positions, not four. If your
x axis shows only Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, you picked the date part instead of the truncated date,
and every chart built on top of it will average four different years into one point.
Two axis settings matter. Right click an axis, choose Edit Axis, and you canfixthe range, which is
what every problem below means by “start the scale at 14K”. Tableau otherwise fits the range to the
data and re-scales the chart every time a filter changes. The same menu holdsSynchronize Axis
for a dual axis chart, which puts both measures on one shared scale. Leave two axes independent and
two measures of very different size look identical in height, the fastest way to publish a misleading
chart by accident.
29

39	1 Introduction
40	Tableau is a data visualization tool. You connect it to data, drag fields onto a canvas, and it draws
41	charts, maps, and dashboards without you writing formulas or code for the drawing itself. What
42	you do write, when the built in options run out, is a small amount of formula style logic that looks
43	a lot like an Excel IF statement.
44	You already have the two skills this module builds on. In Module 1 you used PivotTables to
45	summarize Excel data by dragging fields into rows, columns, and values, and Tableau’s canvas
46	works the same way, drag a field, watch the chart update. In Module 2 you used JOIN to combine
47	tables that share a key, and this module’s data connection does that same combining before you
48	ever open a worksheet, using the same inner and left join logic.
49	Business angle
50	Business intelligence tools like Tableau (Power BI is the other major one) exist because a
51	spreadsheet or a raw query result is not something you hand to a vice president. A VP wants
52	a chart of sales by region that updates itself every morning, or a dashboard she can click
53	through without asking you for a new report every time a filter changes. Tableau, Power BI,
54	and similar tools are what analysts use to turn a query result into something a non technical
55	audience can actually use, and fluency with one of them is a near universal requirement in
56	analyst job postings.
57	This module uses a different dataset than Modules 1 and 2. You will work with four years of

210	5 Joining the tables
211	Transactions is the center of a star, every other table exists to describe one column of Transactions
212	in more detail. This is the exact same shape as the Northwind database in Module 2, one busy
213	transactional table (there, OrderDetails, here, Transactions) surrounded by smaller lookup tables
214	that each describe one dimension of it.
215	How the tables relate.Each transaction is either a sale, a purchase, or a return. Every transac-
216	tion hasexactly onesite, one employee (the manager), and one entity (the customer or supplier).
217	Going the other way, a site, an employee, or an entity can have zero or many transactions.
218	Materials and products work differently. A transaction haszero or onematerial andzero or one
219	product. A sale is linked to a product but not to a material. A purchase is linked to a material but
220	not to a product. So every row matches one of the two tables, never both, and the joins must allow
221	for that.
222	Join to Type Matching columns
223	Sites inner Transactions.TR SiteCode = Sites.Site SiteCode
224	Employee Master inner Transactions.TR Manager = Employee Master.Emp EmployeeID

227	Product Master left outer Transactions.TR Item = Product Master.Prod Product

229	innerjoins because every transaction genuinely has a site, a manager, and a customer or supplier,

232	never both, so an inner join to either table alone would silently drop half your data. A left join

389	7 Dimensions and measures
390	Tableau splits every field into one of two roles, shown as two groups in the Data pane.Dimensions
391	are fields that describe or categorize a row, a name, a code, a date, a category, things you group by.
392	Measuresare fields that hold a number you aggregate, sum, average, count, things you calculate
393	with. Older versions of Tableau print the words Dimensions and Measures as headers over the two
394	groups. Newer versions print nothing at all, just a light gray line, dimensions above it and measures
395	below.
396	Vocabulary
397	Dimension.Discrete data that either cannot be aggregated (summing every customer name
398	is meaningless) or has no practical meaning when aggregated (summing every zip code is
399	meaningless).
400	Measure.Numerical data that is meaningful when aggregated, for example the sum of
401	TR Quantityacross sales rows tells you total units sold.
402	The picture below shows why the role matters. It is the same field both times, and the two roles
403	produce two completely different charts.
404	TR Quantity
405	1
406	2
407	3
408	4
409	four rows of data
410	Used as a dimension
411	1 2 3 4
412	it slices,
413	four marks, one per value
414	Used as a measure
415	10
416	SUM
417	it aggregates,
418	one mark, one number
419	Tableau guesses a field’s role from its data type when you connect, and it guesses wrong more often
420	than you would expect. Any column of numbers, even an ID number likeTR EntityIDor a zip
421	code, is imported as a measure by default, because it is numeric, even though summing a customer
422	ID number is meaningless. You have to fix these by hand.
423	What the role changes.You can use a field either way, but the role sets Tableau’s default
424	behavior. DragTR Itemonto Rows while it is a measure and Tableau showsSUM(TR Item), which
425	adds up item codes. Convert it to a dimension, drag it onto Rows again, and Tableau now groups
426	by item and aggregates your other measures within each group. You can still override this for one
427	chart. Right click a dimension pill and choose Continuous or a function like Sum. It is simply easier
428	when every field starts in the right role.

532	to the far right to read one of the lines. Right click the right axis and chooseSynchronize
533	Axis. Only leave them unsynchronized if seeing the lines close together truly matters.
534	5.Remove the extra axis.Once synchronized, the right axis repeats the left one. Right
535	click it and uncheckShow Header. Then right click the left axis, chooseEdit Axis, and
536	delete its title, since it now covers both measures.
537	6.Label the lines.DragMeasure NamesontoLabelin the All tab. Each line now shows
538	its name, Purchases or Sales. To label only one line, drag Measure Names onto Label in
539	that measure’s tab instead. Drag a label to move it if the two overlap. Now you can hide
540	the color legend, since the labels do its job.
541	7.Tidy the x axis.The title MONTH of TR TransDate looks clumsy. Rename it, for
542	example Month of transaction, or remove it. Right click the axis, chooseEdit Axis, and
543	on the Tick Marks tab set fixed tick marks, for example one per quarter.
544	8.Soften the gridlines.Right click the chart, chooseFormat, open theLinessection,
545	and set Grid Lines to None. The Format pane has many other options worth exploring.
546	18
547	
548	=====PAGE=====
549	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
550	T utorial 7b, independent axis ranges
551	1. Open a new sheet. DragTR TransDateonto Columns and set it to the lowerMonth
552	option. DragPurchasesonto Rows.
553	2. DragTR Manager(employee ID) onto Rows. An employee name would be more readable,
554	but the ID keeps this simple. Filter out the null values. You now have one panel per
555	employee, showing purchases over time.
556	3. Notice every panel uses the same y axis range, up to about 7 million, since the largest
557	month for one employee is about 6.8 million. That is useful forcomparing employees.
558	You can quickly see that one employee buys far less than another.
559	4. But it makes it hard to seehow one employee changes over time, because a small
560	buyer’s line looks flat. Right click the y axis, chooseEdit Axis, and selectIndependent
561	axis ranges for each row or column. Each employee now gets an axis that fits their
562	own data.
563	Rule of thumb, use the same axis range when comparing rows or columns against each other.
564	Use independent ranges when the focus is on change within one row or column.
565	19
566	
567	=====PAGE=====
568	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
569	T utorial 8a, quick table calculations
570	1. Open a new sheet. DragPurchasesonto Rows andTR SiteCodeonto Rows as well, so
571	each site gets its own row.
572	2. DragMat MaterialDescriptiononto Columns so you see purchases of each raw material.
573	Filter out the null values.
574	3. DragTR TransDateonto Rows, next to the site. You now see, for California, then Florida,
575	and so on, the sum of purchases of each material in each year.
576	4. Right click the Purchases pill and chooseQuick Table Calculation. The main options
577	are below.
578	5. ChoosePercent of Total. Each row now adds up to 100 percent. For example, the
579	California 2013 row shows each material’s share of California’s 2013 purchases. Think of
580	it as a pie chart drawn as bars.
581	Option What it shows
582	Running Total each value added to all the values before it
583	Difference the dollar change from one value to another
584	Percent Difference the same change, as a percentage
585	Percent of Total each value as a share of the total
586	Rank, Percentile where each value stands among the others
587	YTD Total date based total, which need a date in the view
588	Moving Average the average of a value and its neighbors
589	For Difference and Percent Difference you can choose what each value is compared with, for
590	example the previous value or the first value.
591	20
592	
593	=====PAGE=====
594	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
595	T utorial 8b, quick table calculations, compute using
596	Compute Usingdecides which values add up to 100 percent. Keep working in the Tutorial
597	8a chart. Right click the Purchases pill, chooseCompute Using, and try each option. The
598	exact choices change a little with the type of table calculation.
599	Option What adds up to 100 percent
600	Table (across) each full row
601	Table (down) each full column, for example all the Ceramic values from
602	top to bottom
603	Table (across then down) every cell in the whole table together, so each value be-
604	comes very small
605	Pane (down) each column, within one pane only
606	Cell each cell on its own, so every value is 100 percent
607	Choosing specific dimensions.Compute Using also lists the dimensions in your view.
608	Tick the ones the calculation should runacross. Everything you leave unticked is held fixed,
609	and gets its own 100 percent.
610	•Tick onlyyear. For each site and each material, the years add up to 100 percent.
611	•Tickyearandsite. For each material, all sites and years together add up to 100 percent,
612	which works like Table (down).
613	•Tick onlysite. For each material in each year, the sites add up to 100 percent.
614	•Tick onlymaterial. For each site in each year, the materials add up to 100 percent.
615	Check your setting with the calculation assistance.Right click the pill and choose
616	Edit Table Calculation. In the window that opens, checkShow calculation assistance.
617	Tableau numbers the cells. Cells numbered in the same sequence are added together into one
618	100 percent. Change the options and watch the numbering change before you trust the result.
619	21
620	
621	=====PAGE=====
622	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
623	T utorial 9a, trend lines and forecasting
624	Trend lines
625	1. Open a new sheet. DragTR TransDateonto Columns and set it to the lowerMonth
626	option. DragPurchasesonto Rows. You see monthly total purchases, around 30 million
627	a month in 2012.
628	2. Right click the chart and chooseTrend Lines, thenShow Trend Lines. You can also
629	use theAnalysismenu, or dragTrend Linefrom theAnalyticspane (the tab next to
630	Data) onto the chart.
631	3. The trend line is a simple regression, with month as the independent variable and purchases
632	as the dependent variable. Hover over the line to see the regression equation, theR
633	squared, which tells you how much of the variation in purchases the line explains, and
634	the p value. For the full output, right click the line and chooseDescribe Trend Model.
635	4. Right click the line and chooseEdit Trend Lines. Linear (a straight line) is the default.
636	You can switch to Logarithmic, Exponential, Power, or Polynomial of different degrees,
637	and show confidence bands. When the chart has one line per color, uncheckAllow a
638	trend line per colorto get one overall trend line instead of one per line.
639	5. Remove the trend line before you move on.
640	Forecasts
641	1. Right click the chart and chooseForecast, thenShow Forecast. You can also use
642	Analysis,Forecast. The line continues past your data in a different shade, with shaded
643	confidence bounds around it.
644	2. Right click again and openForecast,Forecast Resultsto choose what is shown, for
645	example Actual and Forecast, or the trend only.
646	3. ChooseAnalysis,Forecast,Forecast Options. Here you set how far ahead to forecast
647	(Automatic, Exactly a number of periods, or Until a date), the forecast model, and the
648	prediction interval (90, 95, or 99 percent).
649	4. The model can beAutomatic,Automatic without seasonality, orCustom. Custom
650	lets you choose whether the trend and the seasonality are additive or multiplicative. Au-
651	tomatic usually works well, because Tableau compares several models and picks the best
652	one.
653	Tableau forecasts with exponential smoothing, which weights recent observations more heavily
654	than older ones when it predicts the future.
655	22

658	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
659	T utorial 9b, reference lines, bands, and distributions
660	Keep working in the Tutorial 9a chart. Right click the y axis and chooseAdd Reference
661	Line, or drag one from theAnalyticspane. The dialog has four types at the top,Line,
662	Band,Distribution, andBox Plot.
663	Line
664	1. ChooseLineand set the value toAverage. An average line appears. You can also choose
665	Total, Sum, Minimum, Maximum, Median, or a constant.
666	2.Scope.Entire Table draws one line across all the data. Per Pane draws a separate line in
667	each pane. Per Cell draws one in each cell. This matters once you add another dimension
668	to Rows, such asTR SiteCode. Entire Table gives one average for all sites, while Per Pane
669	gives each site its own average.
670	3.Label.Choose None, Computation, Value (for example the actual average of Purchases),
671	or Custom, where you type your own text. You can also format the line and fill the area
672	above or below it.
673	Band
674	1. ChooseBand. Set a lower and an upper value, for example Minimum to Maximum, or
675	Average to Maximum, or constants.
676	2. Change the formatting to add lines at the edges of the band. If you checkShow recal-
677	culated band for highlighted or selected data points, the band changes when you
678	select points.
679	Distribution
680	1. ChooseDistribution. Instead of fixed values, the band comes from a calculation, such as
681	percentages, percentiles, quantiles, or standard deviation.
682	2. For example, set percentiles to 5 and 95 to shade the middle 90 percent of the data.
683	Quantiles splits the data into equal groups.
684	3. ChooseStandard Deviationand set the factor to 2. The band now runs from two
685	standard deviations below the average to two above. As before, choose Entire Table or
686	Per Pane.
687	23
688	
689	=====PAGE=====
690	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
691	Business angle, control charts
692	A two standard deviation band turns your chart into acontrol chart. If a business process,
693	such as generating sales, normally varies around an average, points outside the band may
694	signal something abnormal. One catch, data with an upward trend will naturally drift above
695	the band later on, without anything being wrong. Two fixes help. Use a Percent Difference
696	quick table calculation to remove the slope, or addTR TransDateby year to Rows so each
697	year gets its own average and band, Per Pane.
698	T utorial 10, level of detail expressions (LOD)
699	Build the chart first.
700	1. Open a new sheet. DragTR SiteCode,Emp LastName, andTR UnitPriceonto Rows. Set
701	the unit price toAverage.
702	2. DragTR TransDateonto Columns and choose the lowerMonthoption (month with year).
703	3. DragTR TransTypeonto Filters and keep onlyO. You now see each employee’s average
704	monthly unit price paid for purchases, grouped by site.
705	Where reference lines stop.Add a reference line, Average, Per Pane. Each employee gets
706	their own average, for example 4.225 for one and 4.724 for another. Switch it to Entire Table
707	and every employee shows the same company average, about 3.347. But what if you want
708	each employee compared with theirsite’saverage? A reference line cannot do that. You need
709	an LOD expression.
710	What an LOD expression does.It aggregates the data by fields you choose, even fields
711	that are not in the view. You create one as a calculated field, written inside curly brackets.
712	There are three types.
713	24
714	
715	=====PAGE=====
716	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
717	The three LOD types
718	EXCLUDEremoves a field from the view’s grouping.
719	{EXCLUDE [Emp LastName] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])}
720	The view groups by site, employee, and month. This keeps site and month but drops employee,
721	so it gives thesiteaverage for each month.
722	INCLUDEadds a field to the view’s grouping.
723	{INCLUDE [TR Item] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])}
724	This averages each employee’s unit price for each item, and the view then averages those
725	averages.
726	FIXEDsets its own grouping, independent of the view.
727	{FIXED [TR SiteCode], [TR TransType] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])}
728	This gives one average per site and transaction type, no matter what else is in the view.
729	Separate the grouping from the aggregate with acolon, not a semicolon.
730	T ry it now, add each LOD to the chart
731	1.EXCLUDE.Right click in the Data pane, choose Create Calculated Field, and enter the
732	EXCLUDE expression above. Drag it onto Rows. If Tableau shows it as an attribute
733	(ATTR), right click it, chooseMeasure, thenAverage. Right click its axis, chooseDual
734	Axis, set it to Line,Synchronize Axis, and hide the right header. Within each site,
735	every employee now shows the same line, the site’s average for each month. In California
736	it moves between about 3.22 and 3.78. Florida has its own line, between 3.16 and 3.89.
737	2.INCLUDE.Duplicate the sheet. Replace the EXCLUDE field with the INCLUDE ex-
738	pression above and repeat the dual axis steps. For example, in June 2014 Baro (CA)
739	bought three items, with average unit prices of 2.40, 6.08, and 1.77. The INCLUDE line
740	shows 3.42, the average of those three. His actual average unit price that month is 3.57,
741	because it averages every transaction. The two would only match if he bought each item
742	the same number of times.
743	3.FIXED.Duplicate the sheet again and use the FIXED expression above. The lines are
744	now flat over time, and differ slightly by site, for example 3.518 for California and 3.500
745	for Illinois.
746	4.Why include TR TransType in FIXED?FIXED ignores what is in the view. Without
747	TR TransType, it would average sales and purchases together. Including it keeps them
748	separate, and the filter then keeps only the purchase groups.
749	5.Make FIXED vary by month.Create a calculated field namedTransaction Date
750	MonthwithMONTH([TR TransDate]), and add it to the FIXED grouping. The site
751	averages now change from month to month.
752	25
753	
754	=====PAGE=====
755	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
756	Common mistake, averages of averages
757	An LOD returns its results first, and the view may then aggregate them further. If the LOD
758	groups at a finer level than the view, as with INCLUDE or a FIXED that names more fields
759	than the view, the view takes an average of averages. That is usually not the same as the
760	plain average of all transactions.
761	T utorial 11, ranking and filtering T op N within categories
762	Goal, show the top two employees by purchases within each site.
763	1. Open a new sheet. DragTR SiteCodeandEmp LastNameonto Rows andPurchasesonto
764	Columns. Filter out null purchases.
765	2. Sort the employees by purchases, largest first, so the top employees in each site are easy
766	to see.
767	3. DragPurchasesonto Columns asecondtime, so you keep the original bars. Right click
768	the second pill, chooseQuick Table Calculation, thenRank.
769	4. Check the ranks. By default Tableau ranks across the entire table, so only one employee
770	in the whole company is number 1. That is not what you want.
771	5. Right click the rank pill, chooseEdit Table Calculation, and set Compute Using to
772	Pane (down), so the ranking restarts within each site. Now each site reads 1, 2, 3, 4,
773	and so on.
774	6. Drag the rank pill ontoFilters(hold Ctrl, or Option on a Mac, to copy it instead of
775	moving it) and keep only ranks 1 to 2. Click Apply. You now see the top two employees
776	in each site.
777	Tableau’s own guides show another way to do this, using the INDEX() function. It works well
778	but is less intuitive.
779	26
780	
781	=====PAGE=====
782	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
783	9 Building your first chart
784	Every Tableau worksheet has the same handful of parts, and once you can name them the rest
785	of this module is just combinations of them. Dragging a field onto any shelf changes the chart
786	immediately, there is no separate step to run or refresh. Here is the whole window.
787	Dimensions
788	fields you group by
789	(names, codes, dates)
790	Measures
791	numbers you aggregate
792	(sum, average, count)
793	Data pane
794	a thin gray line is
795	all that separates
796	the two groups
797	Columns shelfwhat goes across, the x axis
798	Rows shelfwhat goes up and down, the y axis
799	Marks card
800	chart type
801	Color, Size, Label,
802	Detail, Tooltip
803	how each
804	mark is drawn
805	Canvas
806	the chart itself, redrawn on every drag
807	TheData paneon the left lists every field, dimensions above the line and measures below it. The
808	ColumnsandRowsshelves decide what sits on each axis. TheMarks cardcontrols how each
809	data point is drawn, and its five buttons matter later in this module, Color and Size encode a
810	measure visually, Label prints the value on the mark, Detail splits the marks finer without adding
811	a row or column, and Tooltip is what appears on hover.
812	T ry it now, your first bar chart
813	1. Open a new worksheet.
814	2. DragMat MaterialDescriptiononto Columns.
815	3. DragPurchasesonto Rows.
816	Check your result, a bar chart, one bar per raw material, height equal to total purchases of
817	that material across all four years. Tableau automatically aggregates a measure with SUM
818	when you drop it onto a shelf, this is the same automatic aggregation you saw with GROUP
819	BY in Module 2, except here it happens the instant you drag the field, with no GROUP BY
820	clause to write.
821	A few formatting moves come up in nearly every problem in this module. Right click an axis and
822	choose Format to control decimals, currency symbols, or a fixed start and end point for the scale.
823	Right click a field on a shelf and choose Rotate Label to change its orientation. The Marks card’s
824	Label button turns on or off the little text values drawn directly on each bar or point.
825	27
826	
827	=====PAGE=====
828	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
829	Quick table calculations
830	Right click a measure already on a shelf, choose Quick Table Calculation, and pick from
831	options including Percent of Total, Running Total, Difference, and Rank. A quick table
832	calculation does not change the underlying data, it recomputes the value already on the shelf
833	relative to the other values in the view, for example turning a dollar amount into that value’s
834	share of the total across everything currently shown.
835	Common mistake
836	A Percent of Total quick table calculation defaults to computing across the entire table, which
837	is not always what you want. Right click the pill again, go to Compute Using, and choose
838	which dimension the percentages should add up to 100 percent within, for example Table
839	(across everything) versus a specific field (within each group separately). Getting this setting
840	wrong is the most common reason a percentage chart’s bars do not add up the way you expect.
841	28
842	
843	=====PAGE=====
844	MGT 153, Module 3 Tableau tutorials 1 to 11
845	10 Dates and axes
846	Dates get special treatment in Tableau, and half the confusion in Problems 6 through 10 comes
847	from not knowing which of two things a date pill is doing. DragTR TransDateonto Columns and
848	Tableau gives youYEAR(TR TransDate)with a little plus sign on it. Click the plus and it drills
849	down, year to quarter to month to day.
850	Two ways to put a date on a shelf
851	Date part.Quarter on its own, so every Q1 from every year piles into one position. Four
852	positions total across four years of data. Tableau writes this asQUARTER([TR TransDate]).
853	Truncated date.Quarter and year together, so 2012 Q1 and 2015 Q1 stay separate. Sixteen
854	positions across four years. Tableau writes this asDATETRUNC(’quarter’, [TR TransDate]),
855	and the right click menu on a date pill lists both options, the truncated versions grouped lower
856	down and showing a full date like May 2012.
857	Adiscrete(blue) date pill makes headers and separate panes. Acontinuous(green) date
858	pill makes a real axis you can add a trend line to.
859	Common mistake
860	Problems 6 through 10 all want quarter and year together, sixteen positions, not four. If your
861	x axis shows only Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, you picked the date part instead of the truncated date,
862	and every chart built on top of it will average four different years into one point.
863	Two axis settings matter. Right click an axis, choose Edit Axis, and you canfixthe range, which is
864	what every problem below means by “start the scale at 14K”. Tableau otherwise fits the range to the
865	data and re-scales the chart every time a filter changes. The same menu holdsSynchronize Axis
866	for a dual axis chart, which puts both measures on one shared scale. Leave two axes independent and
867	two measures of very different size look identical in height, the fastest way to publish a misleading
868	chart by accident.
869	29

MGT 153 · Module 3 Tableau: Skills Test Cheat Sheet

Built from the Tutorials 1–11 PDF, the Problems 1–16 PDF, and the actual data in "Tableau Workbook with Data Loaded" (all numbers below were computed from that data and match the solution screenshots). Dataset: fictional hip-implant maker, 5 sites (CA, FL, IL, NY, TX), 2012–2015.

1. The data in 60 seconds

Tables (star schema, Transactions in the center)
FileRowsHolds
Transactions.txt258,6021 row per purchase or sale
Sites.txt5site code + state name
Employee Master57managers: name, site, position
Entity Master1,072customers (S) / suppliers (O)
Material Master8raw materials
Product Master6finished hip implants
Joins
TableTypeOn
SitesInnerTR SiteCode = Site SiteCode
Employee MasterInnerTR Manager = Emp EmployeeID
Entity MasterInnerTR EntityID = Ent EntityID
Material MasterLeftTR Item = Mat Material
Product MasterLeftTR Item = Prod Product
Why Left: a purchase's TR Item is a material, a sale's is a product, never both. Inner on Material → only 11,268 rows (all sales lost).
TR TransType: S = sale (to customer), O = purchase order (from supplier). Return = sale row with negative TR Subtotal.
Rows: 247,334 sale + 11,268 purchase = 258,602. Return rows: 2,680.
Two sale rows (returns, 10/19/2015) have TR Item 7053, not in Product Master → need Left join.
Check figures (validation)
Records 258,602 · TR TransDate min 1/1/2012, max 12/31/2015 · TR CompleteDate min 1/3/2012, max 1/20/2016
SUM TR Quantity 1,168,069,907.55 · TR UnitPrice 2,047,028.33 · TR Subtotal 5,058,319,249.64 · TR Tax 354,113,001.27
Dates look wrong? File → Workbook Locale → English (US).
Products (6): Metal-on-Metal Hip (Titanium / Cobalt chrome / Stainless steel), Metal and Plastic Hip, Metal and Crosslinked Polyethylene Hip, Ceramic-on-Ceramic Hip.
Materials (8): Ceramic, Cobalt chrome, Plaster, Polyethylene (highly crosslinked), Polyethylene (standard grade), Silicone, Stainless steel, Titanium.
Sheet / Dashboard / Story. Sheet = one analysis. Dashboard = several sheets on one screen. Story = sheets/dashboards in sequence. Tabs at the bottom create each.

2. Calculated fields (Data pane ▾ → Create Calculated Field)

Sales      IF [TR TransType] = "S" AND [TR Subtotal] > 0 THEN [TR Subtotal] END
Returns    IF [TR Subtotal] < 0 THEN -[TR Subtotal] END
Net sales  IF [TR TransType] = "S" THEN [TR Subtotal] END
Purchases  IF [TR TransType] = "O" THEN [TR Subtotal] END
  • Sales = gross (positive sales only). Returns = negatives flipped positive (ABS also works). Net sales = sales minus returns (keeps negatives). Purchases = purchase orders.
  • No ELSE needed; other rows become null.
  • Text in "quotes"; numbers/years not quoted (= 2012, not "2012"). O is the letter O.
IF cond THEN result END
IF c1 THEN r1 ELSEIF c2 THEN r2 ELSE r3 END
Purchases in 2012  IF YEAR([TR TransDate]) = 2012 THEN [Purchases] END
Purchases in 2015  IF YEAR([TR TransDate]) = 2015 THEN [Purchases] END
Price per Item     [TR Subtotal]/[TR Quantity]        (use as AVG)
Sales per Customer SUM([TR Subtotal])/COUNTD([Ent EntityID])

Why: SUM(TR Subtotal) by site mixes sales, returns and purchases (CA ≈ $1B, meaningless). CA alone ≈ $323M purchases + $688M sales.

3. Core concepts

Dimension vs. Measure
Dimension = group by (names, codes, dates), above the gray line. Measure = aggregate (SUM/AVG/COUNT), below the line. Dimensions → GROUP BY, measures → SUM/AVG, like SQL/PivotTable.
Convert ID numbers to dimensions: TR TransNumber, TR Manager, TR EntityID, TR Item, Emp EmployeeID, Ent EntityID, Ent Zip, Mat Material, Prod Product. Keep as measures: TR Quantity, TR UnitPrice, TR Subtotal, TR Tax + 4 calc fields. Hide unused: Emp Order Approval Authority, Ent RelationshipManager.
Test: "Would I ever sum or average this?"
Discrete (blue) vs. Continuous (green)
Blue = headers / separate panes. Green = a real axis (needed for trend lines). Right-click pill → Discrete/Continuous.
Dates: date part vs. truncated
Date part (upper menu options): QUARTER([TR TransDate]) → all Q1s combined, only 4 positions.
Truncated (lower options, show year, e.g. "Q1 2014", "May 2014"): DATETRUNC('quarter',[TR TransDate]) → 16 quarters / 48 months.
Problems 6–10 need truncated quarter (16 points). If the axis shows only Q1–Q4 you picked the wrong one.
Click + on YEAR pill to drill down: year → quarter → month → day.
Marks card: mark type dropdown (Automatic/Bar/Line/Circle/Shape/Map…), Color, Size, Label (prints values), Detail (splits marks finer without new rows/columns), Tooltip (hover text). Show Me (top right) suggests chart types; hover a grayed one to see what it needs.
Filters: drag a field to Filters. Filters remove rows before calculated fields and table calcs (except FIXED LOD, which ignores dimension filters). Exclude nulls: right-click the null mark/header → Exclude, or uncheck Null in the filter. Show a filter on the view: right-click pill → Show Filter.
Axis edits (right-click axis → Edit Axis): rename title; Fixed range ("start at 14K" = Fixed start 14,000); Tick Marks tab (fixed increments, e.g. 1M); Independent axis ranges for each row or column. Same range to compare panes; independent to see change within a pane.

4. How-to recipes (the moves the test checks)

Dual axis
  1. Put 2 measures on Rows.
  2. Right-click the second pill/axis → Dual Axis.
  3. Right-click right axis → Synchronize Axis.
  4. Right-click right axis → uncheck Show Header (hides it).
  5. Set each measure's mark type on its own Marks tab (or the All tab).
  6. If Measure Names lands on Color automatically and you don't want it, drag it off.
  7. Move circles to the front: right-click the axis/pill → Move marks to front, or reorder the pills on Rows.
Quick table calc: Percent of Total
Right-click measure pill → Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total. Then right-click → Compute Using (or Edit Table Calculation → Specific Dimensions).
OptionWhat adds to 100%
Table (across)each full row
Table (down)each full column
Table (across then down)whole table
Pane (down)each column within one pane
Celleach cell alone (all 100%)
Specific dimensionsticked = calculated across; unticked = held fixed, each gets its own 100%
Per-site material shares (P2): tick only Mat MaterialDescription so each site's 8 materials = 100%.
Verify: Edit Table Calculation → Show calculation assistance.
Other quick calcs: Running Total, Difference, Percent Difference, Rank, Percentile, YTD Total, Moving Average.
Trend line: right-click view → Trend Lines → Show (or Analytics pane → drag Trend Line). Linear default; also Log, Exponential, Power, Polynomial. Needs continuous axis. One line for all colors: Edit Trend Lines → uncheck "Allow a trend line per color". Remove from one series: Edit Trend Lines → uncheck that measure. Hover = equation, R², p-value; Describe Trend Model for details.
Forecast: right-click → Forecast → Show Forecast (or Analysis → Forecast). Uses exponential smoothing (recent data weighted more). Options: length (Automatic / Exactly N / Until), model (Automatic, Automatic without seasonality, Custom: additive/multiplicative trend and season), prediction interval 90/95/99%.
Reference line / band / distribution / box plot: right-click y-axis → Add Reference Line (or Analytics pane). Scope: Entire Table (one line), Per Pane, Per Cell. Value: Average, Median, Sum, Total, Min, Max, Constant. Label: None / Computation / Value / Custom. Band = between two values. Distribution = percentiles/quantiles/std dev (±2 SD = control chart).
Annotations: right-click a mark → Annotate → Mark (or Point/Area). Type text. Remove the box border / arrow: right-click annotation → Format → Border None, Line (arrow) None.
Labels: Marks Label button → "Show mark labels". Only Min & Max: Label → Marks to Label → Min/Max. Vertical labels: Label → Alignment → Direction (rotated). Format numbers: right-click pill → Format → Pane → Numbers → Percentage, 1 decimal.
Axis/field label tweaks: Rotate header text: right-click header → Rotate Label. Hide "Mat MaterialDescription" title: right-click field label → Hide Field Labels for Columns/Rows. Gridlines off: Format → Lines → Grid Lines None. Borders on bars: Color → Border. One blue palette: Color → Edit Colors → Blue.
Top N within each group (Tutorial 11 / P15)
  1. Rows: TR SiteCode, Emp LastName. Columns: SUM(Sales). Sort descending.
  2. Drag Sales to Columns again → Quick Table Calc → Rank.
  3. Edit Table Calc → Compute Using Pane (down) → rank restarts per site.
  4. Ctrl/Option-drag the rank pill to Filters → keep 1 to N.
  5. Remove the rank pill from Columns.
Alternative: INDEX().

5. LOD expressions (Level of Detail)

{ FIXED   [dim1],[dim2] : AGG([measure]) }   own grouping, ignores view
{ INCLUDE [dim]         : AGG([measure]) }   view grouping + dim (finer)
{ EXCLUDE [dim]         : AGG([measure]) }   view grouping − dim (coarser)
{ FIXED : AVG([Sales]) }                      no dims = one grand number
  • Use a colon, not a semicolon. Curly braces.
  • FIXED ignores dimension filters (e.g. NY site filter) and dims in view. INCLUDE/EXCLUDE respect filters.
  • If it shows as ATTR, right-click → Measure → Average.
  • FIXED/INCLUDE finer than view → view takes an average of averages ≠ plain average.

Tutorial 10 examples (view: site, employee, month; filter TransType = O; AVG unit price):

{EXCLUDE [Emp LastName] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])}            site avg per month
{INCLUDE [TR Item] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])}                avg of per-item avgs
{FIXED [TR SiteCode],[TR TransType] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])} flat per site

Ref line Entire Table ≈ 3.347 company avg. EXCLUDE: CA 3.22–3.78, FL 3.16–3.89. INCLUDE: Baro June 2014 → 3.42 (actual 3.57). FIXED: CA 3.518, IL 3.500. TransType in FIXED keeps sales and purchases from mixing. Add MONTH([TR TransDate]) to FIXED to vary by month.

Ref line vs. LOD: ref lines can do per-pane or entire-table averages, but not "each employee vs. their site's average". That needs an LOD.

8. Fast troubleshooting / traps

Percentages don't add to 100% per site → wrong Compute Using. Tick only the dimension you want to run across (material).
Only Q1–Q4 on x-axis → you used date part; switch to truncated quarter (with year).
Record count ≠ 258,602 after joins → an inner join should be left (Material/Product), or the wrong column was matched.
Calc says invalid → check quotes on text, no quotes on numbers, END at the end, brackets match field names, LOD uses colon.
One trend line per employee → uncheck "Allow a trend line per color".
Dual-axis lines on different scales → Synchronize Axis. Extra Measure Names color legend → drag it off Color.
"Company-wide" line changes with the site filter → you didn't use FIXED (or grouped by employee). FIXED ignores dimension filters.
Scatter shows 1 point → turn off Analysis → Aggregate Measures (P11) or add Detail (P12).
Null bar/state shows up → exclude Null (right-click → Exclude) or filter it out.

MGT 153 · Module 3 Tableau: Skills Test Cheat Sheet

Built from the Tutorials 1–11 PDF, the Problems 1–16 PDF, and the actual data in "Tableau Workbook with Data Loaded" (all numbers below were computed from that data and match the solution screenshots). Dataset: fictional hip-implant maker, 5 sites (CA, FL, IL, NY, TX), 2012–2015.

1. The data in 60 seconds

Tables (star schema, Transactions in the center)
FileRowsHolds
Transactions.txt258,6021 row per purchase or sale
Sites.txt5site code + state name
Employee Master57managers: name, site, position
Entity Master1,072customers (S) / suppliers (O)
Material Master8raw materials
Product Master6finished hip implants
Joins
TableTypeOn
SitesInnerTR SiteCode = Site SiteCode
Employee MasterInnerTR Manager = Emp EmployeeID
Entity MasterInnerTR EntityID = Ent EntityID
Material MasterLeftTR Item = Mat Material
Product MasterLeftTR Item = Prod Product
Why Left: a purchase's TR Item is a material, a sale's is a product, never both. Inner on Material → only 11,268 rows (all sales lost).
TR TransType: S = sale (to customer), O = purchase order (from supplier). Return = sale row with negative TR Subtotal.
Rows: 247,334 sale + 11,268 purchase = 258,602. Return rows: 2,680.
Two sale rows (returns, 10/19/2015) have TR Item 7053, not in Product Master → need Left join.
Check figures (validation)
Records 258,602 · TR TransDate min 1/1/2012, max 12/31/2015 · TR CompleteDate min 1/3/2012, max 1/20/2016
SUM TR Quantity 1,168,069,907.55 · TR UnitPrice 2,047,028.33 · TR Subtotal 5,058,319,249.64 · TR Tax 354,113,001.27
Dates look wrong? File → Workbook Locale → English (US).
Products (6): Metal-on-Metal Hip (Titanium / Cobalt chrome / Stainless steel), Metal and Plastic Hip, Metal and Crosslinked Polyethylene Hip, Ceramic-on-Ceramic Hip.
Materials (8): Ceramic, Cobalt chrome, Plaster, Polyethylene (highly crosslinked), Polyethylene (standard grade), Silicone, Stainless steel, Titanium.
Sheet / Dashboard / Story. Sheet = one analysis. Dashboard = several sheets on one screen. Story = sheets/dashboards in sequence. Tabs at the bottom create each.

2. Calculated fields (Data pane ▾ → Create Calculated Field)

Sales      IF [TR TransType] = "S" AND [TR Subtotal] > 0 THEN [TR Subtotal] END
Returns    IF [TR Subtotal] < 0 THEN -[TR Subtotal] END
Net sales  IF [TR TransType] = "S" THEN [TR Subtotal] END
Purchases  IF [TR TransType] = "O" THEN [TR Subtotal] END
  • Sales = gross (positive sales only). Returns = negatives flipped positive (ABS also works). Net sales = sales minus returns (keeps negatives). Purchases = purchase orders.
  • No ELSE needed; other rows become null.
  • Text in "quotes"; numbers/years not quoted (= 2012, not "2012"). O is the letter O.
IF cond THEN result END
IF c1 THEN r1 ELSEIF c2 THEN r2 ELSE r3 END
Purchases in 2012  IF YEAR([TR TransDate]) = 2012 THEN [Purchases] END
Purchases in 2015  IF YEAR([TR TransDate]) = 2015 THEN [Purchases] END
Price per Item     [TR Subtotal]/[TR Quantity]        (use as AVG)
Sales per Customer SUM([TR Subtotal])/COUNTD([Ent EntityID])

Why: SUM(TR Subtotal) by site mixes sales, returns and purchases (CA ≈ $1B, meaningless). CA alone ≈ $323M purchases + $688M sales.

3. Core concepts

Dimension vs. Measure
Dimension = group by (names, codes, dates), above the gray line. Measure = aggregate (SUM/AVG/COUNT), below the line. Dimensions → GROUP BY, measures → SUM/AVG, like SQL/PivotTable.
Convert ID numbers to dimensions: TR TransNumber, TR Manager, TR EntityID, TR Item, Emp EmployeeID, Ent EntityID, Ent Zip, Mat Material, Prod Product. Keep as measures: TR Quantity, TR UnitPrice, TR Subtotal, TR Tax + 4 calc fields. Hide unused: Emp Order Approval Authority, Ent RelationshipManager.
Test: "Would I ever sum or average this?"
Discrete (blue) vs. Continuous (green)
Blue = headers / separate panes. Green = a real axis (needed for trend lines). Right-click pill → Discrete/Continuous.
Dates: date part vs. truncated
Date part (upper menu options): QUARTER([TR TransDate]) → all Q1s combined, only 4 positions.
Truncated (lower options, show year, e.g. "Q1 2014", "May 2014"): DATETRUNC('quarter',[TR TransDate]) → 16 quarters / 48 months.
Problems 6–10 need truncated quarter (16 points). If the axis shows only Q1–Q4 you picked the wrong one.
Click + on YEAR pill to drill down: year → quarter → month → day.
Marks card: mark type dropdown (Automatic/Bar/Line/Circle/Shape/Map…), Color, Size, Label (prints values), Detail (splits marks finer without new rows/columns), Tooltip (hover text). Show Me (top right) suggests chart types; hover a grayed one to see what it needs.
Filters: drag a field to Filters. Filters remove rows before calculated fields and table calcs (except FIXED LOD, which ignores dimension filters). Exclude nulls: right-click the null mark/header → Exclude, or uncheck Null in the filter. Show a filter on the view: right-click pill → Show Filter.
Axis edits (right-click axis → Edit Axis): rename title; Fixed range ("start at 14K" = Fixed start 14,000); Tick Marks tab (fixed increments, e.g. 1M); Independent axis ranges for each row or column. Same range to compare panes; independent to see change within a pane.

4. How-to recipes (the moves the test checks)

Dual axis
  1. Put 2 measures on Rows.
  2. Right-click the second pill/axis → Dual Axis.
  3. Right-click right axis → Synchronize Axis.
  4. Right-click right axis → uncheck Show Header (hides it).
  5. Set each measure's mark type on its own Marks tab (or the All tab).
  6. If Measure Names lands on Color automatically and you don't want it, drag it off.
  7. Move circles to the front: right-click the axis/pill → Move marks to front, or reorder the pills on Rows.
Quick table calc: Percent of Total
Right-click measure pill → Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total. Then right-click → Compute Using (or Edit Table Calculation → Specific Dimensions).
OptionWhat adds to 100%
Table (across)each full row
Table (down)each full column
Table (across then down)whole table
Pane (down)each column within one pane
Celleach cell alone (all 100%)
Specific dimensionsticked = calculated across; unticked = held fixed, each gets its own 100%
Per-site material shares (P2): tick only Mat MaterialDescription so each site's 8 materials = 100%.
Verify: Edit Table Calculation → Show calculation assistance.
Other quick calcs: Running Total, Difference, Percent Difference, Rank, Percentile, YTD Total, Moving Average.
Trend line: right-click view → Trend Lines → Show (or Analytics pane → drag Trend Line). Linear default; also Log, Exponential, Power, Polynomial. Needs continuous axis. One line for all colors: Edit Trend Lines → uncheck "Allow a trend line per color". Remove from one series: Edit Trend Lines → uncheck that measure. Hover = equation, R², p-value; Describe Trend Model for details.
Forecast: right-click → Forecast → Show Forecast (or Analysis → Forecast). Uses exponential smoothing (recent data weighted more). Options: length (Automatic / Exactly N / Until), model (Automatic, Automatic without seasonality, Custom: additive/multiplicative trend and season), prediction interval 90/95/99%.
Reference line / band / distribution / box plot: right-click y-axis → Add Reference Line (or Analytics pane). Scope: Entire Table (one line), Per Pane, Per Cell. Value: Average, Median, Sum, Total, Min, Max, Constant. Label: None / Computation / Value / Custom. Band = between two values. Distribution = percentiles/quantiles/std dev (±2 SD = control chart).
Annotations: right-click a mark → Annotate → Mark (or Point/Area). Type text. Remove the box border / arrow: right-click annotation → Format → Border None, Line (arrow) None.
Labels: Marks Label button → "Show mark labels". Only Min & Max: Label → Marks to Label → Min/Max. Vertical labels: Label → Alignment → Direction (rotated). Format numbers: right-click pill → Format → Pane → Numbers → Percentage, 1 decimal.
Axis/field label tweaks: Rotate header text: right-click header → Rotate Label. Hide "Mat MaterialDescription" title: right-click field label → Hide Field Labels for Columns/Rows. Gridlines off: Format → Lines → Grid Lines None. Borders on bars: Color → Border. One blue palette: Color → Edit Colors → Blue.
Top N within each group (Tutorial 11 / P15)
  1. Rows: TR SiteCode, Emp LastName. Columns: SUM(Sales). Sort descending.
  2. Drag Sales to Columns again → Quick Table Calc → Rank.
  3. Edit Table Calc → Compute Using Pane (down) → rank restarts per site.
  4. Ctrl/Option-drag the rank pill to Filters → keep 1 to N.
  5. Remove the rank pill from Columns.
Alternative: INDEX().

5. LOD expressions (Level of Detail)

{ FIXED   [dim1],[dim2] : AGG([measure]) }   own grouping, ignores view
{ INCLUDE [dim]         : AGG([measure]) }   view grouping + dim (finer)
{ EXCLUDE [dim]         : AGG([measure]) }   view grouping − dim (coarser)
{ FIXED : AVG([Sales]) }                      no dims = one grand number
  • Use a colon, not a semicolon. Curly braces.
  • FIXED ignores dimension filters (e.g. NY site filter) and dims in view. INCLUDE/EXCLUDE respect filters.
  • If it shows as ATTR, right-click → Measure → Average.
  • FIXED/INCLUDE finer than view → view takes an average of averages ≠ plain average.

Tutorial 10 examples (view: site, employee, month; filter TransType = O; AVG unit price):

{EXCLUDE [Emp LastName] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])}            site avg per month
{INCLUDE [TR Item] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])}                avg of per-item avgs
{FIXED [TR SiteCode],[TR TransType] : AVG([TR UnitPrice])} flat per site

Ref line Entire Table ≈ 3.347 company avg. EXCLUDE: CA 3.22–3.78, FL 3.16–3.89. INCLUDE: Baro June 2014 → 3.42 (actual 3.57). FIXED: CA 3.518, IL 3.500. TransType in FIXED keeps sales and purchases from mixing. Add MONTH([TR TransDate]) to FIXED to vary by month.

Ref line vs. LOD: ref lines can do per-pane or entire-table averages, but not "each employee vs. their site's average". That needs an LOD.

Record count ≠ 258,602 after joins → an inner join should be left (Material/Product), or the wrong column was matched.
